UPPSC 2025

  • 42nd Amendment 1976 added three words: Socialist, Secular, Integrity. ×8 →
  • Executive is taken from, responsible to and controlled by the legislature. ×2 →
  • Chairman Fazal Ali; members K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru. →
  • Core aim: social and economic democracy. →
  • Speakers: 11th P.A. Sangma; 12th G.M.C. Balayogi; 14th Somnath Chatterjee; 17th and 18th Om Birla. →
  • That resolution needs 2/3 of members present and voting, not of total membership. →
  • Vice-President is not a member of Rajya Sabha; so it is presided by a non-member. ×3 →
  • Article 108: President summons joint sitting to end deadlock on a Bill; not Article 109. ×2 →
  • Three financial committees: Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings. →
  • PAC presents its report to Lok Sabha (Parliament); to Speaker when House not in session. ×3 →
  • PIL widened locus standi (right to file); it helps weaker sections but is not essential for rule of law. →
  • National Integration Council formed in 1962, not 1961. →
  • Order: EVM (1982, Parur, Kerala) → voter photo identity card EPIC (1993) → VVPAT (4 September 2013, Noksen, Nagaland) → NOTA (Supreme Court order, 27 September 2013). →
  • Not in Eighth Schedule: Bhojpuri, English, Angika. →
  • Article 243E: Panchayat term 5 years from date of its first meeting. ×2 →
  • Article 243T(3): 1/3 of directly elected municipal seats for women; minimum age 21 (Article 243V). →
  • National Voters' Day 25 January; Constitution Day 26 November; Human Rights Day 10 December. →
  • BHARATPOL portal (7 January 2025): built by CBI for international police cooperation. →
  • Rules of Procedure Committee · Dr. Rajendra Prasad →
  • IX-A · Municipalities · 243-P–243-ZG ×2 →
  • Seventh · Division of powers: Union, State, Concurrent Lists ×4 →

  • Concurrent: adulteration of foodstuffs and goods (Entry 18); trade and commerce is not counted as Concurrent. →

  • Freedom to own, acquire and sell property, 19(1)(f), was removed by 44th Amendment 1978. →
  • Right against Exploitation = Article 23 (trafficking, forced labour) and Article 24 (child labour). →

  • Article 155: Governor appointed by the President by warrant; it is not about removal. ×3 →
  • Article 352: President proclaims emergency, even on imminent danger, for whole or part of India. →
  • Selection Committee: PM (chair), Lok Sabha Speaker, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, CJI or nominee judge, one eminent jurist. →
  • Lokpal chairperson from 10 March 2024: Justice Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar. →
  • Article 350B (7th Amendment, 1956): one Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities for all India, appointed by President. →
  • UPSC functions come from Constitution, Parliament's laws, executive rules and conventions. →
  • EC does not elect Speaker, Deputy Speaker or Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman; the Houses elect them. →

UPPSC 2023

  • 1919 Act → Chamber of Princes, 120 members (proclamation 23 December 1919); advisory; Viceroy presided. →

  • Fundamental Rights can be amended but not removed; "right to die" is not a Fundamental Right. →

  • Article 20 has three protections; torture ban is not one of them (it is under Article 21). →

    Chapter 1

    The Constitutional Development of India

    British laws from 1773 to 1947 that slowly shaped how India is governed.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 1935 Act: dyarchy at Centre (never implemented); dyarchy in provinces abolished.PCS Pre ’08; PCS Mains ’13; RI ’143 papers
    2. 1935 Act proposed All India Federation ("Federation of India") of provinces and princely states; never came into being.PCS Mains ’12; UDA/LDA ’102 papers
    3. Federal Court set up 1 October 1937 under 1935 Act; first Chief Justice Sir Maurice Gwyer.PCS Pre ’14; PCS Mains ’152 papers
    4. Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (set up 1774): Chief Justice + 3 judges.PCS Mains ’101 paper
    5. First Chief Justice of Calcutta Supreme Court: Sir Elijah Impey (not Lemaister).RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’161 paper

    Company rule Acts 1773–1853

    • Regulating Act 1773: Governor of Bengal (Warren Hastings) became Governor General of Bengal; Madras, Bombay put under Bengal.
    • Governor General got 4-member executive council; decisions by majority; he had only casting vote (tie-breaker).
    • Regulating Act 1773 → Supreme Court at Fort William, Calcutta (set up 1774): Chief Justice + 3 judges.UPPSC
    • First Chief Justice of Calcutta Supreme Court: Sir Elijah Impey (not Lemaister).UPPSC
    • 1773 Act banned Company servants from private trade, gifts and bribes.
    • Pitt's India Act 1784: split commercial and political work; Board of Control (6 members) for political, Court of Directors for commercial.UPPSC
    • Act of 1786: Governor General could overrule council; also became Commander-in-Chief; Cornwallis first to use this.
    • Charter Act 1793: Company's trade monopoly extended 20 years.
    • Charter Act 1813: ended Company's trade monopoly except tea and China trade.UPPSC
    • 1813 Act: Rs 1 lakh a year for Indians' education; missionaries allowed; Crown's sovereignty over Company lands asserted.
    • 1813 Act: local governments could tax people and punish non-payers.
    • General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) handled the Rs 1 lakh grant.
    • Orientalists: H.T. Prinsep, H.H. Wilson; Anglicists led by Charles Trevelyan.
    • 7 March 1835: Macaulay's proposal accepted under Bentinck (1828–35); English = medium of higher education.
    • Charter Act 1833: Governor General of Bengal → Governor General of India; first = Lord William Bentinck.
    • 1833 Act: Company ended as trading body, became purely administrative.
    • 1833 Act: law member (4th member) added to council, only for law-making; first = Macaulay.
    • 1833 Act Section 87: no Indian barred from Company posts for religion, birthplace, descent or colour → first share in administration.UPPSC
    • Charter Act 1853: first split council's legislative and executive work; separate central legislative council.
    • 1853 Act: open competition for civil servants.
    • Merit civil service introduced 1854 on Macaulay Report; Civil Service Commission in London, exams from 1855.

    Crown rule Acts 1858–1909

    • Government of India Act 1858: Crown took over from Company; Governor General also called Viceroy; first Viceroy = Lord Canning.
    • 1858 Act ended Board of Control and Court of Directors; created Secretary of State for India with 15-member advisory council.
    • Indian revenue came under British Parliament's direct control by 1858 Act (not 1813).
    • Indian Councils Act 1861: Indians first joined law-making; Madras, Bombay got back law-making power (decentralization begins).
    • 1861 Act: Viceroy could issue ordinances in emergency, valid up to 6 months.
    • 1861 Act: portfolio system; 5 council members held Revenue, Finance, Law, Home, Military; 6th (Public Works) added 1874.
    • 1861 Act: 6–12 additional members for law-making, nominated for 2 years, half non-official; no Central–Provincial subject split.
    • Indian Councils Act 1892: council could discuss budget (no vote) and ask questions with 6 days' notice; no supplementary questions.UPPSC
    • 1892 Act: more non-official members but official majority kept; indirect election started, word "election" avoided.
    • 1892 Act: royal assent 20 June 1892, in force 3 February 1893; additional members 10–16.
    • Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms): separate electorates for Muslims; Lord Minto = father of communal electorate.
    • 1909 Act: Indians joined executive councils; S.P. Sinha first Indian in Viceroy's council (law member).
    • 1909 Act: legislatures enlarged; members could ask supplementary questions.

    Government of India Act 1919

    • Also called Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; first used term "responsible government".
    • 1919 Act made central legislature bicameral (two houses) for first time: Council of State + Legislative Assembly.UPPSC
    • Council of State: 60 members (max 20 officials); Legislative Assembly: 140 (100 elected, 40 nominated), later 145.
    • 1919 Act: direct elections for first time; Central and Provincial subjects separated.
    • Dyarchy (Greek di-arche = double rule) in provinces: provincial subjects split into reserved and transferred.
    • Reserved (Governor + executive council): justice, police, prisons, land revenue, finance, irrigation, forests, press.
    • Transferred (ministers answerable to legislature): education, health, local self-government, public works, agriculture.
    • Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Europeans, Anglo-Indians.
    • Women got no vote in 1919 Act; provincial councils could decide on it.
    • 1919 Act: separate Indian Civil Service exam in India (from 1922, Allahabad then Delhi); by 1941 Indians outnumbered Europeans in ICS.UPPSC
    • 1919 Act → Chamber of Princes, 120 members (proclamation 23 December 1919); advisory; Viceroy presided.UPPSC
    • First Chancellor of Chamber of Princes: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.
    • Review commission due after 10 years; 7-member Simon Commission named November 1927, 2 years early.
    • Central Assembly elections of 1926 and 1945 held under 1919 Act; 1945 was last.
    • Provincial autonomy began with 1919 Act (separate provincial budgets); 1935 Act extended it.

    Government of India Act 1935

    • 1935 Act: dyarchy at Centre (never implemented); dyarchy in provinces abolished.UPPSC ×3
    • 1935 Act proposed All India Federation ("Federation of India") of provinces and princely states; never came into being.UPPSC ×2
    • Residuary powers (left-over subjects) given to Governor General.UPPSC
    • Federal Court set up 1 October 1937 under 1935 Act; first Chief Justice Sir Maurice Gwyer.UPPSC ×2
    • Burma separated from India (April 1937) by 1935 Act; new provinces Sindh and Orissa.UPPSC
    • President's ordinance power (Article 123) comes from Section 42 of 1935 Act.UPPSC
    • 1935 Act = main source of Constitution: federal scheme, Centre–State power division, Federal Court.UPPSC
    • 1935 Act had no provision for a written Constitution; that demand accepted in August Offer 1940.UPPSC
    • Cripps (1942) brought draft proposal for constitution-making after World War II.
    • Reserve Bank of India set up under 1935 Act to control currency and credit.
    • Separate electorates extended to Scheduled Castes, women, labourers; women got reserved seats.
    • Bicameral legislature in 6 of 11 provinces: Bihar, Bengal, United Provinces, Bombay, Madras, Assam.
    • 1935 Act abolished Council of Secretary of State (made 1858); British Parliament stayed supreme.
    • 1935 Act brought "constitutional autocracy": executive power with Governors and Governor General.
    • Governor General alone handled Defence, External Affairs, Ecclesiastical (church) Affairs, Tribal Areas.

    Indian Independence Act 1947

    • Declared India an independent dominion on 15 August 1947.
    • Abolished Viceroy's office; a Governor General for each dominion.
    • Dropped title "Emperor of India" from British King's titles.

    Chapter 2

    Constituent Assembly and Making of the Constitution

    How the Constituent Assembly was formed, how it worked, and when the Constitution was made.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Constitution adopted, enacted, completed on 26 November 1949 (last day of 11th session) by Constituent Assembly.PCS Pre ’02; PCS Mains ’10, ’12, ’13, ’15; UDA/LDA ’066 papers
    2. First meeting: 9 December 1946, Constitution Hall (now Central Hall), New Delhi; 207 members; Muslim League boycotted.PCS Pre ’90, ’95; PCS Mains ’113 papers
    3. B.N. Rau = Constitutional Advisor; he prepared first draft (243 Articles, 13 Schedules).PCS Pre ’14; Lower Sub ’98, ’093 papers
    4. First meeting chaired by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, oldest member, temporary President.PCS Pre ’90; PCS Mains ’132 papers
    5. Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy, 1934.GIC ’171 paper

    Demand for a Constituent Assembly

    • Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy, 1934.UPPSC
    • First formal demand: Swaraj Party, Ranchi conference, May 1934; Congress demanded it officially in 1934 at Patna.
    • 1938: Nehru (for Congress) wanted Assembly elected by adult franchise (vote for all adults), no outside interference.
    • Gandhi, "The Only Way", Harijan, 19 November 1939: only a Constituent Assembly can give an indigenous (home-made) Constitution.
    • Demand accepted in principle in August Offer 1940.
    • Cripps Mission (March 1942) proposed an elected Constituent Assembly to frame Constitution after the war.UPPSC
    • Cripps plan: dominion status; members elected by provincial assemblies, nominated by princely states; unwilling province could make separate union.
    • Wavell Plan (June 1945): equal Hindus and Muslims in Executive Council; all Indian except Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief; Shimla conference.

    Cabinet Mission and composition

    • Constituent Assembly formed under Cabinet Mission Plan 1946.UPPSC
    • Cabinet Mission (reached 24 March 1946): Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander.UPPSC
    • Seats by population: about 1 member per 10 lakh people.UPPSC
    • Total 389 seats: 296 British India (292 from 11 governors' provinces + 4 chief commissioners' provinces), 93 princely states.
    • Members elected indirectly by provincial legislative assemblies; princely states' members nominated by rulers.UPPSC
    • Not based on adult franchise: voters limited by tax, property, education (1935 Act, Sixth Schedule).
    • Elections July–August 1946: Congress 208, Muslim League 73, others 15.
    • Multi-party body; worked through committees (8 major).
    • Princely states began joining from third session, 28 April 1947.
    • Ambedkar first elected from East Bengal; later from Pune seat, Bombay Presidency (vacated by M.R. Jayakar).
    • 15 women members.UPPSC
    • Women: Vijayalakshmi Pandit, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Sarojini Naidu, Sucheta Kripalani, Purnima Banerjee, Leela Roy, G. Durgabai, Hansa Mehta.
    • Women (contd): Kamala Choudhry, Renuka Ray, Malati Choudhury, Dakshayani Velayudhan, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Annie Mascarene, Ammu Swaminathan.

    Interim Government 1946

    • Interim Government announced 24 August 1946; took charge 2 September 1946.UPPSC
    • Viceroy = ex-officio President of Executive Council; Nehru = Vice-President.
    • No Muslim League member at first; 5 League members joined 26 October 1946.
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was not a member of the Interim Government.UPPSC
    MemberPortfolio

    Sardar PatelHome, Information and Broadcasting

    Sessions and office-bearers

    • First meeting: 9 December 1946, Constitution Hall (now Central Hall), New Delhi; 207 members; Muslim League boycotted.UPPSC ×3
    • First meeting chaired by Dr. Sachchidanand Sinha, oldest member, temporary President.UPPSC ×2
    • Rajendra Prasad elected permanent President unanimously, 11 December 1946; name proposed by J.B. Kripalani.
    • Frank Anthony: first temporary Vice-President (nominated 9 December 1946); H.C. Mukherjee: first permanent Vice-President.
    • Nehru moved Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946 (fifth meeting); it later became the Preamble.UPPSC
    • Objectives Resolution adopted unanimously on 22 January 1947.UPPSC
    • 11 sessions (165 days) + signing meeting of 24 January 1950 = 12 sittings.UPPSC
    • Last meeting 24 January 1950: members signed; national anthem and song adopted; Rajendra Prasad elected first President.UPPSC
    • Time taken: 2 years, 11 months, 18 days.UPPSC

    Check Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha websites count 2 years, 11 months, 17 days; exams key 18 days.

    • First session ran 9–23 December 1946.
    • V.T. Krishnamachari represented Rajasthan's princely states; K.M. Munshi = at first only Congress member of Drafting Committee.

    Drafting, adoption, enforcement

    • B.N. Rau = Constitutional Advisor; he prepared first draft (243 Articles, 13 Schedules).UPPSC ×3
    • Third reading: 17–26 November 1949.
    • Constitution adopted, enacted, completed on 26 November 1949 (last day of 11th session) by Constituent Assembly.UPPSC ×6
    • In force at once on 26 November 1949: citizenship, interim Parliament, temporary and transitional provisions.
    • Whole Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.UPPSC
    • 26 January chosen: Congress observed it as Independence Day from 1930 (Purna Swaraj, Lahore session 1929).
    • Order: Assembly first met 1946 → Drafting Committee 1947 → adopted 1949 → commenced 1950.UPPSC
    • Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) = 26 November; notified 19 November 2015 by Ministry of Social Justice.
    • President is elected by people's representatives, not directly by people.UPPSC

    Views and quotes

    • Called an "adopted" Constitution (borrowed from many countries); it meets all needs, can be amended.UPPSC
    • Gandhi advised disbanding Congress as a political party after independence.UPPSC
    • Ivor Jennings: founding fathers minimized minority interests and emotions.UPPSC
    • Granville Austin ("The Indian Constitution"): "Constituent Assembly was Congress and Congress was India".UPPSC
    • Maulana Azad wanted adult franchise put off 15 years; Prasad and Nehru backed it.
    • Rajendra Prasad (26 November 1949): "A Constitution, like a machine, is a lifeless thing".
    • Ambedkar: born 14 April 1891, Mhow (MP); died 6 December 1956, Delhi.
    • Third Round Table Conference (November–December 1932, London; Congress absent) led to 1935 Act.

    Chapter 4

    Sources of the Constitution

    Which country or law each feature of the Indian Constitution was borrowed from.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Australia · Concurrent List (Seventh Schedule)PCS Mains ’11, ’12, ’14, ’16; Lower Sub ’155 papers
    2. USA · Fundamental Rights (US Bill of Rights)RO/ARO ’14; UDA/LDA ’06, ’103 papers
    3. USA · Judicial review (courts can strike down unconstitutional acts); exists in both India and USAPCS Pre ’98, ’08; PCS Mains ’123 papers
    4. Ireland · Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51)PCS Pre ’98; Lower Sub (Spl) ’042 papers
    5. Canada · Federation with strong CentrePCS Mains ’06, ’172 papers

    Borrowed features by source

    SourceFeatures taken
    Government of India Act 1935Major portion; "blueprint" of the Constitution
    BritainRule of law, parliamentary government, cabinet system, single citizenship, bicameral legislature, law-making procedure, parliamentary privileges, prerogative writs
    USAFundamental Rights (US Bill of Rights)UPPSC ×3
    USAJudicial review (courts can strike down unconstitutional acts); exists in both India and USAUPPSC ×3
    USAPreamble, independence of judiciary, Vice-President's post, impeachment of President, removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges
    IrelandDirective Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51)UPPSC ×2
    IrelandNominating members of talent, experience, service to Rajya SabhaUPPSC
    IrelandMethod of electing President
    CanadaFederation with strong CentreUPPSC ×2
    Canada"Union of States" wording (Article 1), from British North America Act 1867UPPSC
    CanadaResiduary powers with CentreUPPSC
    CanadaGovernors appointed by Centre, Governor reserving bills for President, Supreme Court's advisory jurisdiction
    AustraliaConcurrent List (Seventh Schedule)UPPSC ×5
    AustraliaJoint sitting of Parliament, language of Preamble, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
    Germany (Weimar)Emergency provisions (except financial emergency)
    JapanProcedure established by lawUPPSC
    South AfricaConstitutional amendment procedure, election of Rajya Sabha members
    USSRFundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment 1976 on Swaran Singh Committee advice)UPPSC
    USSRIdeals of social, economic and political justice in Preamble
    FranceRepublic; liberty, equality, fraternity in Preamble

    Related facts

    • The Constitution is supreme in the Indian political system.UPPSC
    • Constitution is world's longest written one: originally 22 Parts, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules; borrowing Fundamental Rights is not the reason.UPPSC
    • Concurrent List: originally 47 items, now 52 (11A, 17A, 17B, 20A, 33A added).
    • India and USA both have a federal Supreme Court to interpret the Constitution.
    • India: single citizenship, three lists; USA: dual citizenship, dual court system, no three lists.
    • Election Commission was not borrowed from any country.
    • USA has first written Constitution, also the shortest (7 Articles).

    Parts of Indian Constitution

    The Parts of the Constitution, their subjects and Article ranges.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. IX · Panchayats (three-tier, by 73rd Amendment) · 243–243-OPCS Pre ’13, ’16, ’203 papers
    2. XIV-A · Tribunals · 323-A–323-BPCS Pre ’23; RO/ARO ’16; RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’163 papers

    5. IX-A · Municipalities · 243-P–243-ZGPCS Pre ’25; PCS Mains ’092 papers

    Number of Parts

    • Originally 22 Parts, 395 Articles, 8 Schedules; at present 25 Parts.UPPSC ×2
    • Part IV-A and Part XIV-A added by 42nd Amendment 1976.
    • Part IX-A added by 74th Amendment 1992; Part IX-B by 97th Amendment 2011.

    Points inside the Parts

    • Part XI Chapter I = legislative relations; Chapter II = administrative relations.UPPSC
    • Three tiers: Gram Panchayat, Block/Mandal/Taluka Panchayat, Zila Panchayat; middle tier optional if state population below 20 lakh.
    • 74th Amendment 1992 = urban local bodies (Nagarpalikas).
    • Article 323-A: administrative tribunals; Article 323-B: tribunals for other matters.
    • Part XV covers Election Commission, electoral rolls, elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President, Vice-President.
    • Idea of Fundamental Rights (Part III) borrowed from USA.UPPSC
    • Abolition of titles = Fundamental Right; organising village panchayats = Directive Principle.
    • Giving education chance to child aged 6–14 = Fundamental Duty.

    Chapter 6

    Articles of the Constitution

    Important Articles of the Constitution and the subject each one covers.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 164 · Governor appoints Chief Minister; other ministers on CM's advicePCS Mains ’05, ’11; Lower Sub ’023 papers

    Chapter 7

    Schedules

    The twelve Schedules of the Constitution and the subjects in the three legislative lists.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Seventh · Division of powers: Union, State, Concurrent ListsPCS Pre ’25; RO/ARO ’16; RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’16; RO/ARO Mains ’214 papers
    2. Concurrent: criminal law and criminal procedure.PCS Mains ’05, ’06, ’113 papers
    3. Eleventh Schedule = Panchayati Raj powers (Article 243G); added by 73rd Amendment 1992; 29 items.PCS Pre ’15, ’19; RI ’143 papers
    4. Fourth · Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States and Union TerritoriesPCS Pre ’19, ’23; PCS Mains ’153 papers
    5. Sixth · Administration of tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, MizoramPCS Pre ’19; PCS Mains ’16; RO/ARO ’233 papers

    The twelve Schedules

    • Originally 8 Schedules; now 12 (9th to 12th added by amendments).
    ScheduleContent
    FirstStates and Union Territories with their territories; amended when a new state is createdUPPSC ×2
    SecondSalaries and allowances of Union office-holders, judges, CAG
    ThirdForms of oaths and affirmationsUPPSC ×2
    FourthAllocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States and Union TerritoriesUPPSC ×3
    FifthAdministration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
    SixthAdministration of tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, MizoramUPPSC ×3
    SeventhDivision of powers: Union, State, Concurrent ListsUPPSC ×4
    EighthLanguages: originally 14, now 22UPPSC
    NinthValidation of certain Acts (originally 13, now 284); added by 1st Amendment 1951
    TenthDisqualification for defection (Anti-Defection Law); added by 52nd Amendment 1985UPPSC ×2
    EleventhPowers of Panchayats, 29 subjects; added by 73rd Amendment 1992
    TwelfthPowers of Municipalities, 18 subjects; added by 74th Amendment 1992
    • Third Schedule oaths: Union and State ministers, election candidates, MPs, state legislators, Supreme Court and High Court judges, CAG.
    • President's oath is in Article 60, not Third Schedule.
    • Eighth Schedule: Sindhi added by 21st Amendment 1967; Konkani, Nepali, Manipuri by 71st Amendment 1992.
    • Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali added by 92nd Amendment 2003; Oriya renamed Odia by 96th Amendment 2011.

    Ninth Schedule

    • Ninth Schedule protects state land reform and zamindari abolition laws from court challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds.UPPSC
    • Added June 1951 under Prime Minister Nehru; Parliament can place a law in it.
    • I.R. Coelho case (2007, "Ninth Schedule case"): laws added after 24 April 1973 open to judicial review against basic structure.UPPSC

    Seventh Schedule: three lists

    ListOriginal subjectsNowWho makes law
    Union List (List I)9798Only Centre
    State List (List II)6659Mainly States
    Concurrent List (List III)4752Both; Parliament's law prevails in conflict
    • Union List: defence, foreign affairs, railways, banking, insurance, census, post office savings bank, radio and television, corporation tax (Entry 85).
    • Stock exchanges and futures markets are in Union List, not Concurrent.UPPSC ×2
    • Union List: inter-state trade and commerce (Entry 42); inter-state migration and quarantine (Entry 81); elections to Parliament and legislatures (Entry 72).
    • State List: police, public order, prisons, public health and sanitation (Entry 6), agriculture, land reforms, local government/Panchayati Raj (Entry 5).
    • Gas is in State List, not Union List.UPPSC
    • Railway police is in State List, though railways are Union.UPPSC ×2
    • State List: treasure trove (Entry 44), agricultural income tax (Entry 46), electricity tax (Entry 53), trade within state (Entry 26), state legislature elections (Entry 37).
    • Concurrent: economic and social planning (Entry 20); Planning Commission was set up under it.UPPSC
    • Concurrent: criminal law and criminal procedure.UPPSC ×3
    • Concurrent: marriage, divorce, adoption, succession (Entry 5).UPPSC
    • Concurrent: adulteration of foodstuffs and goods (Entry 18); trade and commerce is not counted as Concurrent.UPPSC

    Check Concurrent Entry 33 does cover trade in some goods (foodstuffs, cattle fodder, raw cotton, raw jute); UPPSC still excluded trade.

    • Concurrent: population control and family planning (Entry 20A, by 42nd Amendment), electricity, price control (Entry 34), prevention of cruelty to animals (Entry 17).
    • 42nd Amendment 1976 moved education from State List (Entry 11) to Concurrent List.UPPSC ×2
    • 42nd Amendment also moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds (Entry 17B) to Concurrent List.
    • Residuary subjects (in no list, with Centre), example: space research.UPPSC
    • Article 246 with Seventh Schedule gives Union and States the power to tax.

    Fifth and Sixth Schedules

    • Both Schedules protect interests of Scheduled Tribes.
    • Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas in all states except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
    • President notifies Scheduled Areas (Article 244(1)); states having them must form a Tribes Advisory Council (para 4).UPPSC
    • 10 states have Scheduled Areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan.
    • Largest unit of a Scheduled Area = district; smallest = cluster of villages in a block.
    • Governor reports to President on Scheduled Areas yearly or when asked; can stop transfer of tribal land to non-tribals (para 5).
    • President alters Scheduled Area boundaries after consulting Governor.
    • Samatha vs State of Andhra Pradesh (1997): transfer of tribal land to private parties for mining is void.
    • Sixth Schedule flows from Articles 244(2) and 275(1); aims to save tribal culture; Manipur not covered.
    • Education touches Directive Principles (Article 45), local bodies (Articles 243G, 243W), Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Schedules.

    Schedules carried over

    • Eleventh Schedule = Panchayati Raj powers (Article 243G); added by 73rd Amendment 1992; 29 items.UPPSC ×3
    • Scheduled Area status does not take away State Government's executive power; Centre cannot take over its administration.
    • Sixth Schedule: tribal areas run as autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
    • District Council: at most 30 members; at most 4 nominated by Governor, rest elected by adult suffrage.

    Chapter 8

    The Preamble

    The Preamble: its words, changes, legal status and what leaders and courts said about it.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 42nd Amendment 1976 added three words: Socialist, Secular, Integrity.PCS Pre ’91, ’09, ’10, ’25; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; PCS Mains ’10, ’13, ’178 papers
    2. Preamble is called the "soul" of the Constitution; Thakur Das Bhargava said so.PCS Pre ’08; PCS Mains ’13, ’15; UDA/LDA ’06; GIC ’085 papers
    3. On 26 January 1950 India was a "Sovereign Democratic Republic".PCS Mains ’09; Lower Sub (Spl) ’082 papers
    4. Its ideals are elaborated in Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.PCS Mains ’04; UDA/LDA ’022 papers
    5. Preamble secures 3 types of justice: social, economic, political.PCS Mains ’16; RO/ARO ’212 papers

    Text of the Preamble

    • Begins "We, the People of India" → people are sovereign.
    • Order of words: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.UPPSC
    • Preamble has 3 kinds of justice, 5 of liberty, 2 of equality, 1 of fraternity.UPPSC
    • Justice: social, economic, political; no "religious justice".UPPSC
    • Liberty: thought, expression, belief, faith, worship; no "economic liberty".UPPSC
    • Equality of status and opportunity; fraternity assuring dignity of individual and unity and integrity of Nation.UPPSC
    • Date in Preamble: 26 November 1949 (adopt, enact, give to ourselves).
    • Words not in Preamble: "federal", "public welfare", "people's" ("people's" is in China's Constitution).UPPSC
    • Idea of Preamble taken from USA.

    42nd Amendment changes

    • On 26 January 1950 India was a "Sovereign Democratic Republic".UPPSC ×2
    • 42nd Amendment 1976 added three words: Socialist, Secular, Integrity.UPPSC ×8
    • "Unity of the Nation" became "Unity and Integrity of the Nation"; Integrity was absent in 1975.UPPSC
    • Preamble amended only once so far; amendment held valid; based on Swaran Singh Committee.
    • Preamble, with the word Secular, declares India a secular state.UPPSC
    • Secular in India = State has no religion of its own; treats all religions equally.UPPSC
    • Universalism = "all individuals are fully and equally human".

    Nature and legal status

    • Nehru's Objectives Resolution (moved 13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947) became the Preamble.
    • Preamble can be amended; it cannot override specific provisions of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Preamble is non-justiciable: not enforceable in court.UPPSC
    • Preamble reflects objectives of Constitution and mind of its makers; helps interpret unclear provisions.UPPSC
    • Its ideals are elaborated in Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.UPPSC ×2
    CaseRuling on Preamble
    Berubari (1960)Not a part of Constitution; key to minds of makersUPPSC
    Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967)Core soul of Constitution
    Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973, 13 judges)Part of Constitution and of basic structureUPPSC
    S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994)Integral part of ConstitutionUPPSC

    What leaders said

    • Preamble is called the "soul" of the Constitution; Thakur Das Bhargava said so.UPPSC ×5
    • Ambedkar called Article 32 (constitutional remedies) the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.
    • K.M. Munshi: Preamble = "political horoscope" of our sovereign democratic republic.
    • Subhash Kashyap: Constitution = body, Preamble = soul; Preamble = foundation, Constitution = building.
    • Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar: Preamble "expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long".
    • Ambedkar called the Constitution a sacred (pious) document.

    Preamble: leftover facts

    • Idea of Preamble taken from USA; its language from Australia.UPPSC
    • Preamble secures 3 types of justice: social, economic, political.UPPSC ×2
    • Economic justice is given in Preamble and Directive Principles (Article 38(1)).
    • Social equality is guaranteed: Right to Equality, Articles 14–18; Preamble also aims at it.UPPSC
    • Berubari case (1960): Preamble not a part of Constitution.
    • Kesavananda Bharati (1973), 13 judges: Preamble is part of Constitution and of basic structure.
    • S.R. Bommai (1994): Preamble is an integral part of Constitution.
    • Preamble: not enforceable in court; no legal effect on its own.
    • Preamble amended only once: 1976, 42nd Amendment.
    • Preamble's ideals are detailed in Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.
    • K.M. Munshi: Preamble = "horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic".
    • Ambedkar: Constitution = sacred document; Article 32 = "heart and soul".

    Chapter 9

    The Governance System

    Types of government, and why India is parliamentary, republican and federal with a strong Centre.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. India has parliamentary government (UK model), not presidential.PCS Pre ’90, ’05; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; PCS Mains ’154 papers
    2. Quasi-federal: "unitary state with subsidiary federal features" (book Federal Government) · K.C. WhearePCS Pre ’19; RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’23; GIC ’103 papers
    3. Republic: head of State is elected, no hereditary ruler.PCS Pre ’97; PCS Mains ’172 papers
    4. Executive is taken from, responsible to and controlled by the legislature.PCS Pre ’25; PCS Mains ’102 papers
    5. Cardinal features of India: democratic republic, parliamentary form, supreme power with people; no unified authority.PCS Pre ’09; Lower Sub ’082 papers

    State and forms of government

    • Autocracy: supreme power with one person; includes absolute monarchy (inherited post) and dictatorship.
    • Democracy: final power with people; they choose and change the government.
    • Democracy never puts supreme power in one person like a king.UPPSC
    • State has 4 elements: population, territory, government, sovereignty.
    • Sovereignty (full independent power) = most important element of State.UPPSC
    • India before 1947 not a State: sovereignty missing under British control.
    • Garner: State = people on fixed territory, free of outside control, with organised government.
    • India is a Commonwealth member; this does not reduce its sovereignty.UPPSC
    • Republic: head of State is elected, no hereditary ruler.UPPSC ×2
    • India's President is elected indirectly: parliamentary system combined with republicanism.
    • People are the source of political power: "We the People of India".
    • Centre and State governments both get authority from the Constitution.UPPSC
    • India is democratic and has its own Constitution, but Constitution is not the reason.UPPSC
    • UK is democratic without a written constitution; non-democratic countries also have constitutions.
    • India: democratic polity, sovereign State, democratic society, welfare State (through Directive Principles).UPPSC
    • Indian polity: rule of law, democratic and constitutional government; not authoritarian.UPPSC
    • Constitution's philosophy: welfare State, socialist State, political equality (adult franchise); not communist State.UPPSC
    • Welfare State: State protects social and economic well-being, mainly of weaker sections.
    • "The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap" = welfare State.
    • Rule of Law (A.V. Dicey): limited powers, equality before law, liberty and civil rights.
    • Law and liberty: no laws, no liberty.
    • Good governance: accountability, transparency, rule of law; red tapism is not.
    • Political parties = life-blood of democracy; people blame them for bad governance.UPPSC
    • Party-less democracy proposed by Mahatma Gandhi and Jayaprakash Narayan.
    • Indian political system has "continuity and change": modern, traditional and saintly styles.UPPSC
    • Women, Dalits, poor and minorities = biggest stakeholders of Indian democracy.

    Parliamentary system

    • India has parliamentary government (UK model), not presidential.UPPSC ×4
    • Parliamentary government first began in Great Britain.UPPSC
    • Also called Cabinet form, responsible government, Westminster model.
    • Executive is taken from, responsible to and controlled by the legislature.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 75(3): Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
    • Article 164(2): State Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly.
    • Article 75(5): minister not an MP for 6 months in a row loses office.
    • Cabinet is headed by Prime Minister (head of government); President = head of State, nominal executive.
    • Other features: majority party rule, political homogeneity, double membership, PM's leadership, dissolution of lower House, secrecy.
    • Cardinal features of India: democratic republic, parliamentary form, supreme power with people; no unified authority.UPPSC ×2
    • India differs from British system by judicial review (taken from USA).UPPSC
    • British Parliament is sovereign; Indian Parliament is limited by Constitution and basic structure.
    • Constitution bench: at least 5 judges, set up by Chief Justice (Articles 143, 145(3)).
    • Judicial review Articles: 13, 32, 136, 137, 226, 227.

    Presidential system

    • All executive powers lie with the President: head of State and of government.UPPSC
    • Basic feature = single executive; power is centralised.UPPSC
    • President appoints his own ministers but cannot dissolve the legislature.UPPSC
    • First and purest example: USA; President elected indirectly for a fixed term.

    Federal and unitary features

    • Federal = powers divided between Centre and States (7th Schedule, Articles 245–255).
    • Federal features: written and rigid Constitution, its supremacy, division of powers, independent judiciary, two Houses, dual government.
    • Independent judiciary is essential for federalism: it interprets the Constitution.
    • Single citizenship is a unitary, not federal, feature.UPPSC
    • Other unitary features: strong Centre, single Constitution, President appoints Governors, emergency powers, All India Services, integrated judiciary.
    • More unitary features: integrated audit and election machinery, veto over State bills, unequal Rajya Sabha seats.
    • Parliament can make law on State List: Article 249 (national interest), Article 250 (emergency).
    • Federal system is basic structure, with strong unitary bias.UPPSC
    • Only Union is sovereign, not States; judicial power is not divided, only a hierarchy.
    • Constitution is federal and also creates a very strong Centre; second is not reason for first.UPPSC
    • India is a federal State, though not completely; federal in form, unitary in spirit.UPPSC
    • Ambedkar: federal in normal times, works as unitary in war or emergency.
    • Indian federation is not the result of agreement among units; units cannot leave ("Union").
    • Article 1: India is a Union of States; 28 States and 8 Union Territories.
    • Federal system chosen for two reasons: large size and socio-cultural diversity.
    • Constitution is partly rigid, partly flexible: simple majority, special (2/3) majority, ratification by half the States.UPPSC
    • Constitution is the longest written one in the world.
    • USA is a federal republic of 50 States.

    Who said what on federalism

    Term or statementPerson
    Quasi-federal: "unitary state with subsidiary federal features" (book Federal Government)K.C. WheareUPPSC ×3
    Cooperative federalismGranville AustinUPPSC
    Bargaining federalismMorris-Jones
    Federalism with centralising tendencyIvor Jennings
    "Good balance between rigidity and flexibility"K.C. WheareUPPSC
    "Not set in a tight mould of federalism"B.R. AmbedkarUPPSC
    Neither purely federal nor unitary, a combinationD.D. Basu
    • Quasi-federal = neither fully federal nor unitary; Centre has more power.UPPSC
    • Quasi-federal nature and independent judiciary with judicial review are both true but unlinked.UPPSC

    Public administration thinkers

    ThinkerKnown for
    Herbert SimonRejected principles of administration as "myths and proverbs"
    Fred W. RiggsConcept of development administration
    Henri Fayol14 principles of management; public and private administration similar
    B. Donham"If our civilization fails… breakdown of administration"

    Governance: leftover facts

    • Chief purpose of a Constitution: define and limit powers of government.
    • Constitutional government = limited government; State authority restricted to protect individual liberty.
    • Liberty (positive meaning) = opportunity to develop oneself fully.
    • Equality in society means absence of privileges.
    • Pocket veto (keeping a bill unsigned) is common to Presidents of India and USA.UPPSC
    • US President must return a bill within 10 days; Indian President has no time limit.
    • Residuary (left-over) powers: Centre in India, States in USA.
    • Rajya Sabha has 12 members nominated by President; US upper House is fully elected.
    • Indian parliamentary system shifted from centralism to federalism in the 1970s; Congress lost many States.UPPSC
    • 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission, Report 12 "Citizen-Centric Administration": lists barriers to good governance.
    • Bodies promoting unity in diversity: Inter-State Council, National Development Council, Finance Commission, Regional Councils, single judiciary, All India Services.
    BodyArticle or head
    Inter-State CouncilArticle 263
    Finance CommissionArticle 280
    All India ServicesArticle 312
    National Development CouncilHeaded by Prime Minister

    Chapter 10

    National Symbols

    National flag, emblem, anthem, song, calendar and other national symbols.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Constituent Assembly adopted National Flag on 22 July 1947 (fourth session).PCS Pre ’90, ’20; PCS Mains ’043 papers
    2. National Animal: Tiger (Panthera tigris); Project Tiger began April 1973.RO/ARO Mains ’141 paper
    3. National Calendar: Saka era, first month Chaitra, last Falgun; adopted 22 March 1957.PCS Pre ’191 paper

    National Flag

    • Tricolour, rectangular; length : width = 3 : 2.
    • Saffron (top) = strength, courage; white = peace, truth; green = fertility, growth.
    • Navy blue Ashoka Chakra with 24 spokes, from Sarnath lion capital; stands for justice (Dharma Chakra).
    • Designed by Pingali Venkayya; adopted by Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947.
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan's explanation of colours and wheel is given in Flag Code of India.

    Emblem, anthem and song

    • State emblem: from Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka; adopted 26 January 1950.
    • "Satyameva Jayate" from Mundaka Upanishad, in Devanagari, at base of emblem.
    • National Anthem "Jana Gana Mana": by Rabindranath Tagore, originally in Bengali; Hindi version adopted 24 January 1950.
    • Anthem first sung 27 December 1911, Calcutta Congress session (President Bishan Narayan Dar).
    • Anthem playing time: about 52 seconds; short version 20 seconds.
    • National Song "Vande Mataram": from Anand Math by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee; adopted 24 January 1950.
    • Song first sung at 1896 Congress session (President Rahimatullah Sayani).

    Chapter 11

    States and Union Territories

    How India's States and Union Territories were formed, reorganised and can be changed by Parliament.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 2: Parliament may admit or establish new States.PCS Pre ’90; PCS Mains ’13; RO/ARO Mains ’143 papers
    2. Article 3: Parliament may form new States and alter area, boundaries or name of any State.PCS Mains ’08, ’152 papers
    3. 2002: 28 States, 7 UTs → Telangana 29th State (2 June 2014) → now 28 States, 8 UTs.PCS Pre ’02; PCS Mains ’132 papers
    4. 36th Amendment 1975: Sikkim a full State, the 22nd.PCS Mains ’05; UDA/LDA ’062 papers
    5. Meghalaya · 21 January 1972PCS Pre ’10; PCS Mains (Spl) ’082 papers

    Integration and original classes

    • Indian Independence Act 1947: two Dominions, India and Pakistan.
    • Princely States (over 560) could join India, join Pakistan or stay independent.
    • Hyderabad joined by military action, Junagadh by referendum, Kashmir by Instrument of Accession (Maharaja Hari Singh).
    Class in 1950 (First Schedule)What it wasHead
    Part AFormer British provincesGovernor
    Part BFormer Princely StatesRajpramukh
    Part CPrincely States and Chief Commissioner's provincesChief Commissioner
    Part DAndaman and Nicobar Islands onlyPresident through Chief Commissioner
    • Part C States and Part D territory later became the base for Union Territories.

    Articles 1 to 4

    • Article 1: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States", not a federation.UPPSC
    • Territory of India: States, Union Territories, any acquired territories; names listed in First Schedule.
    • Article 2: Parliament may admit or establish new States.UPPSC ×3
    • Article 3: Parliament may form new States and alter area, boundaries or name of any State.UPPSC ×2
    • Admission of new States comes under Article 2, not Article 3.UPPSC
    • Article 3 powers: form new State, increase area, reduce area, alter boundaries, alter name.UPPSC
    • In Article 3 clauses (a)–(e) "State" includes Union Territory; in the proviso it does not.
    • Changing a State's name is Parliament's power, not the State Legislature's.UPPSC
    • New State bill needs only a simple majority in Parliament.UPPSC
    • Article 4(2): such law is not a constitutional amendment under Article 368.UPPSC
    • Such law also amends First and Fourth Schedules.
    • Bill needs President's prior recommendation; he first refers it to the State Legislature for views.
    • Legislature's views within the fixed period are not binding on President or Parliament.UPPSC
    • India is a Union; Parliament can change a State's area, boundary, name without its consent.UPPSC
    • States have no right to secede (leave); advocacy of secession is not protected speech.UPPSC
    • Article 19(1) gives 6 freedoms; State can put reasonable restrictions only on listed grounds.
    • Article 14: equality before law for citizens and non-citizens; Article 16: job equality for citizens only.

    Linguistic reorganisation

    • S.K. Dhar Commission (1948): reorganise on administrative convenience, not language.UPPSC
    • JVP Committee (December 1948): Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya; report April 1949 rejected linguistic basis.
    • Potti Sriramulu died after 56-day fast; Andhra formed on 1 October 1953 as first linguistic State.
    • States Reorganisation Commission: set up 29 December 1953; report 30 September 1955.
    • Chairman Fazal Ali; members K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.UPPSC
    • Commission accepted language as basis but rejected "one language, one state".
    • Commission did not support splitting Bombay and Punjab.
    • States Reorganisation Act 1956 and 7th Amendment 1956 ended Part A, B, C classes.
    • Result on 1 November 1956: 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

    Number of States and Union Territories

    • 2002: 28 States, 7 UTs → Telangana 29th State (2 June 2014) → now 28 States, 8 UTs.UPPSC ×2

    Check Key says "none of the above" for the 2002 count and "28" after Telangana; the explanation says 28 and 7 then, 29 after Telangana.

    • Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh UTs made it 28 and 9; merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu (26 January 2020) made 8.
    • Goa is a State, not a Union Territory (full statehood 1987).UPPSC
    • Delhi: Union Territory; special status as National Capital Territory by 69th Amendment 1991.UPPSC

    • Article 240(1): (a) Andaman and Nicobar, (b) Lakshadweep, (c) merged Dadra–Daman UT, (d) repealed, (e) Puducherry.
    • Dadra and Nagar Haveli: under Portuguese rule till 1954.
    • Daman and Diu separated from Goa by 56th Amendment.

    Sikkim and north-east States

    • 35th Amendment 1974: Sikkim an Associate State (new Article 2A).
    • 36th Amendment 1975: Sikkim a full State, the 22nd.UPPSC ×2
    • Sikkim: part of India in 1975, "botanist's paradise", people mainly Lepchas (also Bhutias, Nepalis).UPPSC
    • Sikkim Assembly: at least 32 members.
    • Mizoram: State by 53rd Amendment; formed 20 February 1987 (accord 30 June 1986).
    • Nagaland: created by ordinary law, State of Nagaland Act 1962, not by amendment.
    • Tripura: Part C State → Union Territory 1956 → full State 21 January 1972.
    • Arunachal Pradesh: capital Itanagar named after Ita Fort; two national parks, Namdapha and Mouling.

    Chapter 12

    The Citizenship

    Who is an Indian citizen, how citizenship is gained and lost, and recent citizenship laws.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Citizenship is in Part II of the Constitution.PCS Pre ’18; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’102 papers
    2. India has single citizenship for the whole country, taken from Britain.PCS Pre ’94, ’152 papers
    3. It covers Articles 5 to 11.PCS Pre ’201 paper
    4. 3 ways to lose it: renunciation, termination (voluntarily taking foreign citizenship), deprivation.PCS Mains ’171 paper
    5. Not eligible: person whose self, parent, grandparent or great-grandparent was citizen of Pakistan or Bangladesh.PCS Mains ’161 paper

    Constitutional provisions

    • Citizenship is in Part II of the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • It covers Articles 5 to 11.UPPSC
    • India has single citizenship for the whole country, taken from Britain.UPPSC ×2
    • USA has dual citizenship: of the federation and of the State.
    • One person has only one citizenship and one domicile (permanent home).
    • Any citizen, by birth or naturalised, can become President.
    ArticleSubject
    6Citizenship rights of persons who migrated to India from Pakistan
    7Citizenship rights of certain migrants to Pakistan
    8Citizenship rights of persons of Indian origin living outside India
    9Person who voluntarily takes foreign citizenship is not a citizen
    11Parliament may make laws on citizenship

    Citizenship Act 1955

    • Passed by Parliament in 1955; amended in 1957, 1985, 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019.
    • 5 ways to gain citizenship: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory.
    • 3 ways to lose it: renunciation, termination (voluntarily taking foreign citizenship), deprivation.UPPSC
    • Marrying a foreigner or criticising the government does not end citizenship.
    • Section 5(1)(a): person of Indian origin can register after 7 years' residence in India.
    • Registered or naturalised citizenship can be cancelled for fraud, disloyalty, trading with enemy in war, 7 years abroad.

    OCI and the 2019 amendment

    • Section 7A (added by 2015 amendment): Centre may register a person as Overseas Citizen of India cardholder.
    • Not eligible: person whose self, parent, grandparent or great-grandparent was citizen of Pakistan or Bangladesh.UPPSC
    • Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019: passed 11 December 2019; in force 10 January 2020.
    • Section 6B: Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Parsi, Buddhist, Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan not illegal migrants.
    • Condition: came to India on or before 31 December 2014 due to religious persecution; Muslims not included.
    • Citizenship (Amendment) Rules 2024 notified on 11 March 2024.
    • Act not applicable to Sixth Schedule tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura.
    • Also not applicable to Inner Line areas under Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873.

    Citizenship: leftover facts

    • Article 11: only Parliament can make law on gaining and losing citizenship.UPPSC
    • Central Government made Citizenship Rules 2009 under Section 18 of Citizenship Act 1955.
    • Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2019: Lok Sabha 9 December, Rajya Sabha 11 December 2019, President's assent 12 December.UPPSC
    • It gives citizenship on religious basis for the first time, to non-Muslim migrants from three countries.
    • OCI card eligible: former Indian citizens and their children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren; minor child of Indian citizen.
    • Foreign spouse of Indian citizen or OCI holder eligible after 2 years of registered marriage, with security clearance.
    • Naturalised citizen can lose citizenship under Section 10 of the Act.
    • Articles 371-A to 371-I: special provisions for Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa.

    Chapter 13

    Fundamental Rights

    The six Fundamental Rights in Part III, their Articles, key court cases, writs and limits.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 44th Amendment 1978 (Janata Party government) removed Right to Property from Fundamental Rights.PCS Pre ’90, ’02, ’07; PCS Mains (Spl) ’04; PCS Mains ’13, ’14, ’15; Lower Sub (Spl) ’04; Lower Sub ’13; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’1010 papers
    2. Guardian of Fundamental Rights = judiciary (Supreme Court and High Courts), not the President.PCS Pre ’92; PCS Mains ’10, ’12, ’15; Lower Sub ’04, ’13, ’157 papers
    3. Article 24: no child below 14 in factory, mine or hazardous work; an absolute ban.PCS Pre ’05, ’18; PCS Mains ’09, ’11, ’12; UDA/LDA (Spl) ’106 papers
    4. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.PCS Pre ’94; PCS Mains ’03, ’13, ’15; RO/ARO ’175 papers
    5. Equal pay for equal work: drawn from "socialist" in Preamble with Articles 14, 16 and 39(d); Randhir Singh case.PCS Pre ’99, ’01, ’03; UDA/LDA ’024 papers

    Background and nature

    • First demand for rights: Constitution of India Bill 1895, inspired by Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
    • Nehru Report (1928) asked for Fundamental Rights in the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Karachi Congress session 1931 (President Sardar Patel) passed resolution on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme.
    • Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35.UPPSC
    • Part III = "Magna Carta of India"; similar to US Bill of Rights.
    • They are a guarantee against arbitrary State action, written in Part III.UPPSC
    • They are justiciable (enforceable in court) and needed for personality development.
    • Originally 7 rights; now 6: equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational, constitutional remedies.
    • Right to protest is not among the six Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Not granted: right to equal shelter; right to information is not written, but read into Article 19(1)(a).
    • Dr. S. Radhakrishnan: rights are "a pledge to our people and a pact with the civilized world".UPPSC
    • Nehru: a Fundamental Right is something "you want to make permanent in the Constitution".
    • Patanjali Sastri: Part III protects freedoms against arbitrary invasion by State.
    • Article 13: laws against Fundamental Rights are void; secures their paramountcy (supremacy).UPPSC
    • Best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy: separation of powers.
    • Fundamental Rights can be amended but not removed; "right to die" is not a Fundamental Right.UPPSC

    Articles at a glance

    RightArticles
    Right to Equality14–18UPPSC ×3
    Right to Freedom19–22UPPSC
    Right against Exploitation23–24
    Right to Freedom of Religion25–28UPPSC
    Cultural and Educational Rights29–30
    Right to Constitutional Remedies32

    Article-wise subjects

    ArticleSubject
    14Equality before law, equal protection of laws
    15No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
    16Equal opportunity in public employment
    17Abolition of untouchability
    18Abolition of titles, except military and academic
    19Six freedoms
    20Protection in respect of conviction for offences
    21Protection of life and personal liberty
    21ARight to education
    22Protection against arrest and detentionUPPSC ×2
    23Ban on human trafficking and forced labour (begar)
    24Ban on child labour in factories, mines

    30Minorities' right to set up and run educational institutionsUPPSC ×4

    Right to Equality

    • Article 14 applies to all persons, citizens and foreigners.UPPSC
    • Article 14 puts an absolute limit on legislative power.UPPSC
    • "Equal protection of laws" is taken from the American Constitution.
    • Law giving unguided discretion to the executive violates Article 14.
    • State may treat unequals differently (reasonable classification); among equals law must be equal.UPPSC
    • Rule of law: no one above the law; one law and one judiciary for all.
    • Right to equality covers legal, social and opportunity equality; not economic equality.UPPSC
    • Champakam Dorairajan case (1951) led to change in right against discrimination: Article 15(4) added by 1st Amendment.UPPSC
    • Same case: Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles in a conflict.
    • Article 15(4): special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.
    • Article 15(5): reservation in admissions, including private institutions, except minority ones; 93rd Amendment 2005 (27% OBC).
    • Article 16(1), 16(2): equal opportunity in State jobs; no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, birthplace, residence.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 16(4): reservation in posts for backward classes.
    • Article 16(4A): reservation in promotion for SCs and STs; 77th Amendment 1995.
    • Indra Sawhney (1993) and M. Nagaraj (2006): Article 16(4) reservation limited by Article 335 (efficiency of administration).
    • Article 335 does not define "efficiency of administration".
    • Equal pay for equal work: drawn from "socialist" in Preamble with Articles 14, 16 and 39(d); Randhir Singh case.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.UPPSC ×5
    • Untouchability is a punishable offence under Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955.
    • Untouchability can be ended by laws, education and public awareness; not by giving jobs.UPPSC
    • Untouchability = worst structural violence, because it was practised with religious approval.UPPSC

    Article 19 freedoms

    Article 19(1)Freedom
    (a)Speech and expression
    (b)Assemble peacefully without arms
    (c)Form associations, unions, co-operative societies
    (d)Move freely throughout India
    (e)Reside and settle anywhere in India
    (g)Practise any profession, occupation, trade or business
    • Freedom to own, acquire and sell property, 19(1)(f), was removed by 44th Amendment 1978.UPPSC
    • Freedom of the press is not stated directly; it is part of Article 19(1)(a) (Sakal Papers case 1961).UPPSC ×2
    • Hoisting the National Flag on private buildings is a right under Article 19(1)(a).
    • Bijoe Emmanuel case: no one can be forced to sing the National Anthem; Articles 19(1)(a), 25(1).
    • Article 19(2) limits on speech: sovereignty and integrity, State security, foreign relations, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence.
    • Article 19(3): reasonable limits on assembly for public order; gherao is not protected.
    • Reasonable restrictions (Articles 19(2)–19(6)) must guard public interest and social needs.

    Articles 20, 21, 21A, 22

    • Article 20 has three protections; torture ban is not one of them (it is under Article 21).UPPSC
    • Article 20(1): no ex-post-facto (back-dated) criminal law or higher penalty.
    • Article 20(2): no second prosecution and punishment for same offence (double jeopardy).UPPSC
    • Article 20(3): accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself.UPPSC
    • Article 21: no one loses life or liberty except by "procedure established by law".UPPSC

    Check Key places "due process of law" in Article 21; the Article's words are "procedure established by law".

    • Maneka Gandhi case (1978), 7 judges: right to travel abroad is under Article 21.UPPSC
    • Maneka Gandhi: procedure must be fair, like US due process; Articles 14, 19, 21 are linked; life means life with dignity.
    • Supreme Court recognised right to shelter (Chameli Singh 1995), to travel abroad (Satwant Singh), to equal pay.UPPSC
    • Right to privacy: from Article 19(1)(d) read with Article 21 (Govind 1975, Malak Singh 1980).UPPSC ×3
    • K.S. Puttaswamy case (24 August 2017), 9 judges: privacy is a Fundamental Right under Article 21.
    • Article 21 also covers: marriage of choice (Lata Singh 2006, Hadiya), livelihood, speedy trial, food, clean air, water, environment.
    • Also under Article 21: medical aid to injured (Parmanand Katara 1989), safety from workplace sexual harassment (Vishakha 1997), pollution-free water (Subhash Kumar 1991).
    • Capital punishment does not violate Article 21 (Bachan Singh case).UPPSC
    • Article 21 cannot be suspended even in National Emergency (after 44th Amendment).UPPSC
    • Unnikrishnan case (1993): right to education flows from Article 21.
    • Article 21A (86th Amendment 2002): free, compulsory education for children aged 6–14 is a Fundamental Right.UPPSC ×2
    • Right to Education Act 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.
    • Article 22(1): arrested person must be told grounds and may consult a lawyer of choice.
    • Article 22(2): produce before nearest magistrate within 24 hours.
    • Article 22(4): preventive detention without trial for at most 3 months.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 22(5): detained person must be told grounds and allowed to make a representation.
    • Article 355: Union must protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance.
    • Parole is not a right in India; States have their own parole rules.

    Exploitation, religion, minorities

    • Right against Exploitation = Article 23 (trafficking, forced labour) and Article 24 (child labour).UPPSC
    • Article 24: no child below 14 in factory, mine or hazardous work; an absolute ban.UPPSC ×6
    • Article 24 of ICCPR (International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights) also protects child rights.UPPSC
    • Article 25 covers propagation of religion, Sikhs carrying kirpans, State's power to make social reform laws; not conversion by religious bodies.UPPSC
    • "Hindu" in Article 25 includes Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists; not Parsis.UPPSC
    • Articles 25 and 26 are subject to public order, morality and health.
    • Article 26: religious groups may set up institutions, manage own affairs, own and administer property.
    • Article 29(2): no citizen denied admission to State-aided institution on religion, race, caste, language.
    • Article 30 does not define "minority"; Constitution recognises religious and linguistic minorities.UPPSC
    • Article 30(2): State cannot discriminate in aid against minority-run institutions.

    Remedies and writs

    • Guardian of Fundamental Rights = judiciary (Supreme Court and High Courts), not the President.UPPSC ×7
    • Article 32 enforces only Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution; it gives effective remedy.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 32(2): Supreme Court issues five writs; Article 32(3): Parliament may empower any other court too.UPPSC
    • High Courts (Article 226) issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose.
    WritMeaningUse
    Habeas CorpusTo have the bodyProduce detained person; greatest safeguard of personal liberty; also against private personsUPPSC ×2
    MandamusWe commandOrders public official or body to do its dutyUPPSC ×2
    ProhibitionTo forbidHigher court stops lower court exceeding jurisdiction
    CertiorariTo be certifiedHigher court transfers case from, or quashes order of, lower courtUPPSC
    Quo WarrantoBy what authorityChecks legality of a claim to public office

    Suspension, amendment, property

    • Fundamental Rights can be suspended only during Emergency (Articles 358, 359).UPPSC
    • Article 358: Article 19 suspended automatically in war or external aggression emergency.
    • Article 359: President can suspend enforcement of rights, except Articles 20 and 21.
    CaseYearRuling
    A.K. Gopalan1950Early Fundamental Rights case
    Shankari Prasad1951Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights
    Sajjan Singh1965Same view repeated
    Golaknath1967Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
    Kesavananda Bharati1973Can amend rights, but not the basic structureUPPSC ×3
    Minerva Mills1980Approved basic structure doctrineUPPSC
    • Fundamental Duties came by 42nd Amendment.
    • 44th Amendment 1978 (Janata Party government) removed Right to Property from Fundamental Rights.UPPSC ×10
    • Right to Property is now a legal (statutory) right under Article 300-A, Part XII, for any person.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 31 (compulsory acquisition of property) was repealed; Article 301 deals with freedom of trade.

    Citizens only vs all persons

    • Only for citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.
    • Freedom of speech and expression is not available to foreigners.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 14 (equal protection of law) is available to all persons.UPPSC
    • Citizens only: right against discrimination, free movement, contesting elections.UPPSC
    • For all persons: Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 23, 24, 25–28 and constitutional remedies.
    • A British citizen in India cannot claim freedom of trade and profession, Article 19(1)(g).

    Exploitation, rights and duties

    • Article 23(1): bans human trafficking and forced labour.
    • Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act passed 1976; replaced the Ordinance of 25 October 1975.UPPSC ×2
    • Hazardous child labour (below 14) banned by Article 24, UN Charter and Supreme Court (M.C. Mehta vs Tamil Nadu, 10 December 1996).UPPSC ×2
    • Right against exploitation covers children, women and tribals; word "Dalit" is not in the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Rights = claims of citizens against the State; they limit State power.UPPSC
    • Rights and duties are correlative (two faces of one thing).
    • Ernest Barker: "Rights without duties are like men without shadows."
    • Right to Service (time-bound public services): idea began in Great Britain.
    • First Right to Services Act: Madhya Pradesh (25 September 2010); second: Bihar (15 August 2011).
    • Central Bill of 2011 on time-bound delivery of services was not passed.
    • Right to Service Act order: Punjab → Assam → Gujarat → Maharashtra.
    • Citizen's Charter aims: quality time-bound service, citizen-friendly and accountable government; not a hearing system for public demands.

    Chapter 14

    Directive Principles of State Policy

    Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36–51): guidelines the State should follow to build a welfare state.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 39(d) · Equal pay for equal work for men and womenPCS Pre ’98; PCS Mains ’12, ’14; Lower Sub ’04; UDA/LDA Mains ’105 papers
    2. Idea borrowed from the Irish Constitution.PCS Pre ’94; PCS Mains ’05; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; Lower Sub ’154 papers
    3. Welfare state idea is in the DPSP.PCS Mains ’04; Lower Sub ’04; Lower Sub Mains ’133 papers
    4. Article 37: DPSP are non-justiciable (courts cannot enforce), yet fundamental in governance; State's duty to apply them in making laws.RO/ARO ’23; Lower Sub ’042 papers
    5. Aims: welfare state, socio-economic justice, secular state; not a religious state.PCS Mains ’17; RO/ARO Mains ’132 papers

    Basics of Directive Principles

    • Directive Principles (DPSP): Part IV, Articles 36–51.
    • Idea borrowed from the Irish Constitution.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 37: DPSP are non-justiciable (courts cannot enforce), yet fundamental in governance; State's duty to apply them in making laws.UPPSC ×2
    • Core aim: social and economic democracy.UPPSC
    • Aims: welfare state, socio-economic justice, secular state; not a religious state.UPPSC ×2
    • Welfare state idea is in the DPSP.UPPSC ×3
    • Welfare state idea is found in both Preamble and DPSP.UPPSC
    • DPSP guide both Centre and States.
    • DPSP are instructions to legislature and executive; they impose no legal duty and no limit on their functions.
    • Concentration of wealth violates the DPSP (Article 39(c)).
    • Constitution gives no classification; for study: socialist, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual.UPPSC
    • Gandhian: Articles 40, 43 (cottage industry), 47, 48.
    • Not Gandhian: Uniform Civil Code (liberal-intellectual), right to work (socialist).

    Rights versus Directive Principles

    Mostly negativePositive
    Legal sanctionsMoral and political sanctions

    Welfare of the individualWelfare of the community

    40Organise village panchayats as units of self-governmentUPPSC ×2
    41Right to work, education and public assistance in certain casesUPPSC ×2
    42Just and humane work conditions; maternity relief
    43Living wage, decent life and leisure for workers; promote cottage industry; MGNREGA serves this goalUPPSC
    43AWorkers' participation in management of industries; added by 42nd AmendmentUPPSC ×2
    43BPromotion of cooperative societiesUPPSC
    44Uniform Civil Code for citizens
    45Early childhood care and education below age 6
    46Educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections
    47Raise nutrition, living standard, public health; prohibit intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs (except medicinal)
    48Organise agriculture and animal husbandry; prohibit cow slaughterUPPSC
    48AProtect and improve environment; safeguard forests and wildlifeUPPSC
    49Protect monuments, places and objects of national importance
    50Separate judiciary from executive in public services
    51International peace and security: India's foreign policy ArticleUPPSC ×2
    • Article 51 also: just relations between nations, respect for international law and treaties, settling disputes by arbitration.

    Changes and special points

    • 42nd Amendment added Articles 39(f), 39A, 43A; Uniform Civil Code was original.UPPSC
    • Free education up to 14 is no longer a DPSP: 86th Amendment, 2002 moved it from Article 45 to Article 21A.UPPSC ×2
    • Environment protection is in both DPSP (48A) and Fundamental Duties (51A(g)).UPPSC ×2
    • DPSP are silent on adult education.UPPSC
    • Equal pay for equal work: read as a Fundamental Right through Articles 14, 16, 39(d) (Randhir Singh vs Union of India, 1982).
    • Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 gives effect to Article 39(d).
    • MGNREGA: at least 100 days of work a year per rural household; right to employment is not in Part III.UPPSC
    • Trafficking and forced labour ban is a Fundamental Right (Article 23), not a DPSP.

    Directive Principles: more points

    • Free legal aid (Article 39A) inserted in 1976 by 42nd Amendment, in force 3 January 1977.
    • NALSA (National Legal Services Authority): set up under Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
    • NALSA gives free, competent legal services to weaker sections; organises Lok Adalats; guides and funds State authorities.
    • Patron-in-Chief of State Legal Services Authority = Chief Justice of that High Court.
    • Free legal services (Section 12): SC/ST member, trafficking or begar victim, woman, child, disabled person, industrial workman, low-income person.
    • Income limit: 1 lakh in most States; Andhra Pradesh 3 lakh; Delhi 2 lakh for senior citizens and transgender persons.
    • OBCs and all senior citizens are not automatically covered.
    • Right to Information is not a DPSP; it is a legal right (RTI Act, 2005).UPPSC ×2
    • Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) is a DPSP.UPPSC ×2
    • Prohibition of liquor (Article 47) is a DPSP; bans on child labour (24), forced labour (23), untouchability (17) are Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Abolition of untouchability is not a DPSP.UPPSC
    • K.T. Shah: DPSP are "a cheque payable at the bank's convenience".UPPSC
    • National Social Assistance Programme (15 August 1995) fulfils DPSP (Article 41).
    • It began with old age pension (NOAPS), family benefit (NFBS), maternity benefit (NMBS); NMBS moved out on 1 April 2001.
    • Small family norm and mother-tongue primary education (Article 350A) are not DPSP.

    Chapter 15

    Fundamental Duties

    The eleven duties of citizens in Part IV-A (Article 51A).

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Placed in Part IV-A.PCS Mains ’06, ’11, ’12; GIC ’104 papers
    2. Added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976).PCS Pre ’12; PCS Mains (Spl) ’082 papers
    3. Added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (in force 3 January 1977); ten duties then.PCS Pre ’93; Lower Sub ’022 papers
    4. Duties are non-justiciable moral obligations; cannot be enforced by writs.PCS Pre ’03; UDA/LDA ’002 papers
    5. Fundamental Duties now number eleven.PCS Mains ’14; RO/ARO Mains ’142 papers

    Origin of Fundamental Duties

    • Inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR.
    • Added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976).UPPSC ×2
    • Added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (in force 3 January 1977); ten duties then.UPPSC ×2
    • Placed in Part IV-A.UPPSC ×4
    • Part IV-A has only one Article: 51A.UPPSC
    • Now 11 duties; the 11th added by 86th Amendment, 2002 (in force 1 April 2010).
    • Committee was set up by the Congress Party during the internal emergency (1975–77).
    • Its 12 members: Swaran Singh (chairman), A.R. Antulay, S.S. Ray, Rajni Patel, H.R. Gokhale, V.S. Sayed Muhammed, V.N. Gadgil, C.M. Stephen, D.P. Singh, Dinesh Goswami, Vasanth Sathe, B.N. Banerjee.
    • Duties are non-justiciable moral obligations; cannot be enforced by writs.UPPSC ×2
    • No legislative process to enforce them; not correlative to legal duties.

    The eleven duties (Article 51A)

    ClauseDuty of every citizen
    (a)Abide by the Constitution; respect its ideals, institutions, National Flag and National Anthem
    (b)Cherish and follow noble ideals of the freedom struggle
    (c)Uphold and protect sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
    (d)Defend the country; render national service when called
    (e)Promote harmony and common brotherhood; renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity
    (f)Value and preserve rich heritage of composite culture
    (g)Protect natural environment (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife); compassion for living creatures
    (h)Develop scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry and reform
    (i)Safeguard public property; abjure (give up) violence
    (j)Strive for excellence in individual and collective activity
    (k)Parent or guardian to give education chances to child aged 6–14 (86th Amendment, 2002)
    • Voting in elections is not a Fundamental Duty.UPPSC

    Fundamental Duties: tested points

    • Fundamental Duties now number eleven.UPPSC ×2
    • They are in Part IV-A, not part of Fundamental Rights.UPPSC
    • Part V = Union Executive, not Fundamental Duties.UPPSC
    • Article 51A(g): duty to protect natural environment, including wildlife.UPPSC ×2
    • Not a duty: abolition of untouchability (Article 17, a Fundamental Right).UPPSC
    • Not a duty: organising village panchayats (Article 40, a Directive Principle).UPPSC
    • Not a duty: paying income tax.UPPSC
    • Not a duty: protecting monuments of national importance (Article 49, a Directive Principle).UPPSC ×2
    • Not a duty: respecting parents and teachers.UPPSC
    • Not a duty: protecting weaker sections from social injustice.
    • Article 51(c): respect for international law; 51A(h): spirit of inquiry; Article 50: separating judiciary from executive.UPPSC
    • Child labour ban below 14 in factories = Fundamental Right (Article 24).
