    Chapter 16

    The President

    The President: election, term, removal, powers, and the persons who held the office.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Both offices vacant: Chief Justice of India acts (President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969), then senior-most Supreme Court judge.PCS Pre ’92; PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’05, ’14; RO/ARO ’14; RO/ARO Mains ’216 papers
    2. Article 53: Union's executive power vested in President; used directly or through subordinate officers.PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’08, ’10; RO/ARO ’23; RO/ARO Mains ’215 papers
    3. Article 54: indirect election by an electoral college of elected MPs (both Houses) and elected MLAs of States.PCS Pre ’93; PCS Mains ’11, ’15; UDA/LDA ’014 papers
    4. Article 62(2): vacancy by death, resignation or removal filled within six months.PCS Pre ’98, ’05; PCS Mains ’13, ’164 papers
    5. Removal before term only by impeachment: Article 61.PCS Pre ’94; PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’173 papers

    Position of the President

    • President = head of the Indian State (Republic), first citizen, symbol of national unity.UPPSC
    • Article 52: there shall be a President of India.
    • Article 53: Union's executive power vested in President; used directly or through subordinate officers.UPPSC ×5
    • President heads the Union Executive, but powers are limited by the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Article 53(2): supreme command of Defence Forces with President; its use is regulated by law.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 77: all executive action of Government of India is taken in President's name.UPPSC
    • President is elected indirectly, British King is hereditary; US President is far more powerful.UPPSC
    • President "represents the nation but does not lead it"; Prime Minister leads.UPPSC
    • Authority: titular (formal) and de jure; constitutional and nominal.UPPSC
    • Union Cabinet prepares the President's address to Parliament.

    Election of the President

    • Article 54: indirect election by an electoral college of elected MPs (both Houses) and elected MLAs of States.UPPSC ×4
    • 70th Amendment, 1992 (from 1 June 1995): elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry included.UPPSC
    • Nominated members and Legislative Council members do not vote.UPPSC
    • Jammu and Kashmir UT Assembly members not yet included.
    • A Chief Minister who sits in the Legislative Council cannot vote.
    • Article 55(3): proportional representation, single transferable vote, secret ballot.
    • Article 55: uniform scale of representation among States; parity between States and Union.
    • MLA's vote value = State population ÷ elected MLAs ÷ 1000.
    • MP's vote value = total value of all MLA votes ÷ total elected MPs; same for both Houses.
    • Population = 1971 census, until first census after 2026 (84th Amendment, 2001).
    • MLA vote values: Uttar Pradesh 208, Kerala 152, Madhya Pradesh 131, Rajasthan 129, Puducherry 16, Arunachal Pradesh 8.
    • More Assembly seats → lower vote value per MLA.
    • Nomination needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders; security deposit Rs. 15,000.
    • Deposit lost if votes are not above one-sixth of those needed to win.
    • Article 71: Supreme Court decides all election doubts and disputes; decision final.
    • Article 71(2): if election is declared void, acts done till that date stay valid.
    • Election cannot be postponed or challenged because the electoral college is incomplete.UPPSC
    • A dissolved Assembly cannot take part in the election.
    • Election of successor must be held before the term ends.

    Check No UPPSC key printed for three questions on electoral college and proposers; follow Article 54 and the 50-proposer rule.

    Qualification, term, oath, pay

    • Article 58: citizen of India, age 35, qualified for Lok Sabha; no education condition.UPPSC
    • Citizenship by birth not needed; must qualify for Lok Sabha, not just "Parliament".UPPSC
    • Article 58(2): must not hold an office of profit.
    • Article 59(1): an MP or MLA elected President vacates that seat on entering office.UPPSC
    • Article 56: term five years from the date he enters office; continues till successor enters.
    • Article 57: eligible for re-election any number of times.
    • Article 60: oath given by the Chief Justice of India.
    • Salary: currently 5 lakh per month, from Consolidated Fund of India.
    • Article 56(1)(a): resigns to the Vice-President, who at once informs Lok Sabha Speaker (56(2)).
    • Article 361: no criminal case during term; civil case allowed after two months' written notice.

    Impeachment and vacancy

    • Removal before term only by impeachment: Article 61.UPPSC ×3
    • Only ground: violation of the Constitution (phrase not defined).
    • Charge can start in either House of Parliament.UPPSC ×2
    • Needs 14 days' written notice signed by one-fourth of that House's members.UPPSC
    • Resolution passed by two-thirds of total membership; other House investigates and passes likewise.
    • President may appear and be represented in the investigation.
    • Impeachment is quasi-judicial; no President impeached so far.
    • State Assemblies elect the President but have no role in impeachment.
    • Article 62(2): vacancy by death, resignation or removal filled within six months.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 65(1): Vice-President acts as President till new President enters; at most six months.
    • Both offices vacant: Chief Justice of India acts (President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969), then senior-most Supreme Court judge.UPPSC ×6

    Powers over Parliament and Bills

    • Article 79: President is a part of Parliament; no Bill becomes law without his assent (Article 111).UPPSC ×2
    • He addresses both Houses together every year but does not join their discussions.UPPSC
    • Article 85: summons and prorogues Houses, dissolves Lok Sabha, on advice of Council of Ministers.
    • He may prorogue a House even in session; prorogation usually follows adjournment sine die.
    • Article 108: President summons a joint sitting; Lok Sabha Speaker presides (Article 118(4)).UPPSC ×3
    • Joint sitting: Bill rejected, final disagreement, or six months' delay; President notifies his "intention".
    • Article 111: President assents, withholds assent, or returns a non-money Bill.UPPSC ×3
    • A Bill passed again must get assent; no time limit is fixed for his decision.
    • He cannot return a Money Bill or financial Bill; it is introduced only on his recommendation.UPPSC
    • Absolute veto: Rajendra Prasad, PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954.
    • Pocket veto: Giani Zail Singh, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986; used only once.
    • Article 86(2): may send messages to either House (a right, not a "power").
    • Discretionary: return a Bill, keep a Bill, ask Prime Minister for information, ask for reconsideration of advice.
    • Article 123: ordinance when Parliament is not in session.UPPSC ×3
    • Ordinance has force of an Act; lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles; President can withdraw it.
    • Ordinance can amend a Central Act and act retrospectively; cannot amend Constitution or abridge Fundamental Rights.
    • He lays before Parliament: Finance Commission recommendations (281), CAG report (151), SC Commission report (338).

    Appointments, courts, other powers

    • Appoints Finance Commission Chairman (Article 280) and Chief Ministers of Union Territories (Article 239AA); Planning Commission Vice-Chairman was appointed by Prime Minister.UPPSC
    • Appoints Attorney General (76), CAG (148), Governors (155).UPPSC
    • Vice-President is elected (Article 66), not appointed.UPPSC
    • State Chief Minister is appointed by Governor (Article 164).
    • Article 160: President provides for Governor's duties in any contingency.UPPSC
    • Article 143: may consult the Supreme Court on law or fact.UPPSC
    • He is not bound to accept the Supreme Court's advice.UPPSC
    • Cannot remove a Supreme Court judge alone; needs address of both Houses (Article 124(4)).
    • Article 72: pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, suspend, commute; a judicial power.UPPSC
    • Covers Union-law offences, court-martial sentences, death sentences; used on ministers' advice; limited judicial review.
    • Declares any area a Scheduled Area (Fifth Schedule).UPPSC
    • 42nd Amendment, 1976: President bound by Council of Ministers' advice.
    • 44th Amendment, 1978: may ask for reconsideration once, then must follow.

    • Acting Presidents: V.V. Giri (3 May – 20 July 1969), B.D. Jatti (11 Feb – 25 July 1977).
    • Chief Justice M. Hidayatullah acted as President, 20 July – 24 Aug 1969.UPPSC ×2

    Presidents: special facts

    • Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was never Vice-President before becoming President.UPPSC ×2
    • Reddy was Lok Sabha Speaker twice (1967–69, March–July 1977).UPPSC
    • V.V. Giri: trade union leader; twice chairman of All India Trade Union Congress.UPPSC
    • Giri appeared in person before the Supreme Court in his election case; election upheld.
    • Giri won on counting second-preference votes.
    • 15th Presidential election: UPA candidate was Meera Kumar.
    • Droupadi Murmu: former Jharkhand Governor, NDA candidate.
    • Rashtrapati Bhavan designed by Edwin Lutyens.UPPSC
    • Called Viceroy House till 1947, then Government House; C. Rajagopalachari first Indian resident (21 June 1948).

    Chapter 17

    The Vice-President

    The Vice-President's election, role, term, removal and office-holders.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 67(b): removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution (majority of all then members), agreed to by Lok Sabha; moved only in Rajya Sabha.PCS Mains ’03, ’04, ’07, ’134 papers
    2. Article 66(1): elected by all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament.PCS Pre ’12; PCS Mains ’122 papers
    3. Election is indirect; State legislatures have no role.RO/ARO Mains ’161 paper
    4. Article 66(3): citizen, age 35, qualified for Rajya Sabha (not Lok Sabha).UDA/LDA (Spl) ’101 paper
    5. Vice-President is the second-highest dignitary; acts as President on vacancy, does his functions in absence.Lower Sub ’131 paper

    Vice-President: election and role

    • Office modelled on the American Vice-President.
    • Article 63: there shall be a Vice-President of India.
    • Article 64: ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha; holds no other office of profit.
    • Article 66(1): elected by all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament.UPPSC ×2
    • Election is indirect; State legislatures have no role.UPPSC
    • Method: proportional representation, single transferable vote, secret ballot.
    • 2022 (16th election) electoral college: 233 + 12 Rajya Sabha + 543 Lok Sabha = 788.
    • Article 66(3): citizen, age 35, qualified for Rajya Sabha (not Lok Sabha).UPPSC
    • Salary 4 lakh per month, drawn as Rajya Sabha Chairman; none fixed as Vice-President.
    • While acting as President: no Chairman duties; gets President's pay (Article 65(3)).
    • If he resigns while acting as President, Chief Justice of India takes over.

    Vice-President: term

    • Article 67: term five years; resigns in writing to the President.
    • Article 67(b): removal resolution needs 14 days' notice.

    • K.R. Narayanan was Ambassador to China, 1976–78.

    Vice-President: tested points

    • Vice-President is the second-highest dignitary; acts as President on vacancy, does his functions in absence.UPPSC
    • He must qualify for Rajya Sabha, not Lok Sabha; an MLA may contest; removal is not formal impeachment.UPPSC
    • Article 67(b): removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution (majority of all then members), agreed to by Lok Sabha; moved only in Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×4
    • Rajya Sabha is presided over by a non-member (the Vice-President).UPPSC
    • Article 71(2): if his election is declared void, acts done on or before that date stay valid.UPPSC
    • First Vice-President: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1952–62); Zakir Husain was second.UPPSC
    • Constitutional cases in Supreme Court need at least five judges; press freedom is part of free speech.

    Chapter 18

    The Council of Ministers

    Prime Minister and Council of Ministers: appointment, size, responsibility to Lok Sabha, Cabinet and past Prime Ministers.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 75(3): Council collectively responsible to Lok Sabha only; a constitutional duty.PCS Pre ’12, ’21; PCS Mains ’12; RO/ARO ’16; BEO ’195 papers
    2. Article 75(5): a non-MP minister must enter either House within six months or cease.PCS Pre ’93, ’95; PCS Mains ’153 papers
    3. No-confidence motion needs support of 50 Lok Sabha members.PCS Mains ’09, ’13; Lower Sub ’153 papers
    4. Prime Minister is the real head of the Council of Ministers; need not be an MP when appointed.PCS Mains ’11, ’132 papers
    5. Council itself can move a Confidence Motion.PCS Pre ’06; PCS Mains ’102 papers

    Council of Ministers: basics

    • Article 300: legal name of the Government of India = "The Union of India".UPPSC
    • Council has Prime Minister, Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (independent charge), Ministers of State; ranks are convention, not in Constitution.
    • Article 74(1): Council headed by Prime Minister aids and advises President, who acts on it.
    • President may send advice back once; then must follow (44th Amendment, 1978).
    • Article 74(2): courts cannot inquire into advice given to President.
    • Article 75: appointment and other provisions for ministers.UPPSC
    • Article 75(1): President appoints Prime Minister; other ministers on Prime Minister's advice.
    • Article 75(1A): ministers, including Prime Minister, at most 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment, 2003).
    • Same 15% cap for States under Article 164(1A).
    • Article 75(2): ministers hold office during President's pleasure, not Prime Minister's.
    • President gives oath of office and secrecy to Prime Minister and ministers.
    • Article 77(3): President makes rules for business and allots portfolios on Prime Minister's advice.
    • Ministries are created by President on Prime Minister's advice (Allocation of Business Rules, 1961).
    • Ministries: 18 on 15 August 1947; 53 at present.

    Prime Minister

    • Prime Minister is the real head of the Council of Ministers; need not be an MP when appointed.UPPSC ×2
    • Prime Minister = head of Government; President = head of State.
    • Article 78: Prime Minister's duty to tell President all Council decisions and proposals for legislation.UPPSC
    • He chairs Cabinet meetings, freely picks ministers, resigns to the President.
    • Minimum age 25 (same as Lok Sabha member).
    • Usually from Lok Sabha; Indira Gandhi was first from Rajya Sabha when appointed.
    • A minister can speak in both Houses but votes only in his own.
    • So a Rajya Sabha Prime Minister cannot vote on a no-confidence motion.

    Membership and collective responsibility

    • Article 75(5): a non-MP minister must enter either House within six months or cease.UPPSC ×3
    • Cabinet membership is not limited to the Lower House.UPPSC
    • Article 75(3): Council collectively responsible to Lok Sabha only; a constitutional duty.UPPSC ×5
    • Article 74(3) does not exist.
    • Council itself can move a Confidence Motion.UPPSC ×2
    • It must resign if Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion.UPPSC
    • No-confidence motion needs support of 50 Lok Sabha members.UPPSC ×3
    • It is not in the Constitution; Lok Sabha Rule 198; only in Lok Sabha.
    • Written notice goes to Lok Sabha Secretary-General.
    • First no-confidence motion: 1963, J.B. Kripalani against Nehru government.
    • Till 15 August 2023: 28 no-confidence and 11 confidence motions discussed; 12 against Indira Gandhi governments.
    • Prime Minister resigning on losing Lok Sabha majority is a convention, not written.
    • After Council resigns: it continues till new arrangement; President's Rule is not imposed.UPPSC
    • Resigned minister may make a statement in Lok Sabha with Speaker's permission.
    • Executive is subordinate to the legislature.
    • Ministers make policy, civil servants follow it; parliamentary system runs on Cabinet's collective responsibility.UPPSC
    • Ministerial responsibility: minister answers to Parliament for acts of his officials.

    Cabinet and Cabinet Secretariat

    • Cabinet = Prime Minister and ministers of Cabinet rank only.UPPSC
    • Word "Cabinet" appears only in Article 352(3), added by 44th Amendment.
    • Council seldom meets; Cabinet shapes policy.
    • Cabinet Secretariat is directly under the Prime Minister.
    • Its head, the Cabinet Secretary, is highest civil servant and ex-officio Chairman of Civil Services Board.
    • Cabinet Committees: not in Constitution; set up by Prime Minister under Rules of Business.
    • If Prime Minister is a member of a committee, he chairs it.
    • Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs is chaired by the Defence Minister.
    • Deputy Prime Minister: not in Constitution; a political, extra-constitutional post with no Prime Minister's powers.UPPSC ×2
    • First Deputy Prime Minister: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (15 August 1947 – 15 December 1950), also Home Minister.
    • N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar report (1950), "Reorganization of the Machinery of Central Government": grouping of ministries.
    • Department of Personnel created under Cabinet Secretariat, 1 August 1970.
    • It moved to Home Ministry April 1977; became a full Ministry March 1985.
    • Renamed Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on 10 December 1985; under Prime Minister.
    • Ministry of Tribal Affairs set up 1999, split from Social Justice and Empowerment.

    • Charan Singh never faced Parliament as Prime Minister.

    • He sat in Rajya Sabha from Assam (1991 onward); from Rajasthan in 2019.

    • First Law Minister: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar; in 1946 interim government: Jogendra Nath Mandal.

    • Finance Ministers: Y.B. Chavan (1971–75), R. Venkataraman (1980–82), V.P. Singh (1984–87), Pranab Mukherjee (2009–12).

    Ministries and persons: misc

    • Narayan Desai: chairman of War Resisters International (anti-war body), 1988–91.UPPSC
    • War Resisters International: founded 1921 at Bilthoven, Netherlands; headquarters London.
    • White Paper: official Government of India document explaining policy on a subject.UPPSC
    • Reorganisation of the Union Cabinet rests on the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report.UPPSC
    • Memorials: Nehru – Shanti Van; Shastri – Vijay Ghat; Indira Gandhi – Shakti Sthal; Rajiv Gandhi – Veer Bhumi; Shankar Dayal Sharma – Karma Bhumi.UPPSC
    • "Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan": Lal Bahadur Shastri, 1965, Ramlila Maidan, Delhi.
    • Nagendra Singh: President, International Court of Justice (1985–88).
    • A.N. Ray: Chief Justice of India from 26 April 1973.
    • R.K. Trivedi: Chief Election Commissioner (1982–85); Ashok Desai: Attorney General.
    • UIDAI created June 2009: first chairman Nandan Nilekani; first Director General R.S. Sharma.
    • UIDAI head called CEO since 12 July 2016; presently Bhuvnesh Kumar.
    • Sarosh Zaiwalla: international law (arbitration) expert.
    • Giriraj Singh (Begusarai): Textiles Minister after 18th Lok Sabha election.
    • Ministry of Minority Affairs: created 29 January 2006; minister in 2025: Kiren Rijiju.
    • Notified minorities: Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, Sikh, Parsi, Jain.
    • Cabinet Secretariat work: Cabinet agenda, help to Cabinet Committees, Rules of Business, inter-ministry coordination; not fund allocation.
    • Split system in administration = policy vs implementation.
    • Prime Minister heads CSIR and the National Defence Committee.
    • Office of Parliamentary Secretary first created in 1951.

    Chapter 19

    The Attorney General and the C.A.G.

    Attorney General, Solicitor General, Advocate General and the Comptroller and Auditor General.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 76: Attorney General (AG) = first and highest law officer; chief legal adviser to Government of India.PCS Pre ’95, ’06; PCS Mains ’08; UDA/LDA (Spl) ’104 papers
    2. Article 88: may speak in both Houses, joint sittings and committees he is named to; no vote.PCS Pre ’11; PCS Mains ’03, ’053 papers
    3. Article 76(1): President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge.PCS Pre ’23; RO/ARO Mains ’142 papers
    4. Solicitor General: a legal adviser; second law officer; assists AG; helped by Additional Solicitors General.PCS Pre ’91, ’942 papers
    5. Advocate General: first legal adviser of the State Government.PCS Mains ’14; Lower Sub ’152 papers

    Attorney General of India

    • Article 76: Attorney General (AG) = first and highest law officer; chief legal adviser to Government of India.UPPSC ×4
    • Article 76(1): President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge.UPPSC ×2
    • That means: citizen; High Court judge 5 years, or High Court advocate 10 years, or eminent jurist.
    • Article 76(2): advises Government on legal matters referred by President.
    • Article 76(3): right of audience (to be heard) in all courts in India.UPPSC
    • Article 76(4): holds office during the pleasure of the President; no fixed term or removal procedure.UPPSC
    • Remuneration fixed by the President, not Parliament.UPPSC
    • Article 88: may speak in both Houses, joint sittings and committees he is named to; no vote.UPPSC ×3
    • He enjoys all privileges and immunities of an MP.UPPSC

    Check Key treats "not entitled to MP privileges" as correct; the chapter text says he enjoys them.

    • Need not be an MP; not removed by impeachment; not a full-time government servant.
    • May do private practice with permission; need not resign when the government changes.
    • Vice-President takes part only in Rajya Sabha; AG in both Houses.

    Solicitor General and Advocate General

    • Solicitor General: a legal adviser; second law officer; assists AG; helped by Additional Solicitors General.UPPSC ×2
    • Advocate General: first legal adviser of the State Government.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 165(1): Governor appoints a person qualified to be a High Court judge.
    • Article 165(2): advises State Government; 165(3): holds office during Governor's pleasure.
    • Article 177: may speak in the State Legislature; no vote.

    Comptroller and Auditor General

    ArticleSubject
    148CAG: appointment, service conditions
    149Duties and powers
    150Form of accounts of the Union
    151Audit reports
    • CAG office was created by the Constitution itself.UPPSC
    • Article 148(1): appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.UPPSC ×2
    • Removed only like a Supreme Court judge: both Houses' special-majority address, for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.UPPSC

    Check Key calls "removed by the President" untrue: the President cannot remove him at will.

    • Term: 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier (CAG Act, 1971).UPPSC
    • Article 148(3): Parliament fixes salary and service conditions; salary equals a Supreme Court judge's.
    • Salary appears in the Second Schedule.
    • Article 148(4): no further office under Union or State after retirement.
    • CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971; amended 1976 to separate accounts from audit.
    • Head of Indian Audit and Accounts Department; "guardian of the public purse"; audits Centre and States.
    • Ambedkar: CAG is probably the most important officer under the Constitution.
    • Article 151(1): Union audit reports go first to the President, who lays them before Parliament.UPPSC
    • Article 151(2): State reports go to the Governor, then the State Legislature.
    • Three reports: appropriation accounts, finance accounts, public undertakings.
    • Public Accounts Committee examines them; CAG is its "friend, philosopher and guide" and attends its meetings.UPPSC
    • Parliament has final responsibility to act on CAG's comments.UPPSC
    • Audits: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, Public Accounts, receipts, stores and stock, trading and profit-loss accounts, government companies.
    • Does not control receipt and issue of public money (no exchequer control).UPPSC
    • Checks both legality and propriety of spending; audit types: financial, compliance, performance.
    • No judicial power to prosecute; investigating agencies may use his reports.

    CAG: Articles and removal

    ArticleSubject
    148CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General): office, appointment by President by warrant
    149Duties and powers of CAG
    150Form of accounts of Union and States
    151Audit reports: Union report to President → laid before both Houses
    • CAG audits all receipts and spending of Union and State governments, including stores and stock.
    • Removal: like a Supreme Court judge; President's order after address by both Houses (special majority).
    • Grounds of removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
    • CAG's office expenses, salaries, pensions: charged on Consolidated Fund of India [Art 148(6)]; not voted.
    • Salary and service conditions: fixed by Parliament by law; till then Second Schedule [Art 148(3)].
    • After leaving office, CAG cannot hold any post under Union or State [Art 148(4)].
    • President grants or refuses leave to CAG.
    • CAG has no judicial power to prosecute; no exchequer control during emergency.
    • Investigating agencies can use CAG reports to press charges.

    CAG: role and titles

    • Parliament has final duty to act on CAG reports.
    • CAG = "friend, philosopher and guide" of Public Accounts Committee (PAC); attends its sittings.UPPSC
    • CAG (Duties, Powers, Conditions of Service) Act 1971 amended in 1976: accounts separated from audit, CAG only audits.UPPSC ×2
    • 1976 amendment in force 1 March 1976; for States, CAG still does both accounting and auditing.
    • Accounts of States (and Union) are controlled by CAG, not Governor or Chief Minister.UPPSC
    • CAG = Guardian of Public Purse; head of Indian Audit and Accounts Department.UPPSC
    • CAG = custodian and trustee of public money; no spending without legislature's sanction.
    • Linked bodies: Vice-President → Rajya Sabha; CAG → PAC; Solicitor General → Supreme Court; Attorney General → Lok Sabha meetings.UPPSC
    • Girish Chandra Murmu = 14th CAG; K. Sanjay Murthy = 15th CAG, appointed 2024.

    Chapter 21

    The Parliament (1)

    Lok Sabha: strength, seats, reservation, sessions, elections and the Speaker.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Quorum (minimum members present) of each House = 1/10 of total members, Article 100(3).PCS Pre ’17; PCS Mains ’04, ’06; Lower Sub (Spl) ’084 papers
    2. At most 20 members from Union Territories.PCS Pre ’18; PCS Mains (Spl) ’082 papers
    3. Most ST seats: Madhya Pradesh (6); Jharkhand 5, Odisha 5; Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra 4 each.PCS Pre ’97; PCS Mains ’052 papers
    4. Uttar Pradesh has most seats in both Houses: Lok Sabha 80, Rajya Sabha 31.PCS Pre ’95; PCS Mains ’122 papers
    5. Speaker resigns in writing to Deputy Speaker, and vice versa [Art 94(b)].PCS Mains ’08, ’142 papers

    Parliament and Lok Sabha strength

    • Public Finance = study of government revenue, spending, financial administration; not working of commercial banks.UPPSC
    • Parliament = legislative organ of Union; Articles 79–122, Part V.
    • Article 79: Parliament = President + Lok Sabha (House of the People) + Rajya Sabha (Council of States).
    • Lok Sabha maximum strength = 550 (Article 81).UPPSC
    • At most 530 members from States, chosen by direct election.UPPSC
    • At most 20 members from Union Territories.UPPSC ×2
    • Present strength 543: States 524 + UTs 19.
    • UT Lok Sabha seats: Delhi 7, J&K 5, Dadra-Nagar Haveli-Daman-Diu 2, Andaman 1, Chandigarh 1, Lakshadweep 1, Puducherry 1, Ladakh 1.
    • UT Rajya Sabha seats = 8: Delhi 3, J&K 4, Puducherry 1.
    • Article 331: President could nominate 2 Anglo-Indians to Lok Sabha (old maximum 552).
    • 104th Amendment 2019: Anglo-Indian nomination not extended beyond 25 January 2020; ended.
    • 7th Amendment 1956: Lok Sabha members fixed at 520.
    • 31st Amendment 1973: strength 525 → 545 (States 500 → 525; UTs 25 → 20).UPPSC

    Seat allocation and delimitation

    • Seats given to States on basis of population (Article 81); same population-seat ratio across constituencies.
    • This ratio rule does not apply to States with population up to 6 million.
    • State-wise seats now based on 1971 Census.UPPSC
    • 84th Amendment 2001: seats frozen till first Census after 2026.UPPSC
    • Delimitation Commission divides States into territorial constituencies.

    Reserved seats: SC and ST

    ArticleSubject
    330SC/ST seats in Lok Sabha
    331Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha
    332SC/ST seats in State Assemblies
    333Anglo-Indians in State Assemblies
    • After 2008 delimitation: general 412, SC 84 (earlier 79), ST 47 (earlier 41).
    • Reserved seats are filled by all voters; no separate electorate.
    • Article 330(2): reserved seats in proportion to SC/ST population of the State.
    • West Bengal and old Andhra Pradesh (42 seats each): SC seats 8 and 6 in 1996; 10 and 7 after 2008.
    • No ST seats in Lok Sabha now: Kerala and Tamil Nadu.UPPSC
    • After 2008, Karnataka and Meghalaya got 2 ST seats each.
    • No SC or ST seat: Arunachal Pradesh, UT of Jammu & Kashmir; also Andaman, Chandigarh, Puducherry.UPPSC
    • Most ST seats: Madhya Pradesh (6); Jharkhand 5, Odisha 5; Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra 4 each.UPPSC ×2
    • No ST seat in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
    • Rajasthan: 25 seats (SC 4, ST 3).

    State-wise seats

    StateLok Sabha seats
    Uttar Pradesh80 (highest)
    Maharashtra48 (second)UPPSC

    • Uttar Pradesh has most seats in both Houses: Lok Sabha 80, Rajya Sabha 31.UPPSC ×2
    • Before 2000: Bihar 54 = Madhya Pradesh 40 + Assam 14; Jharkhand took 14.
    • Before 2014: Andhra Pradesh 42 = West Bengal 42; Telangana took 17.
    • Largest constituency by area: Ladakh; then Barmer, Kachchh, Arunachal East, Arunachal West.
    • Smallest by area: Chandni Chowk, Delhi.
    • UP constituency with most voters: Ghaziabad; among Amethi, Unnao, Lucknow, Baghpat it is Unnao.UPPSC

    Term, sessions, quorum

    • Normal term 5 years from first meeting; President can dissolve earlier.
    • Early dissolution [Art 85(2)(b)]: by President on advice of Prime Minister/Council of Ministers.
    • Article 83(2): in National Emergency Parliament can extend term, one year at a time.
    • Extension cannot go beyond 6 months after Emergency ends.
    • Member's qualifications (Article 84): Indian citizen, age 25 (Rajya Sabha 30), oath, other qualifications by law.
    • Article 85(1): President summons each House at time and place he thinks fit.
    • Gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months → at least two sessions a year.
    • No fixed minimum sitting days; Constitution does not name three sessions.
    • Usual sessions: Budget (Feb–May), Monsoon (July–Aug), Winter (Nov–Dec).
    • A sitting ends by adjournment, prorogation or dissolution.UPPSC
    • Adjournment and adjournment sine die (no date fixed): by Speaker.
    • Prorogation (ends a session) and dissolution (ends the House): by President, Article 85(2).UPPSC
    • Quorum (minimum members present) of each House = 1/10 of total members, Article 100(3).UPPSC ×4

    Elections to Lok Sabha

    • Article 326: elections on basis of adult suffrage (all adults vote).
    • Article 324: electoral rolls and elections under Election Commission, not President.UPPSC
    • Nomination: any citizen whose name is on electoral roll of any constituency [RPA 1951, sec 4(d)].
    • First past the post: most votes wins; 50% not needed.
    • Spending limit (Jan 2022): Lok Sabha Rs 95 lakh (was 70); small States 75 lakh (was 54).
    • Assembly limit: Rs 40 lakh (was 28); small States 28 lakh (was 20).
    • Security deposit since 2010: Lok Sabha general 25,000, SC/ST 12,500; Assembly 10,000 and 5,000.
    • Deposit lost if candidate gets not more than 1/6 of valid votes.
    • First general election: 25 Oct 1951 to 21 Feb 1952, for 489 seats.
    • First Lok Sabha first met 13 May 1952.
    • 5th Lok Sabha lasted about 6 years: 15 March 1971 to 18 Jan 1977.
    • 7th Lok Sabha election was in 1980; 9th 1989, 11th 1996, 13th 1999.UPPSC
    • 9th Lok Sabha: 2 Dec 1989 to 13 March 1991.
    • 12th: elected Feb–March 1998, formed 10 March 1998, dissolved 26 April 1999.
    • 13th: 10 Oct 1999 to 6 Feb 2004; did not complete 5 years.
    • 2024 election: 7 phases, 19 April to 1 June; schedule 16 March; result 4 June 2024.UPPSC
    • Malogam (Anjaw, Arunachal Pradesh): polling station for one voter, 2024.
    • Shompen tribe (Great Nicobar) voted first time in 2024, Andaman and Nicobar seat.
    • Leader of Lok Sabha = Prime Minister; if PM is from Rajya Sabha, he names a minister.
    • 14th Lok Sabha: PM Manmohan Singh (Rajya Sabha); Leader of House Pranab Mukherjee.

    Speaker: election and removal

    • Article 93: Lok Sabha chooses Speaker and Deputy Speaker from among its members.
    • Speaker to majority party, Deputy Speaker to Opposition: only convention, not in Constitution.
    • Speaker and Deputy Speaker take no oath of office.
    • Article 94 = vacation, resignation, removal; Article 95 = Deputy Speaker acting as Speaker.
    • Speaker resigns in writing to Deputy Speaker, and vice versa [Art 94(b)].UPPSC ×2
    • Removal: resolution of Lok Sabha passed by majority of all then members [Art 94(c)].UPPSC ×2
    • Removal resolution needs 14 days' notice.
    • Speaker vacates office if he stops being a member [Art 94(a)].
    • On dissolution Speaker stays till just before first meeting of new Lok Sabha.
    • Speaker need not resign from his party under the Constitution.
    • Article 96: during his removal resolution Speaker cannot preside, but can speak and take part.
    • During that resolution he votes in first instance, not on a tie.
    • 1954: first removal motion against Speaker (Mavlankar), by Vigneshwar Missir, J.B. Kripalani; rejected.

    Speaker: powers and names

    • Casting vote (deciding vote) used only in a tie.UPPSC
    • Article 100(1): Speaker/Chairman does not vote first; casting vote on equality of votes.UPPSC
    • Article 100(1): questions decided by majority of members present and voting.
    • Speaker presides over joint sitting [Art 118(4)]; President summons it (Art 108).
    • Speaker certifies a Money Bill [Art 110(4)].
    • Lok Sabha Secretariat works directly under Speaker.
    • Pro-tem (temporary) Speaker gives oath to new members; runs House till Speaker is chosen.UPPSC
    • President appoints one of the senior-most members of new Lok Sabha as pro-tem Speaker.UPPSC
    • First Speaker: Ganesh Vasudev Mavlankar (1952–56); died in office 27 Feb 1956.UPPSC
    • First Deputy Speaker: M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar; Speaker 1956–62.
    • First woman Speaker: Meira Kumar (2009–14).
    • Speaker of 18th Lok Sabha: Om Birla (since 2019).

    Chapter 22

    The Parliament (2)

    Lok Sabha Speaker and Deputy Speaker, then Rajya Sabha: make-up, term, special powers and seats.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Permanent House, never dissolved; one-third members retire every second year [Art 83(1)].PCS Pre ’14; PCS Mains ’11, ’12; RO/ARO Mains ’164 papers
    2. First woman Speaker: Meira Kumar, 15th Lok Sabha, June 2009–June 2014, chosen unopposed.PCS Pre ’23; PCS Mains ’07, ’083 papers
    3. First no-confidence motion against a Speaker: against Mavalankar, 15 Dec 1954; rejected 18 Dec 1954.PCS Pre ’00; Lower Sub (Spl) ’042 papers
    4. Rajya Sabha only: resolution to create new All India Service (Article 312).PCS Pre ’97, ’182 papers
    5. 249 · Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 present and voting, in national interestPCS Mains ’12, ’172 papers

    Speakers and Deputy Speaker

    • First Speaker of Lok Sabha: G.V. Mavalankar, 15 May 1952 till death 27 Feb 1956.UPPSC
    • Nehru called Mavalankar "Father of the Lok Sabha".
    • First no-confidence motion against a Speaker: against Mavalankar, 15 Dec 1954; rejected 18 Dec 1954.UPPSC ×2
    • Motion moved by Vigneshwar Missir and J.B. Kripalani with 21 opposition members.
    • First woman Speaker: Meira Kumar, 15th Lok Sabha, June 2009–June 2014, chosen unopposed.UPPSC ×3
    • Speakers: 11th P.A. Sangma; 12th G.M.C. Balayogi; 14th Somnath Chatterjee; 17th and 18th Om Birla.UPPSC
    • First tribal Speaker: P.A. Sangma, 23 May 1996, 11th Lok Sabha.UPPSC
    • Deputy Speaker's election date is fixed by the Speaker [Rule 8(1)].
    • Motion to choose Deputy Speaker: moved by one member, seconded by another [Rule 8(2)].
    • No rule that Deputy Speaker must be from opposition or ruling party.
    • Article 95: Deputy Speaker does Speaker's duties when office is vacant or Speaker absent.
    • While presiding, Deputy Speaker has Speaker's powers; no appeal against his rulings.
    • Presiding Deputy Speaker votes only on equality of votes (casting vote).UPPSC
    • Deputy Speakers: P.M. Sayeed (1999); 14th Charanjit Singh Atwal; 15th Karia Munda; 16th M. Thambidurai.
    • Post of Deputy Speaker vacant since May 2019.

    Secretariat, women, Opposition

    • Lok Sabha Secretariat is under direct control of the Speaker (Article 98).UPPSC
    • Article 98(3): President makes staff recruitment rules after consulting Speaker; Speaker issues appointment orders.
    • Fewest women in Lok Sabha: 1977 (19); most: 2019 (78).
    • 17th Lok Sabha: women over 14%; BJP 41, Congress 6; UP and West Bengal 11 each.
    • 106th Amendment 2023: one-third seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, Delhi Assembly.
    • Leader of Opposition recognised by Speaker only if party has 10% of House (about 54–55 seats).
    • Leader of Opposition first formally recognised in 1969.
    • Post vacant in 16th and 17th Lok Sabha; Rahul Gandhi in 18th.
    • First Lok Sabha: Congress 364 of 489 seats; Communist Party of India second with 16.

    Rajya Sabha: composition

    • Rajya Sabha = Council of States = Upper House; Article 80.
    • Maximum 250: up to 238 from States and UTs + 12 nominated.
    • President nominates 12 members from literature, science, art, social service.UPPSC
    • Present strength 245: States 225, UTs 8, nominated 12.
    • Only 3 of 8 UTs have seats: Delhi 3, Jammu & Kashmir 4, Puducherry 1.
    • State members elected by elected MLAs (Assembly members) [Art 80(4)].UPPSC
    • Method: proportional representation by single transferable vote.
    • Seats given by population; listed in Fourth Schedule.
    • Permanent House, never dissolved; one-third members retire every second year [Art 83(1)].UPPSC ×4
    • Term of a member = 6 years.UPPSC
    • Minimum age 30 years; must be Indian citizen.UPPSC
    • Since 2003 RPA amendment: candidate may be voter of any parliamentary constituency in India, not that State.
    • Member must not hold office of profit.
    • Nargis Dutt = first actress nominated to Rajya Sabha (1980).

    Chairman and Deputy Chairman

    • Vice-President = ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
    • When acting as President he gets President's salary, not Chairman's.
    • Rajya Sabha elects Deputy Chairman from its members; he resigns to Chairman.
    • Deputy Chairman removed by resolution of majority of all members; 14 days' notice.
    • Deputy Chairman acts when Chairman's post is vacant; has only a casting vote.
    • Chairman or Deputy Chairman cannot preside while his own removal resolution is considered.
    • Rajya Sabha also has a panel of Vice-Chairmen.
    • Leader of House: senior-most minister who is a Rajya Sabha member, named by PM.
    • Quorum = 1/10 of total members.
    • Attorney General can speak in both Houses.
    • Election disputes are decided by courts through election petition, not by Chief Election Commissioner.

    Parliament's power on State List

    ArticleWhen Parliament can make law on State subject
    249Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 present and voting, in national interestUPPSC ×2
    250During Proclamation of Emergency; law lapses 6 months after it ends
    252For two or more States by their consent; other States may adopt
    253To carry out international agreements and conference decisions
    • Article 249 resolution valid 1 year; can be renewed by new resolution.
    • After the resolution, Parliament (not Rajya Sabha alone) makes the law, for whole or part of India.UPPSC

    Powers of two Houses compared

    • Money Bill cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha; only in Lok Sabha, with President's recommendation (Article 109).UPPSC
    • Rajya Sabha must return Money Bill with recommendations within 14 days.
    • Lok Sabha may accept or reject any Rajya Sabha recommendation; not bound.UPPSC
    • Lok Sabha only: Money Bill introduction, its rejection/amendment, Council of Ministers' responsibility [Art 75(3)].UPPSC
    • Demands for Grants voted only by Lok Sabha [Art 113(2)]; Rajya Sabha can discuss Budget.
    • No-confidence motion only in Lok Sabha; defeat in Rajya Sabha does not remove government.
    • Both Houses: approve Emergency, impeach President (Article 61), amend Constitution (Article 368) equally.
    • Rajya Sabha only: resolution to create new All India Service (Article 312).UPPSC ×2
    • That resolution needs 2/3 of members present and voting, not of total membership.UPPSC
    • Article 312 covers All India Judicial Service too.
    • Schedules: 4th Rajya Sabha seats; 5th and 6th Scheduled/Tribal Areas; 7th Union-State powers; 8th 22 languages.

    Chapter 23

    The Parliament (3)

    How Parliament works: members, law-making, joint sitting, Money Bills, Budget and motions.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over joint sitting [Art 118(4)].PCS Pre ’14, ’23; PCS Mains ’05, ’06, ’10, ’13; RO/ARO Mains ’13; Lower Sub ’09; Lower Sub Mains ’139 papers
    2. Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (Article 79).PCS Pre ’12, ’14, ’17; PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’04, ’11; Lower Sub ’02; Lower Sub Mains ’138 papers
    3. Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days; else deemed passed by both Houses.PCS Pre ’92, ’06, ’16; RO/ARO Mains ’14; Lower Sub ’09; Lower Sub Mains ’136 papers
    4. Money Bill is introduced only in Lok Sabha, on President's recommendation; never in Rajya Sabha.PCS Pre ’12; PCS Mains ’11, ’15; UDA/LDA ’06; GIC ’105 papers
    5. Vice-President = ex-officio (by virtue of office) Chairman of Rajya Sabha; Articles 64, 89(1).PCS Pre ’90, ’93; PCS Mains ’11; UDA/LDA ’134 papers

    Rajya Sabha: seats and Chairman

    • Rajya Sabha seats: Karnataka 12, Gujarat 11, Odisha 10, Kerala 9.UPPSC
    • Andhra Pradesh 11, Telangana 7; Tamil Nadu 18; Maharashtra 19; Uttar Pradesh 31.
    • Small numbers: Himachal Pradesh 3, J&K 4 (now UT), Chhattisgarh 5, Jharkhand 6.UPPSC ×2
    • Union Territories are represented in both Houses; Rajya Sabha: Delhi 3, J&K 4, Puducherry 1.UPPSC
    • Vice-President = ex-officio (by virtue of office) Chairman of Rajya Sabha; Articles 64, 89(1).UPPSC ×4
    • Vice-President is not a member of Rajya Sabha; so it is presided by a non-member.UPPSC ×3
    • An MP elected Vice-President vacates his seat on taking office.
    • Deputy Chairman is a Rajya Sabha member, elected by it.
    • Nominated MPs vote in Vice-President's election, not in President's election (Article 54).
    • Rajya Sabha first formed 3 April 1952; idea from Montague-Chelmsford Reforms 1919.UPPSC
    • First Amendment 1951 passed before Rajya Sabha existed.
    • Two consecutive terms as Chairman: S. Radhakrishnan (1952–62), Hamid Ansari (2007–17).
    • Present Chairman: Vice-President C.P. Radhakrishnan.
    • 2024 nominations: Satnam Singh Sandhu (30 Jan), Sudha Murty (8 March, the 12th nominated member).
    • A minister who is a Rajya Sabha member can take part in Lok Sabha debates.
    • No bar on a nominated member becoming minister.

    Parliament: parts and sessions

    • Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (Article 79).UPPSC ×8
    • Vice-President is not a part of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Article 59(1): President is not a member of either House, yet integral part of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Article 87: President addresses both Houses together at first session after each general election and each year; tells causes of summons.UPPSC
    • Six months' maximum gap between sessions → Parliament must meet at least twice a year [Art 85(1)].UPPSC
    • Officers of Parliament: Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Secretary-General of Lok Sabha, Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×2
    • Westminster (British) model of parliamentary government; power to amend Constitution under Article 368.
    • Parliament's Secretariat is independent of government; Parliament controls administration through committees.
    • Estimates Committee: largest financial committee, 30 members, all from Lok Sabha.
    • MLAs vote in both Lok Sabha (as citizens) and Rajya Sabha elections.

    Members: vacancy and privileges

    • Article 101(4): seat may be declared vacant if member absent 60 days without permission.UPPSC
    • The 60 days exclude prorogation or adjournment of over 4 days in a row.
    • First member so disqualified: Barjinder Singh Hamdard, Rajya Sabha (Punjab), 2000.UPPSC
    • Article 101(2): MP also elected to State Legislature must resign that seat in 14 days, or loses Parliament seat.
    • Article 102(1)(a): holding an office of profit (paid government post) disqualifies an MP.
    • "Office of profit" is not defined in Constitution or RPA 1951.
    • Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act 1959 exempts certain offices; amended five times.
    • Which offices are exempt: Parliament by law (States: State Legislature, Article 191).
    • Whether a member is disqualified: President on Election Commission's advice (Art 103); Governor in States (Art 192).UPPSC ×2
    • Article 105: powers, privileges and immunities of Houses, members, committees.
    • Collective privileges: bar publishing proceedings, exclude strangers, regulate own procedure, punish breach of privilege or contempt.
    • Also collective: no arrest inside House without Chair's leave; right to be told of member's arrest.
    • Freedom from attendance as witness = individual privilege, not collective.UPPSC
    • Article 122: courts cannot inquire into proceedings of Parliament.UPPSC
    • Privilege motion against a minister: for hiding facts or giving distorted facts.
    • Article 120(1): business in Hindi or English; Chair may allow member's mother tongue.

    Parliament's law-making reach

    • Parliament can legislate for Union, territory of India, and Indian subjects and their property anywhere.UPPSC
    ArticlePower on State List or beyond
    248Residuary power: subjects in no List → Parliament onlyUPPSC
    249Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 majority, national interest
    250During Proclamation of Emergency
    252Two or more States pass resolutions asking for itUPPSC
    253To give effect to international agreements, treaties, conference decisionsUPPSC ×3
    • Article 253 law needs no consent of any State.UPPSC
    • Only these four routes open State List: national interest, Emergency, States' consent, treaties.UPPSC

    House terms and Zero Hour

    • Yielding the floor: Speaker stops one member and lets another speak.
    • Crossing the floor: member leaves his party for another.
    • Interpellation: asking a government official to explain an act or policy.
    • Zero Hour: Indian innovation, from early 1960s; not in the Rules.UPPSC
    • Zero Hour lasts at most one hour.UPPSC
    • Timing: Lok Sabha 12 noon–1 pm (after Question Hour); Rajya Sabha 11 am–12 noon (before it).UPPSC ×2

    Check Key for Zero Hour time accepts both 11–12 and 12–1, as the two Houses differ.

    • Question Hour: Lok Sabha 11 am–12 noon; Rajya Sabha 12 noon–1 pm since 2014.
    • Bill stages: first reading = introduction; second = general discussion, then clause-by-clause; third = final passing.
    • General discussion on a Bill happens in the second reading.UPPSC
    • Private member's Bill = Bill by any member who is not a minister; about a dozen passed.
    • Ordinary Bill can start in either House.

    Joint sitting and lapse of Bills

    • Article 108: President summons joint sitting to end deadlock on a Bill; not Article 109.UPPSC ×2
    • Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over joint sitting [Art 118(4)].UPPSC ×9
    • If Speaker absent: Deputy Speaker → Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha → person chosen by members present.
    • Joint sitting only for ordinary Bills (and non-money financial Bills); never Money or Constitution Amendment Bills.UPPSC ×2
    • Bill passes by simple majority of members of both Houses present and voting [Art 108(4)].
    • Joint sitting quorum = 1/10 of total members of both Houses.
    • Three joint sittings so far: Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1978, Prevention of Terrorism Bill 2002.
    • First joint sitting was on the Dowry Prohibition Bill.UPPSC
    • Joint sitting still held if Lok Sabha dissolves after President notified it [Art 108(5)].
    • On Lok Sabha dissolution, lapse: Bills pending in Lok Sabha; Bills passed by it, pending in Rajya Sabha [Art 107(5)].
    • No lapse: Bill pending in Rajya Sabha, not passed by Lok Sabha [Art 107(4)].
    • Prorogation never lapses a Bill [Art 107(3)].

    Funds and charged expenditure

    ArticleSubject
    265No tax levied or collected without authority of lawUPPSC
    266Consolidated Fund and Public Account of India and States
    267Contingency FundUPPSC
    300Suits and proceedings
    • Consolidated Fund: all revenues, loans raised, loan repayments received.
    • No one can draw from Consolidated Fund without Parliament's authorisation (Appropriation, Article 114).UPPSC
    • Public Account payments need no Parliament authorisation; executive controls it.
    • Contingency Fund: at President's disposal for unforeseen spending; he spends before Parliament's authorisation.UPPSC
    • Charged expenditure [Art 112(3)]: discussed, not voted.
    • Charged: President's pay and office; Chairman, Deputy Chairman, Speaker, Deputy Speaker salaries; debt charges.
    • Charged: Supreme Court judges' pay and pensions; High Court and Federal Court judges' pensions; CAG's pay and pension; court decrees and awards.
    • Not charged: salary and pension of Election Commission members.UPPSC
    • Not charged: Vice-President's salary as such; he is paid as Rajya Sabha Chairman.UPPSC
    • Not charged: Prime Minister's salary and allowances.UPPSC

    Money Bill and Financial Bills

    ArticleSubject
    109Special procedure for Money Bills
    110Definition of Money BillUPPSC ×2
    111Assent to Bills
    117(1)Financial Bill (I): Article 110 matters plus others
    117(3)Financial Bill (II): spending from Consolidated Fund
    • Money Bill covers only: tax (impose, abolish, remit, alter, regulate); government borrowing and guarantees.
    • Also: custody of, payment into, withdrawal from Consolidated or Contingency Fund; appropriation from Consolidated Fund.
    • Also: declaring expenditure as charged; receipt, custody, issue of public money; audit of Union or State accounts; incidental matters.
    • Fines or penalties are not Money Bill matters.UPPSC
    • Speaker decides if a Bill is a Money Bill; decision final [Art 110(3)]; he certifies it.UPPSC ×3
    • Money Bill is introduced only in Lok Sabha, on President's recommendation; never in Rajya Sabha.UPPSC ×5
    • Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days; else deemed passed by both Houses.UPPSC ×6
    • Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject; Lok Sabha accepts or rejects its recommendations, then Bill is deemed passed.UPPSC
    • President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
    • Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill; not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.
    • Financial Bill (I): only in Lok Sabha, President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha can amend or reject; joint sitting possible.
    • Bill only involving expenditure [Art 117(3)]: can start in either House; President's recommendation needed for consideration.UPPSC
    • All-India Services resolution starts only in Rajya Sabha.

    Budget procedure

    • Article 112: Annual Financial Statement = estimated receipts and spending for the year (1 April–31 March).
    • Word "Budget" is not in the Constitution.UPPSC
    • President causes it to be laid; Finance Minister lays it on President's behalf.
    • Department of Economic Affairs (Finance Ministry) prepares the Budget.
    • Article 113: estimates go to Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants; only on President's recommendation.
    • Lok Sabha may pass, refuse or reduce a demand; 102 demands in Budget 2025-26.
    • Budget stages: presentation, general discussion, committee scrutiny, voting on demands, Appropriation Bill, Finance Bill.
    • Normal financial legislation: presentation, discussion, Appropriation Bill, Finance Bill; Vote on Account not a stage.UPPSC ×2
    • Articles: 114 Appropriation Bill; 115 supplementary grants; 116 votes on account, votes of credit, exceptional grants.
    • Vote on Account (Article 116): money from Consolidated Fund for a short period, not the whole year's demands.UPPSC ×2
    • Needed when regular Budget cannot be passed in time.UPPSC
    • Interim Budget has both receipts and expenditure; Vote on Account only expenditure.
    • Economic Survey is presented before the Budget every year.UPPSC
    • If Lok Sabha does not pass the Budget, PM submits Council of Ministers' resignation.
    • President's prior sanction needed for Bills on: new State, altering State boundaries, taxation affecting States, Money Bill.UPPSC

    Motions and questions

    • Cut motion relates to the Budget: Lok Sabha member's move to reduce a demand for grant.UPPSC
    • Policy cut: demand reduced to Re 1; Economy cut: by a stated amount; Token cut: by Rs 100.
    • Censure motion: strong disapproval of government policy; must state reasons; differs from no-confidence motion.
    • Calling Attention: Indian idea; member draws minister's attention to urgent public matter; no censure part.
    • Calling Attention notices narrowed the scope of the Adjournment Motion.UPPSC
    • Adjournment motion: draws House's attention to urgent matter of public importance.
    • Question Hour = first hour of sitting.
    • Starred question: oral answer, supplementaries allowed; 20 a day.
    • Unstarred question: written answer, no supplementaries.
    • Short notice question: urgent matter, shorter notice, supplementaries allowed.

    House procedure leftovers

    • Starred question: oral answer, marked with asterisk (*); supplementary questions allowed; only 20 listed per day.
    • Unstarred question: written answer; no supplementary questions.
    • Adjournment motion: to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
    • Rule 184 (Lok Sabha): discussion followed by voting; ruling party may lose, so governments avoid it.UPPSC ×2
    • Rule 377: matters that fit no other rule; written notice to Secretary-General; Speaker's consent needed.
    • Rule 377 matters per day raised from 20 to 30 in 2015.
    • Closure motion = cut short a debate; four kinds; Guillotine is one.
    • Guillotine: undiscussed clauses put to vote with discussed ones when allotted time ends.
    • Rajya Sabha can hold a Financial Bill like an ordinary Bill; a Money Bill only 14 days.UPPSC
    • 44th Amendment 1978: Right to Property no longer Fundamental Right; legal right under Article 300-A.

    Chapter 24

    Parliamentary Committees

    How Parliament works through rules, its secretariat and committees, mainly the three financial committees.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. PAC chairman is appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker from its members.PCS Pre ’14; Lower Sub ’04; Lower Sub Mains ’13; UDA/LDA ’064 papers
    2. PAC presents its report to Lok Sabha (Parliament); to Speaker when House not in session.PCS Pre ’25; PCS Mains ’15; Lower Sub ’023 papers
    3. All 30 are from Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha has no representation.PCS Pre ’10; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; PCS Mains ’103 papers
    4. Estimates Committee: 30 members, largest committee of Parliament; first formed 1950.PCS Pre ’20; PCS Mains ’172 papers
    5. Article 98(2): Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and service conditions of secretariat staff.PCS Pre ’231 paper

    Parliament: secretariat and history

    • Separate secretariat idea: Vithalbhai J. Patel, January 1926.
    • Article 98(1): each House has separate secretarial staff, independent of Government; common posts allowed.
    • Article 98(2): Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and service conditions of secretariat staff.UPPSC
    • Parliament's sovereignty is limited by judicial review; laws cannot violate Basic Structure.UPPSC
    • Parliament constituted 13 May 1952; Golden Jubilee on 13 May 2002.UPPSC
    • New Parliament building: architect Bimal Patel; inaugurated by PM Modi on 28 May 2023.
    • Old building: designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and Sir Herbert Baker.
    • Vitthalbhai Patel: first elected Speaker of Central Legislative Assembly, 24 August 1925 to 28 April 1930.UPPSC
    • Indian Parliamentary Group: autonomous body, formed 1949 (motion of 16 August 1948).
    • Group open to MPs and ex-MPs; Lok Sabha Speaker = ex-officio President.
    • It is the National Group of Inter-Parliamentary Union and India branch of Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.

    Types of committees

    • Committees are elected or appointed by the House, or nominated by Speaker/Chairman; report to House or presiding officer.
    • Parliament controls administration through its committees.
    • Standing committees = permanent; Ad hoc = temporary, end when task is done.
    • Six kinds of standing committees: Financial; Department-related (24); Enquiry; Scrutiny and Control; Day-to-day business; Housekeeping/Service.
    • Three financial committees: Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings.UPPSC
    • Most joint committees take Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members in ratio 2:1.UPPSC
    • 24 Department-related Standing Committees: 16 under Lok Sabha, 8 under Rajya Sabha.
    • Enquiry committees: Petitions, Privileges, Ethics.
    • Petitions Committee: Lok Sabha 15 members, Rajya Sabha 10; no minister; examines petitions and representations.
    CommitteeType
    Public Accounts CommitteeFinancial
    Committee on PetitionsFunctional
    Joint Committee on Stock Market ScamAd hoc
    Departmental committeesStandingUPPSC
    • CAG (Article 148) is not a committee tool of Parliament's control over spending.
    • Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs works under Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs; its minister nominates MPs to government bodies.

    Public Accounts Committee

    • PAC: 22 members = 15 Lok Sabha + up to 7 Rajya Sabha; no outsiders.UPPSC
    • Lok Sabha members elected yearly by proportional representation, single transferable vote; term one year.
    • First set up in 1921 under Government of India Act 1919.
    • Main work: examine CAG's audit reports, appropriation and finance accounts.UPPSC
    • CAG reports are laid before Parliament by the President; CAG assists the PAC.
    • PAC presents its report to Lok Sabha (Parliament); to Speaker when House not in session.UPPSC ×3
    • PAC chairman is appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker from its members.UPPSC ×4
    • Since 1967-68 the chairman is from the opposition; till 1966-67 from ruling party.
    • A minister cannot be a PAC member.

    Estimates and Undertakings committees

    • Estimates Committee: 30 members, largest committee of Parliament; first formed 1950.UPPSC ×2
    • All 30 are from Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha has no representation.UPPSC ×3
    • Members elected every year; term one year; chairman appointed by Speaker.UPPSC
    • Work: suggest alternative policies for efficiency and economy in administration.
    • Committee on Public Undertakings: 22 members = 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha; one-year term; no minister.
    • It examines reports and accounts of public undertakings, CAG reports on them, and disinvestment.

    More on committees

    • Financial committees of Parliament: Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings.UPPSC
    • Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances of MPs is a Housekeeping committee, not financial.
    • CAG audit reports are examined by Public Accounts Committee; Public Undertakings Committee examines CAG reports on PSUs.UPPSC

    Check Key gives Public Undertakings Committee; the explanation accepts both it and Public Accounts Committee.

    • Department-related Standing Committees: 17 set up in 1993 (Rules Committee advice); raised to 24 in 2004.
    • Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs is also a standing committee.
    • No parliamentary committee exists for welfare of minorities; a Minority Commission exists instead.UPPSC
    • Committee on Government Assurances: checks whether ministers' promises in the House are carried out.
    • Committee on Subordinate Legislation: checks whether executive uses delegated rule-making power properly.
    • Subordinate Legislation Committee: 15 members in each House; nominated by Speaker/Chairman; no ministers.
    • Rules Committee: procedure of the House; suggests changes in Rules.
    • Business Advisory Committee: fixes programme and time-table of the House.
    • Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee, 1997: first in any Indian legislature.
    • Lok Sabha Ethics Committee: first formed 16 May 2000 by Speaker G.M.C. Balayogi; ad hoc till 2015.
    • Rule 233A: any person or member may complain; a person's complaint must be forwarded by a member.
    • Ethics Committee cannot take up a sub-judice (pending in court) matter.
    • Health and Family Welfare committee is under Rajya Sabha; Labour, Urban Development, Social Justice under Lok Sabha.
    • Consultative Committees of MPs for Railway Zones are formed by Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs.
    • Chairpersons 2024-25: PAC K.C. Venugopal; Estimates Sanjay Jaiswal; Public Undertakings Baijayant Panda.
    • 2024-25: OBC Welfare committee Ganesh Singh; SC/ST Welfare committee Faggan Singh Kulaste.
    • 2G spectrum Joint Parliamentary Committee: 30 members = 20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha.UPPSC
    • 2G JPC chairman: P.C. Chacko; report given to Speaker Meira Kumar.UPPSC
    • Independent regulators (telecom, insurance, electricity) are reviewed by Department-related Standing Committees and ad hoc committees.

    The Parliamentary Act

    Important Acts of Parliament: years, key sections and authorities.

    • Chronological order: Lex Loci → Bengal Tenancy → Age of Consent → Indian Universities Act.UPPSC
    • Women's reservation in urban local bodies came by 74th Amendment, not 73rd.UPPSC
    • Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005: in force 26 October 2006.UPPSC
    • MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) 1971, repealed 1977: a security law, not a social Act.UPPSC

    • PESA 1996: self-rule through gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas.
    • Aadhaar Act 2016 upheld; authentication data kept at most 6 months; private companies cannot use it.
    • Aadhaar may be required for welfare schemes paid from Consolidated Fund of India; not for insurance.

    Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955

    • Punishes preaching and practice of untouchability; extends to whole of India (Section 1(2)).
    • All offences are cognizable (police can arrest without warrant), summarily triable, non-compoundable (Section 15).
    • Tried by Judicial Magistrate First Class; Metropolitan Magistrate in metros.

    • Central ministries concerned: Home Affairs (criminal offences), Social Justice (SCs), Tribal Affairs (STs); states implement.

    SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989

    • President's assent 11 September 1989; in force 30 January 1990; 23 sections.

    • Special Court = a Court of Session named by State Government with concurrence of High Court Chief Justice.
    • Special Court can remove a person, forfeit property, take measurements and photographs; cannot impose collective fine or order non-police investigation.
    • Appeal lies to High Court on both facts and law.
    • Witchcraft allegation causing harm to SC/ST member: jail 6 months to 5 years, with fine.
    • 1995 Rules: investigation by officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police (Rule 7).
    • 1995 Rules: Rule 17 district vigilance and monitoring committee (by District Magistrate); Rule 18 material for annual report.
    • Investigation was 30 days; 2016 Rules: investigation plus charge-sheet within 60 days.

    Right to Information Act 2005

    • RTI Act passed in 2005: Lok Sabha 11 May, Rajya Sabha 12 May.UPPSC
    • President Kalam's assent 15 June 2005; in force 12 October 2005 (after 120 days).UPPSC
    • RTI is a legal right.UPPSC
    • Supreme Court reads RTI into freedom of expression (Article 19), so it is also a fundamental right.UPPSC
    • Raj Narain vs State of Uttar Pradesh 1976: right to information under Article 19.
    • Aim: access to information held by public authorities; transparency, accountability, less corruption, empowered citizens.
    • Section 6(2): applicant need not give any reason.
    • Madras High Court once said the applicant should state the reason.UPPSC
    • MKSS (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan), 1990, Aruna Roy and Nikhil Dey: movement behind RTI.UPPSC
    • Namit Sharma vs Union of India 2012 relates to RTI Act.UPPSC
    • RTI raised bureaucracy's sense of responsibility, but has miles to go; two separate truths.UPPSC
    • Central Information Commission formed 12 October 2005; covers central public authorities.
    • Sections: 12 constitution of CIC; 18 powers; 19 appeal; 20 penalty (by Central or State Commission); 25 annual report.
    • 2019 Amendment: tenure set by Central Government; now 3 years or age 65 (earlier 5 years).
    • State Commissioners: appointed by Governor; panel = Chief Minister (chair), Opposition Leader in Assembly, one Cabinet Minister.
    • State Commission: Chief plus up to 10 Commissioners; MPs and MLAs not eligible.
    • RTI now applies in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
    • Citizen Charter has nine basic elements; inspection of agency's work is not one.

    Forest, environment, disaster laws

    • Forest Rights Act 2006: nodal agency Ministry of Tribal Affairs; Gram Sabha starts rights process (Section 6(1)).
    • National Green Tribunal: set up 18 October 2010 under NGT Act 2010.UPPSC
    • NGT rests on right to healthy environment under Article 21; follows natural justice, not Civil Procedure Code.
    • NGT can review its decisions; appeal to Supreme Court within 90 days.
    • Disaster Management Act passed 2005; assent 23 December 2005; 11 chapters, 79 sections.UPPSC
    • NDMA chairman = Prime Minister (ex-officio); up to 9 members; 5-year tenure.UPPSC
    • COVID lockdown powers came from Disaster Management Act 2005 and Epidemic Diseases Act 1897.UPPSC

    • Aadhaar: 12-digit random number from UIDAI for residents; enrolment voluntary and free.
    • Aadhaar Act 2016, Section 9: proof of identity only, not of citizenship or domicile.
    • Section 23(g): issuing authority can deactivate or omit an Aadhaar number.

    • State Food Commission: Section 16, National Food Security Act 2013.

    Chapter 26

    The Supreme Court

    The Supreme Court: judges, jurisdiction, judicial review, PIL, key cases and rulings.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Constitutional appeals: Article 132 read with Article 134A (certificate for appeal).PCS Pre ’01; PCS Mains ’04; UDA/LDA ’023 papers
    2. Article 137: Supreme Court can review and change its own judgment or order.PCS Mains ’05, ’09, ’113 papers
    3. Basic structure doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala 1973.PCS Pre ’14; PCS Mains ’12; Lower Sub Mains ’133 papers
    4. Judge resigns by writing to the President.PCS Pre ’14, ’232 papers
    5. Article 126: Acting Chief Justice is appointed by the President.PCS Pre ’00; UDA/LDA ’012 papers

    Setting up and strength

    • Single integrated judiciary, Supreme Court at top; taken from Government of India Act 1935.
    • Supreme Court inaugurated 28 January 1950; replaced the Federal Court; created by the Constitution.
    • Articles 124–147, Part V, Chapter IV deal with Supreme Court; Article 124 sets it up.
    • Sapru Committee 1945 (set up by Non-Party Conference, November 1944): basis of judge-appointment provisions.
    • Constituent Assembly's ad hoc committee on Supreme Court: S. Varadachariar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, B.L. Mitter, K.M. Munshi, B.N. Rau; report 21 May 1947.
    • Parliament can increase the number of judges.
    YearJudges including Chief Justice
    19508
    195611

    198626
    200931
    201934
    • Now: Chief Justice of India (CJI) plus up to 33 judges.

    Judges: appointment to removal

    • Article 124(2): President appoints judges by warrant; CJI always consulted for other judges.
    • Qualifications (Article 124(3)): citizen; High Court judge 5 years, or High Court advocate 10 years, or distinguished jurist.
    • No minimum age is fixed; oath is taken before the President.
    • Oath "uphold Sovereignty and Integrity, Constitution and Law" (Third Schedule): for CJI and judges, also CAG.UPPSC
    • Third Schedule has 10 forms of oath.
    • Collegium = CJI + 4 senior-most judges; recommends judges.UPPSC
    • Collegium adopted 1993 (Second Judges Case: consultation = concurrence); then CJI + 2 judges; widened to 4 in 1998.
    • Collegium grew from Three Judges Cases, not from any law of Parliament; majority view prevails.
    • NJAC (99th Amendment 2014) was to replace collegium; struck down by Supreme Court in 2015.
    • NJAC: CJI (chair), 2 senior judges, Law Minister, 2 eminent persons chosen by PM, CJI and Opposition Leader.
    • Second Administrative Reforms Commission: appoint higher judges jointly by Executive, Legislature and Chief Justice.UPPSC
    • Judge resigns by writing to the President.UPPSC ×2
    • Supreme Court judges retire at 65; High Court judges at 62.UPPSC
    • Article 125: salaries fixed by Parliament by law; till then as in Second Schedule.UPPSC
    • Salaries and court expenses are charged on Consolidated Fund of India; High Court expenses on State fund.
    • CJI appoints officers and staff of the Supreme Court.
    • Article 124(7): retired Supreme Court judge cannot practise in any court or authority in India.UPPSC
    • Article 220: retired permanent High Court judge may practise only in Supreme Court and other High Courts.
    • Removal (Article 124(4)): President's order after address by each House in same session.
    • Address needs majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.
    • Grounds: proved misbehaviour or incapacity; Constitution does not define them.
    • Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968 gives the removal procedure; Speaker may reject the motion.
    • Constitution uses "removal" for judges; "impeachment" only for President.
    • Article 126: Acting Chief Justice is appointed by the President.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 127: ad hoc judge only in Supreme Court, when quorum is lacking; no additional judges there.UPPSC ×2
    • Ad hoc judge = High Court judge named by CJI, with President's consent, after consulting that High Court's Chief Justice.
    • Article 128: CJI, with President's consent, may ask a retired judge to sit in the Supreme Court.

    Seat, record and jurisdiction

    • Article 130: Court sits in Delhi, or elsewhere as CJI decides with President's approval.UPPSC
    • Constitution Bench: at least 5 judges for questions of interpreting the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • Benches usually have odd numbers of judges.
    • Article 129: Supreme Court is a Court of Record, not Article 124.UPPSC
    • Court of Record: decisions recorded for ever, have evidence value, cannot be questioned in any court; can punish contempt.UPPSC
    • Both Supreme Court (Article 129) and High Courts (Article 215) are Courts of Record.UPPSC
    • Contempt of Courts Act 1971 followed H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961); it defines contempt, Constitution does not.
    • Section 2(b): wilful disobedience of court order = civil contempt; M.L. Sachdev vs Union of India.
    • Supreme Court has original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 131, original (heard first here) and exclusive: Centre vs State, or State vs State disputes on a legal right.
    • Article 131 does not cover disputes from pre-Constitution treaties and agreements.
    • Articles 132–136: appellate jurisdiction; all cases on interpreting the Constitution come under it.UPPSC
    • Constitutional appeals: Article 132 read with Article 134A (certificate for appeal).UPPSC ×3
    • Article 133: civil appeals; Article 134: criminal appeals; Article 136: special leave to appeal.
    • Under Article 136 the Court can quash orders of quasi-judicial tribunals.
    • Court-martial matters can reach Supreme Court (Armed Forces Tribunal Act 2007).
    • Article 137: Supreme Court can review and change its own judgment or order.UPPSC ×3
    • A High Court, as court of record, can also review its judgments.
    • Article 138: Parliament may by law enlarge jurisdiction on Union List matters.
    • Article 139A: Supreme Court can transfer or withdraw cases from High Courts.
    • Article 141: Supreme Court's law binds all courts in India.
    • Article 142: orders for complete justice; ordinary laws cannot limit this power.
    • Curative petition: from Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra 2002; filed under Article 142.UPPSC
    • Article 143: only the President can seek Supreme Court's advisory opinion.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 143(1): question of law or fact of public importance, such as judges' appointment and transfer.UPPSC
    • Advice is on issues of law or fact of public importance; given only when asked.UPPSC
    • Under 143(1) Court may refuse; on pre-Constitution treaties (143(2)) it must give opinion.
    • Advisory reference heard by 5-judge bench; opinion not binding on government.
    • 2002: President Kalam used Article 143 on deferring Gujarat Assembly elections.
    • Fundamental Rights are enforced by both Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226).UPPSC ×2
    • Writ power is not exclusive to Supreme Court; High Court writ power is wider.UPPSC
    • Article 32: Supreme Court protects Fundamental Rights by writs.UPPSC
    • TDSAT (telecom tribunal, set up 2000): appeals to Supreme Court; cyber matters to High Court.UPPSC

    Judicial review and basic structure

    • Judicial review = courts can strike down any law or order that conflicts with the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Both Supreme Court and High Courts have this power.UPPSC
    • Judicial review exists in India and USA; not in UK, where Parliament is supreme.UPPSC
    • Began in USA: Marbury vs Madison 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall.
    • Articles for judicial review: 13, 32, 136, 137, 226, 227; based on "procedure established by law".
    • Scope of judicial review is limited in India; borrowed Constitution is not the reason.UPPSC
    • 42nd Amendment barred High Courts from judging central laws; 43rd Amendment 1977 restored it.
    • High Courts too can judge validity of central laws; Supreme Court has no exclusive power.UPPSC

    Check Key (d) is printed; the note adds that UPPSC took (a) as correct.

    • Supreme Court = guardian (custodian) and final interpreter of the Constitution.UPPSC
    • Basic structure doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala 1973.UPPSC ×3
    • That bench: 13 judges, largest ever, decided 7:6; Parliament cannot damage basic structure under Article 368.
    • Basic structure comes from judicial interpretation, not the text.UPPSC
    • Articles 32, 226 and 227 declared inviolable basic structure.UPPSC
    • Minerva Mills 1980 confirmed the doctrine; judicial review itself is basic structure.
    • Second largest bench: 11 judges, Golaknath vs State of Punjab 1967.UPPSC
    • Golaknath: "Fundamental Rights enable a man to chalk out his life in the manner he likes best".UPPSC
    • An amendment removing equality before law from Part III can be struck down (Article 13(2)).
    • Due process of law ≈ natural justice; accepted in Maneka Gandhi case.
    • Natural justice: no one a judge in own cause; hear the other side.
    • Equal protection of laws from USA; equality before law from Britain (Article 14).

    • Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act 1983 struck down on 13 July 2005 under Article 355.UPPSC

    Judges: firsts and facts

    • Shortest-serving CJI: Kamal Narain Singh, 25 November to 12 December 1991.
    • Longest-serving CJI: Y.V. Chandrachud, 16th CJI, 22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985; appointed by Neelam Sanjiva Reddy.
    • CJI order: K.G. Balakrishnan, S.H. Kapadia; later H.L. Dattu, T.S. Thakur, J.S. Khehar, Dipak Misra, Ranjan Gogoi, S.A. Bobde, N.V. Ramana, U.U. Lalit, D.Y. Chandrachud.
    • Sanjiv Khanna: CJI from 11 November 2024 (as printed, "till now").
    • A.S. Anand: 29th CJI, 1998–2001; R.C. Lahoti: 35th CJI, 2004–2005.
    • Fathima Beevi: first woman Supreme Court judge (1989), first Muslim woman in higher judiciary; Governor of Tamil Nadu 1997–2001; died 23 November 2023.UPPSC
    • Women judges in order: Fathima Beevi, Sujata Manohar, Ruma Pal, Gyan Sudha Misra (30 April 2010), Ranjana Desai.UPPSC
    • L. Nageswara Rao: 7th person raised directly from the Bar, 13 May 2016; never a High Court judge.UPPSC
    • N. Kotiswar Singh: Chief Justice of J&K and Ladakh High Court before Supreme Court, July 2024.
    • Justice Manmohan (Delhi High Court Chief Justice) joined Supreme Court on 5 December 2024.

    Public Interest Litigation

    • PIL (Public Interest Litigation) began by judicial initiative, not by law or amendment.UPPSC
    • First PIL case: Hussainara Khatoon vs State of Bihar 1979, petition by Kapila Hingorani.
    • CJI then was Y.V. Chandrachud; P.N. Bhagwati became 17th CJI (12 July 1985 to 20 December 1986).
    • Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer pioneered PIL; Iyer was never CJI.
    • PIL fits Article 39A (equal justice); can be filed in High Courts and Supreme Court.
    • PIL lets public-minded citizens seek justice for those who cannot reach court.UPPSC
    • PIL widened locus standi (right to file); it helps weaker sections but is not essential for rule of law.UPPSC
    • PIL concept originated in the United States; first legal aid office, New York 1876.UPPSC
    • Judicial activism in India is linked to PIL; began mid-1970s.UPPSC
    • Justice A.S. Anand: judicial activism should not become "judicial adventurism".

    Rulings and court language

    • Supreme Court (Justice M.B. Shah), 23 September 2003: preferring women as girls' college principal is valid.UPPSC
    • Vishakha guidelines 1997 replaced by Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013.
    • Shayara Bano 2017: Triple Talaq (Talaq-e-Biddat) unconstitutional; violates Article 14.
    • Supreme Court called CBI a "caged parrot" in Coal Gate scam case.UPPSC
    • Homosexuality judgment relates to Section 377 of IPC.UPPSC
    • Article 348(1)(a): all proceedings in Supreme Court and High Courts in English.UPPSC
