    Chapter 27

    The Governor

    The Governor: appointment, term, powers and immunity.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 155: Governor appointed by the President by warrant; it is not about removal.PCS Pre ’12, ’15, ’243 papers
    2. Elected Governor plan dropped: extra election cost, clash with Chief Minister, unsuited to parliamentary system.PCS Pre ’03; PCS Mains ’04; UDA/LDA ’023 papers
    3. Article 159: oath before Chief Justice of High Court, or senior-most judge; not in Third Schedule.PCS Mains ’14; Lower Sub Mains ’132 papers
    4. Article 156(1): holds office during pleasure of the President; responsible to President.PCS Pre ’92; PCS Mains ’042 papers
    5. Article 156(3): normal term five years; continues till successor joins.PCS Mains ’04; GIC ’102 papers

    Appointment, term and conditions

    • Articles 153–167, Part VI: State government; Governor = executive and constitutional head of State.
    • Article 153: a Governor for each State; Article 154: State executive power vests in Governor.
    • 7th Amendment 1956: same person may be Governor of two or more States.UPPSC
    • Article 155: Governor appointed by the President by warrant; it is not about removal.UPPSC ×3
    • Elected Governor plan dropped: extra election cost, clash with Chief Minister, unsuited to parliamentary system.UPPSC ×3
    • Ambedkar and Nehru favoured nominated Governor; Krishnamachari, B.G. Kher, Pant favoured election.
    • Article 157 qualifications: citizen of India (not by birth), completed 35 years.UPPSC
    • Article 158: Governor cannot be member of any House; emoluments cannot be reduced during term.
    • Article 158(3A): for two or more States, President decides how emoluments are shared.UPPSC
    • Article 159: oath before Chief Justice of High Court, or senior-most judge; not in Third Schedule.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 156(1): holds office during pleasure of the President; responsible to President.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 156(3): normal term five years; continues till successor joins.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 156(2): resigns by writing to the President.
    • No removal procedure in Constitution; State Legislature cannot remove the Governor.UPPSC ×2
    • Salary and office expenses charged on Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 202(3)(a)).
    • Sarojini Naidu: first woman Governor, United Provinces, 15 August 1947 to 2 March 1949.

    J&K, Rajpramukh, Union Territories

    • J&K head renamed from Sadar-e-Riyasat to Governor in 1965 by 6th Amendment of J&K Constitution.UPPSC
    • J&K Reorganisation Act 2019: UT of J&K (with legislature), UT of Ladakh (without).
    • First Lt. Governors: J&K Girish Chandra Murmu; Ladakh Radha Krishna Mathur (31 October 2019).
    • Manoj Sinha: J&K Lt. Governor from 7 August 2020; Kavinder Gupta: Ladakh from July 2025.
    • Rajpramukh post ended by 7th Amendment, 1 November 1956, on States Reorganisation Commission advice.
    • States Reorganisation Commission, December 1953: Fazal Ali, K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru.
    • First Governor of Rajasthan: Gurumukh Nihal Singh, 25 October 1956.
    • Article 239: Union Territories administered by the President through an administrator.UPPSC
    • Chief Minister of a UT with legislature (Delhi, Article 239AA) is appointed by the President.

    Powers of the Governor

    • Appoints Chief Minister, and ministers on Chief Minister's advice (Article 164(1)).
    • Appoints Advocate General (Article 165; qualified as High Court judge) and State Public Service Commission members.
    • High Court judges are appointed by the President, not Governor; Governor nominates some Council members (Article 171(3)(e)).UPPSC
    • Governor is part of State Legislature; summons, prorogues, dissolves Assembly; nominates one-sixth of Legislative Council.
    • Anglo-Indian nomination to Assemblies ended 25 January 2020 (104th Amendment 2019).
    • Article 200: Governor may assent, withhold, return (non-money bill) or reserve a Bill for the President.UPPSC
    • No time limit for returning a Bill; if passed again, he assents or reserves it.
    • Article 201: President decides on a reserved Bill; President cannot reserve a State Bill on his own.
    • Assent given cures lack of Governor's prior recommendation for a Bill.
    • Article 213: Governor issues ordinance when Legislature is not in session.UPPSC ×2
    • Ordinance must be approved by State Legislature; lapses six weeks after reassembly.UPPSC
    • Article 163(1): Governor acts on ministers' advice except where Constitution requires his discretion.
    • Discretion: ask for majority proof, dismiss Chief Minister who lost confidence, reserve or return Bills.UPPSC
    • Also discretionary: report for President's Rule (Article 356), dissolving Assembly; he cannot consult High Court.
    • Article 166(3): Governor makes rules for business of State Government.
    • Article 161: pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions for offences under State laws; cannot pardon death sentence.UPPSC
    • Governor has no emergency powers.

    Immunity

    • Article 361: Governor not answerable to any court for official acts.
    • No criminal case against President or Governor during term; civil case allowed after two months' notice.UPPSC
    • President can be impeached (Article 61); Governor can be dismissed by President.
    • State legislators not liable in court for anything said in the House.

    Governor: immunity and firsts

    • Article 361(1): Governor/President not answerable to any court for official acts.
    • Article 361(2): no criminal case against them during term of office.
    • Article 361(4): civil case for personal acts allowed after 2 months' written notice.
    • Article 74(2): courts cannot inquire into advice given by Ministers.UPPSC
    • No impeachment for Governor; he holds office at President's pleasure (Article 156(1)).UPPSC
    • Word "impeachment" used only for the President (Article 61).
    • Vice-President removed by Rajya Sabha resolution agreed by Lok Sabha (Article 67); CJI under Article 124(4).
    • Article 158(4): Governor's pay and allowances cannot be cut during his term.
    • Article 161: Governor's pardon power; he cannot pardon a death sentence.
    • Governor does not appoint High Court judges; President does (Article 217(1)).
    • Governor nominates some Legislative Council members (Article 171(3)(e)).
    • Article 194(2): state legislators not liable in court for speech or vote in House.
    • Sarojini Naidu: first woman Governor of a State (Uttar Pradesh); died in office 1949.UPPSC
    • National Women's Day, 13 February = Sarojini Naidu's birthday (born 1879).UPPSC
    • Padmaja Naidu (her daughter): first woman Governor of West Bengal (1956–67).
    • C. Rajagopalachari: first Governor of West Bengal; C.V. Ananda Bose since 17 November 2022.
    • Sarla Grewal: first woman Governor of Madhya Pradesh (1989–90).
    • Bhagwat Dayal Sharma: first CM of Haryana; later Governor of Odisha and Madhya Pradesh.
    • N.N. Wanchoo: MP Governor who was not a Constituent Assembly member.
    • Rajpramukh post abolished by 7th Amendment from 1 November 1956 (States Reorganisation Commission).
    • Gurumukh Nihal Singh: first Governor of Rajasthan, appointed 25 October 1956.
    • Haribhau Kisanrao Bagde: Rajasthan Governor since 31 July 2024; Gujarat: Acharya Devvrat.
    • First Governor dismissed: Prabhudas Patwari, Tamil Nadu, October 1980.
    • Raghukul Tilak: Rajasthan Governor dismissed in August 1981.UPPSC
    • Sarkaria Commission (report 1988): Governor = eminent outsider, detached from recent politics, not of ruling party.

    Chapter 28

    The State Legislature

    Legislative Council and Assembly, their officers and bills, and the Chief Minister.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Article 169: creation or abolition of a Legislative Council.PCS Pre ’11, ’13; PCS Mains ’07; Lower Sub Mains ’154 papers
    2. Madhya Pradesh has no Council (one house only).PCS Pre ’08; PCS Mains ’06; Lower Sub ’083 papers
    3. Council cannot be dissolved but can be abolished.PCS Pre ’18; PCS Mains ’072 papers
    4. Article 170: Assembly strength minimum 60, maximum 500; direct election.PCS Mains ’14; RO/ARO ’172 papers
    5. Parliament makes the law after the Assembly passes a resolution.Lower Sub (Spl) ’081 paper

    Legislative Council: creation

    • Articles 168–212 (Part VI) deal with the State Legislature.
    • Article 168: State Legislature = Governor + Assembly (+ Council where it exists).
    • Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) = Upper House; Legislative Assembly = Lower House.
    • Article 169: creation or abolition of a Legislative Council.UPPSC ×4
    • Parliament makes the law after the Assembly passes a resolution.UPPSC
    • Resolution needs majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting.
    • Resolution does not bind the Union Government to bring a law.
    • Council cannot be dissolved but can be abolished.UPPSC ×2
    • Rajya Sabha: neither dissolved nor abolished; Lok Sabha and Assemblies: dissolved, not abolished.
    • 6 States have Councils: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana.
    • Rajasthan has no Legislative Council.UPPSC
    • Madhya Pradesh has no Council (one house only).UPPSC ×3
    • Tamil Nadu also has one house only.
    • 1956: 7 of 14 reorganised States had two houses: UP, Bihar, Bombay, Madras, Mysore, Punjab, West Bengal.
    • Councils abolished: West Bengal 1969, Punjab 1970, Tamil Nadu 1986, Jammu & Kashmir 31 October 2019.

    Legislative Council: composition

    • Article 171: composition of the Council.
    • Size: at most 1/3 of the Assembly, but never below 40.UPPSC
    • Uttar Pradesh Council is the largest: 100 members.
    • Permanent House; member's term 6 years; 1/3 retire every second year.
    • Minimum age for Council member: 30 years.
    • Elected by proportional representation, single transferable vote, secret ballot (Article 171(4)).
    • Article 171(3): about 5/6 elected, rest nominated by Governor.
    ShareChosen by
    1/3Legislative Assembly members
    1/3local bodies (municipalities, district boards)
    1/12graduates of 3 years' standing
    1/12secondary school teachers, 3 years' experience
    restGovernor: literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service
    • Actual shares fixed by Section 10 and Schedule 3, Representation of the People Act, 1950.
    • UP: Governor nominates only 10 of 100 (1/10), not a fixed 1/3, 1/4 or 1/6.UPPSC
    • Nominated share: Bihar about 1/6; Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana about 1/7.
    • Article 182: Council elects its own Chairman and Deputy Chairman.
    • Chairman removed by resolution of majority of all then members of Council.

    Legislative Assembly: composition

    • Article 170: Assembly strength minimum 60, maximum 500; direct election.UPPSC ×2
    • Sikkim is the exception: 32 members.UPPSC
    • Largest Assembly: Uttar Pradesh, 403 members.UPPSC
    • Smallest: Sikkim (32) among States, Puducherry (33) among Union Territories.
    StateAssembly seats
    Goa40
    Uttarakhand70
    Himachal Pradesh68
    Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya60
    Manipur60, not 62UPPSC
    • Article 170(2): same population-to-seat ratio across constituencies of a State.
    • 84th Amendment, 2001: Assembly seats frozen till first census after 2026.
    • Article 173: MLA must be Indian citizen, at least 25 years old.
    • Article 332: seats reserved for SCs and STs in Assemblies.
    • Article 333: Anglo-Indian nomination; not extended after 25 January 2020 (104th Amendment, 2019).
    • UTs with Assemblies: Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir; Ladakh has none.
    • J&K Assembly: 90 elected + 5 nominated; 24 seats vacant for POK areas.
    • Election Commission of India conducts Assembly elections (Article 324).UPPSC
    • MLAs vote for President, Rajya Sabha and Council members; not for Vice-President.

    Speaker, sessions and procedure

    • Article 191: disqualifications of state legislators.
    • Article 192: Governor decides disqualification finally, on Election Commission's opinion.UPPSC
    • Defection (Tenth Schedule) cases: Speaker or Council Chairman decides.
    • Article 178: Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Assembly.
    • Article 179: Speaker resigns to Deputy Speaker; removed by Assembly resolution.
    • Speaker vacates office if he stops being an Assembly member.
    • After dissolution, Speaker stays till just before first sitting of new Assembly.UPPSC
    • Speaker has a casting vote on a tie; powers same as Lok Sabha Speaker.
    • 2022 Speakers: Ramesh Tawadkar – Goa; Kultar Sandhwan – Punjab; T. Satyabrat – Manipur; Ritu Khanduri – Uttarakhand.UPPSC
    • Ramkishore Shukla: Protem Speaker, Speaker and Deputy Speaker of MP Assembly.
    • Article 174(2): Governor prorogues (ends session of) the Assembly.
    • Article 176: Governor addresses first session after election and first session each year.
    • No own rule on a matter → State Legislature follows Lok Sabha rule.
    • Article 189(3): quorum = 10 members or 1/10 of House, whichever is greater.UPPSC
    • Article 210: business in State's official language, Hindi or English.
    • Advocate General cannot vote; House cannot discuss judges' conduct.
    • MP Assembly order: oath, Governor's address, introduction of ministers, mention of death.
    • Adjournment motion: Speaker's consent, specific recent matter, one per sitting, no privilege question.
    • Rajasthan: Home Department estimates not under Estimates Committee 'A'.

    Bills and funds

    • State Contingency Fund is at the disposal of the Governor.UPPSC
    • State Legislature sets up the Contingency Fund by law.UPPSC
    • Article 195: members' salaries; Article 199: definition of Money Bill.
    • Article 197: Council can hold an ordinary bill 3 months the first time.UPPSC
    • Second time 1 month more: total delay 4 months.UPPSC
    • Money Bill starts only in Assembly; Council returns it within 14 days (Article 198).
    • Assembly Speaker decides whether a bill is a Money Bill.
    • Article 207: Money Bill introduced only on Governor's recommendation.UPPSC
    • Budget leaked before presentation → Finance Minister resigns; Official Secrets Act, 1923.

    Chief Minister and ministers

    • Article 162: extent of executive power of State.UPPSC
    • Article 163: Council of Ministers aids Governor, except in his discretionary functions.UPPSC
    • Article 164(1): Governor appoints CM; other ministers on CM's advice.UPPSC

    Check Governor formally appoints the CM but does not select him; the majority party chooses.

    • Article 164(1A) (91st Amendment, 2003): ministers at most 15% of Assembly, minimum 12.UPPSC
    • Article 164(4): non-member can be minister for 6 months only.

    Chief Minister and State administration

    • Articles 153–167 (Part VI): State executive = Governor, CM, Council of Ministers, Advocate General.
    • Article 164(5): State Legislature fixes ministers' pay and allowances by law.UPPSC
    • Article 167: duties of CM: tell Governor Cabinet decisions and proposals for laws.UPPSC
    • CM attending National Development Council = administrative duty, not constitutional.
    • Article 163(3): courts cannot inquire into ministers' advice to Governor.
    • Article 164(2): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
    • Article 164(3): Governor gives ministers oath of office and secrecy (Third Schedule).
    • Conviction with 2+ years' jail: disqualified till 6 years after release (RP Act 1951).
    • J&K Assembly term: earlier 6 years; now 5 years (J&K Reorganisation Act 2019).
    • Sucheta Kriplani: first woman CM of a State (Uttar Pradesh, 1963).
    • Ravishankar Shukla: first CM of Madhya Pradesh; Mohan Yadav: 19th CM since 13 December 2023.
    • Govind Narayan Singh (5th MP CM) never held post of Leader of House.
    • State Secretariat: apex of State administration; frames procedure of government work.
    • Chief Secretary: chosen by CM, appointed by Governor; no fixed tenure; sends files to Cabinet.
    • After Ayodhya 1992: Assemblies of UP, MP, Himachal, Rajasthan dissolved; Bihar's not.
    • Andhra Pradesh proposed reservation for Muslims in jobs and education (2004; 4% in 2007).UPPSC
    • Goa: only State with a Common Civil Code (Portuguese Civil Code, 1867).UPPSC

    Check Now out of date: Uttarakhand enforced a uniform civil code on 27 January 2025.

    Chapter 29

    The High Court

    High Court judges, jurisdiction and writs, plus lower courts.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Certiorari: higher court calls record of a lower court's case for review.PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; PCS Mains ’082 papers
    2. Article 217(1): President appoints every High Court judge, not the Governor.PCS Mains ’161 paper
    3. Article 224: additional judges (up to 2 years) and acting judges in High Courts.RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’161 paper
    4. Judges' salaries: charged on Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 202(3)(d)).PCS Mains ’131 paper
    5. Judges' pension: charged on Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112(3)(d)).PCS Mains ’131 paper

    High Court: judges

    • Articles 214–231 (Part VI) deal with High Courts.
    • Article 214: a High Court for every State; Article 215: Court of Record, can punish contempt.
    • 7th Amendment, 1956: Parliament may set up a common High Court for two or more States/UT.
    • Article 216: Chief Justice + other judges; President fixes the number.
    • Article 217(1): President appoints every High Court judge, not the Governor.UPPSC
    • President consults CJI, Governor and Chief Justice of that High Court.
    • Qualification: Indian citizen; 10 years in judicial office or 10 years as High Court advocate.
    • Retirement age 62 (15th Amendment, 1963; earlier 60); resigns to President.
    • 114th Amendment Bill (2010) to raise age to 65 was not passed.
    • Removal same as Supreme Court judge: Parliament's address by special majority; proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
    • Article 222: President transfers a judge after consulting CJI.
    • Third Judges case (1998): CJI consults 4 seniormost judges and both High Court Chief Justices.
    • Article 223: President appoints acting Chief Justice.
    • Article 224: additional judges (up to 2 years) and acting judges in High Courts.UPPSC
    • Judges' salaries: charged on Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 202(3)(d)).UPPSC
    • Judges' pension: charged on Consolidated Fund of India (Article 112(3)(d)).UPPSC
    • Article 220: retired permanent judge can practise only in Supreme Court and other High Courts.

    Number, seats and jurisdiction

    • At present 25 High Courts; 7 cover more than one State/UT.
    • Only 3 cover more than one State: Gauhati, Bombay, Punjab and Haryana.
    • Delhi has its own High Court; J&K and Ladakh share one.
    • High Courts began 1862: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras.
    • 1866: High Court for North-Western Provinces at Agra; shifted to Allahabad 1869.
    High CourtArea and benches
    CalcuttaAndaman & Nicobar; benches Port Blair, Jalpaiguri
    BombayMaharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu; benches Nagpur, Aurangabad, PanajiUPPSC
    GauhatiAssam, Arunachal, Nagaland, Mizoram; benches Kohima, Aizawl, Itanagar
    Punjab and HaryanaPunjab, Haryana, Chandigarh
    MadrasPuducherry
    KeralaLakshadweep
    Madhya Pradeshseat Jabalpur; benches Indore, Gwalior

    Check Largest number of benches: key gives Bombay; explanation says Bombay and Gauhati both have 3.

    • Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura High Courts started work in March 2013.UPPSC
    • Main jurisdictions: original, appellate, supervisory; advisory belongs to Supreme Court (Article 143).UPPSC
    • Second appeal and public interest litigation lie with High Court.
    • Article 227: superintendence over all courts and tribunals, except armed forces ones.
    • Article 233: Governor appoints district judges in consultation with High Court.
    • Article 235: High Court controls subordinate courts.
    • Chief Justice in administrative role is subject to writ jurisdiction of other judges.
    • Parliament can extend a High Court's jurisdiction.
    • Preventive detention: normally up to 3 months.
    • Lok Adalat: settles pending or pre-litigation civil and compoundable criminal cases.
    • Lok Adalat bench: judicial officer + lawyer + social worker.
    • Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008: village courts, civil and criminal cases.

    Writs of High Court

    • Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
    • Certiorari: higher court calls record of a lower court's case for review.UPPSC ×2
    • Prohibition: stops a lower court while the case is pending.UPPSC
    • Prohibition lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies.
    • Mandamus: not against private body unless it has a public duty; lies against government company.
    • Quo Warranto: any public-minded person can ask for it.
    • Article 226: High Court writs cover Fundamental Rights and any other legal right.UPPSC
    • Article 32: Supreme Court writs only for Fundamental Rights; so High Court power is wider.UPPSC

    Judges and lower courts: misc

    • High Court judge resigns in writing to the President (Article 217(1)(a)).
    • Justice Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC): Rajya Sabha passed removal motion 2011; resigned 1 September 2011.
    • Babri Mosque/Ramjanmabhoomi case in Allahabad High Court = title suit.
    • Allahabad HC, Rahmatullah vs State of UP (1994): triple talaq illegal; violates Articles 14, 15.
    • Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019: instant talaq void and illegal.
    • Rajeev Gupta: Chief Justice, Chhattisgarh HC, 2 February 2008; current: Justice Ramesh Sinha.
    • Justice H.R. Khanna (8th Law Commission, 80th report): 1/3 judges of each HC from other States.
    • Article 233: "district judge" term; Governor appoints them consulting High Court.
    • Article 236: district judge includes sessions judge, chief presidency magistrate, small cause court chief judge; not tribunal judge.
    • District Judge: highest judicial authority in district; supervises its subordinate courts.
    • Advocates Act, 1961: one class "advocates"; includes corporate lawyers, patent attorneys.
    • Bar Council of India sets rules for legal education and law colleges.
    • Prisons: State List entry 4; Prisons Act, 1894; Model Prisons Act, 2023 as guide.
    • Police custody = police lock-up; judicial custody = jail, under the magistrate.
    • Arrested person must be produced before magistrate within 24 hours.
    • Judicial custody: police may question only with court's permission.
    • Lok Adalat needs consent of both parties; its decision then binds them.
    • Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008: Section 11 civil and criminal; Section 27 social workers as conciliators.
    • Mobile court: idea of A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; first in Mewat, Haryana, August 2007.

    Chapter 30

    The Centre-State Relations

    How law-making, administrative and money powers are shared between Centre and States.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Sarkaria Commission (9 June 1983): reviewed Centre-State relations.PCS Pre ’08, ’16, ’18; PCS Mains ’03, ’04, ’06; RO/ARO ’147 papers
    2. Part XI: legislative relations (Articles 245–255).PCS Mains (Spl) ’04; RO/ARO ’142 papers
    3. Seventh Schedule holds the three lists.PCS Pre ’93; Lower Sub ’082 papers
    4. Article 248: residuary powers (subjects in no list) lie with Parliament/Union.PCS Pre ’91, ’952 papers
    5. Such resolution stays in force not more than one year.PCS Pre ’16, ’172 papers

    Basics of Centre-State relations

    • Centre-State relations rest on Constitution, conventions, court interpretations and dialogue mechanisms.UPPSC
    • Federal polity covers Union-State relations, inter-State relations, cooperation and dispute-solving mechanisms.UPPSC
    • Also shaped by planning process and conflict of political interests.
    • Centre's control over States in planning = "municipal relations".
    • Part XI: legislative relations (Articles 245–255).UPPSC ×2
    • Part XI also: administrative relations (Articles 256–263).
    • Part XII, Articles 264–293: financial relations.
    • States lack enough resources for development → growing demand to review Centre-State relations.UPPSC
    • Centre → State transfers now: tax sharing, grants-in-aid, centrally sponsored schemes; not Gadgil formula.

    Legislative relations

    • Articles 245 and 246 regulate the three-list division of powers.UPPSC
    • Article 245: Parliament makes law for India; State Legislature for the State.
    • Seventh Schedule holds the three lists.UPPSC ×2
    ListSubjects originallyAt present
    Union List (I)9798
    State List (II)6659
    Concurrent List (III)4752
    • Concurrent List: both Centre and States make law; Union law prevails in conflict.UPPSC
    • Economic and social planning, infants and minors: Concurrent List.UPPSC
    • Article 248: residuary powers (subjects in no list) lie with Parliament/Union.UPPSC ×2
    • In USA residuary powers lie with States.
    • Residuary examples: cyber law, space research, artificial intelligence rules.
    • Article 246A (101st Amendment, 2016): Parliament and States both make GST laws.
    • Article 247: Parliament may set up additional courts.
    • Article 249: Parliament makes law on State List subject in national interest.UPPSC
    • Needs Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting.
    • Such resolution stays in force not more than one year.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 250: Parliament legislates on State List during Emergency.
    • Article 251: Parliament's law under 249/250 prevails over State law.
    • Article 252: Parliament legislates for two or more States by consent.
    • Article 253: law to carry out international agreements, even on State subjects.

    Administrative and financial relations

    • Article 256: State executive power must ensure compliance with Parliament's laws; Union can give directions.UPPSC
    • Article 257: State must not impede Union's executive power.
    • Article 258: President may entrust Union functions to a State with its consent.
    • Article 262: Parliament decides inter-State river water disputes.
    • Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956; River Boards Act, 1956 (not 1970); National Water Policy, 1987.UPPSC
    • Article 265: no tax without authority of law.
    • Article 266: Consolidated Fund of India; Article 267: Contingency Funds of India and State.
    • Article 269A: GST on inter-State trade; Article 279A: GST Council (101st Amendment).
    • Article 275: Union grants to certain States.
    • Article 280: President sets up Finance Commission every 5th year; quasi-judicial body.
    • Article 281: President lays its recommendations before both Houses.

    Inter-State and Zonal Councils

    • Article 263: inter-State relations; provides for Inter-State Council.UPPSC
    • Inter-State Council's source: the Constitution.UPPSC
    • President sets it up by order.UPPSC
    • Set up 28 May 1990 (V.P. Singh government).
    • Members: PM (chairman), all CMs, UT CMs/administrators, 6 Cabinet ministers named by PM.
    • Advisory body on inter-State and Centre-State matters.
    • Zonal (regional) Councils made by Parliament's law: States Reorganisation Act, 1956.UPPSC
    • Zonal Council: statutory and advisory, not constitutional.UPPSC
    • Five zones: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern; Union Home Minister chairs each.
    • Chandigarh, Delhi, Puducherry also included in zones.
    • Zonal Councils called "sub-federal links".
    • North Eastern Council Act, 1971; Sikkim added as 8th member in 2002.
    • NEC members: Governors and CMs of member States + 3 President's nominees.
    • NEC chairman: Union Home Minister; vice-chairman: DoNER Minister.
    • National Development Council, Governors' Conference: extra-constitutional and extra-legal.
    • National Security Council: set up by executive decision.
    • National Integration Council formed in 1962, not 1961.UPPSC
    • Jharkhand Area Autonomous Council: 8 August 1995, 18 districts.

    Sarkaria and other commissions

    • Sarkaria Commission (9 June 1983): reviewed Centre-State relations.UPPSC ×7
    • Chairman Justice R.S. Sarkaria; members B. Shivaraman and S.R. Sen.UPPSC
    • Report January 1988: 247 recommendations, 19 chapters.
    • It advised a permanent Inter-State Council; led to the 1990 Council.UPPSC
    • Suggested name "Inter-Governmental Council".
    • Said Article 356 was misused; use it rarely.
    • Rajamannar Committee, Punchhi Commission: also on Centre-State relations.
    • Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998): state funding of elections, not Centre-State relations.UPPSC
    • Gupta Committee: funds in kind, only to recognised parties, not independents.

    Financial relations: taxes

    • Part XII (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits): Centre-State financial relations.UPPSC
    • Part X: Scheduled and Tribal Areas; Part XIII: trade and commerce within India.
    • Articles 268–281: distribution of revenues between Union and States.UPPSC
    • Article 268: stamp duties levied by Union, collected and kept by States.
    • Article 270: taxes levied and collected by Union, shared with States (income tax, not agricultural income).
    • Tax on stock exchange and futures market deals: levied by Union, not collected by States.UPPSC
    • Land revenue (State List entry 45): levied and collected only by States.
    • Agricultural income tax: given to States by the Constitution (State List entry 46).
    • Article 282: discretionary grants by Union or State for any public purpose.
    • Article 293: State borrows only within India; no direct foreign loans.UPPSC
    • Fiscal disputes between Centre and States: Supreme Court decides (Article 131).UPPSC
    • Article 276: tax on professions, trades, callings capped at Rs. 2,500 a year per person.UPPSC
    • Cap was Rs. 250 before 60th Amendment, 1988.
    • Article 301: trade, commerce and intercourse free throughout India (Part XIII).UPPSC
    • Article 300: suits and proceedings by or against Union and States.

    Chapter 31

    Emergency Provisions

    National Emergency (Article 352), President's Rule (Article 356) and Financial Emergency (Article 360).

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Grounds: war, external aggression or armed rebellion; not internal disturbance or communal clashes.PCS Mains ’10, ’16, ’17; RO/ARO ’16; UDA/LDA ’02; GIC ’106 papers
    2. Three types: National (352: war, external aggression, armed rebellion), President's Rule (356: constitutional machinery fails), Financial (360).PCS Mains ’07, ’09, ’143 papers
    3. Both Houses must approve within one month.PCS Pre ’06; PCS Mains ’03, ’043 papers
    4. Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended.PCS Pre ’15; PCS Mains ’092 papers
    5. Article 360 has never been used.PCS Mains ’16; Lower Sub Mains ’152 papers

    Types of emergency

    • Part XVIII, Articles 352–360: emergency provisions.
    • Three types: National (352: war, external aggression, armed rebellion), President's Rule (356: constitutional machinery fails), Financial (360).UPPSC ×3
    • Article 355: Union's duty to protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance.UPPSC
    • Article 365: effect of State not obeying Union directions.
    • During emergency the Union can direct any State how to use executive power.

    National Emergency: Article 352

    • Grounds: war, external aggression or armed rebellion; not internal disturbance or communal clashes.UPPSC ×6
    • 44th Amendment, 1978 replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion".
    • Article 352: President proclaims emergency, even on imminent danger, for whole or part of India.UPPSC
    • President acts only on written decision of the Union Cabinet (Article 352(3)).
    • Both Houses must approve within one month.UPPSC ×3
    • Earlier 2 months; cut to 1 month by 44th Amendment.
    • Approval by special majority (2/3 present and voting); revoked by simple majority.
    • If Lok Sabha dissolved: survives till 30 days after new Lok Sabha's first sitting.
    • Once approved, runs 6 months; extended 6 months at a time.
    • Proclaimed 3 times: 1962, 1971, 1975.
    • 25 June 1975: declared for "internal disturbance" by Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed; withdrawn 21 March 1977.

    Effects of National Emergency

    • Parliament can make law on State List; such law ends 6 months after emergency.
    • Article 354: President can change Centre-State tax sharing till end of that financial year.
    • Article 358: Article 19 suspended automatically, only for war or external aggression.
    • Article 359: President suspends enforcement of other Fundamental Rights by order.UPPSC
    • Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 83(2): Lok Sabha term extended one year at a time while emergency lasts.UPPSC
    • Extension ends within 6 months after emergency stops.
    • Article 172(1): Parliament extends State Assembly term the same way.

    President's Rule: Article 356

    • Article 356: President's Rule when a State's constitutional machinery fails.
    • President acts on Governor's report or otherwise; Article 365 gives a second ground.
    • Council of Ministers removed; Assembly suspended or dissolved; Parliament makes State laws and budget.
    • No effect on Fundamental Rights; local bodies not dissolved.
    • Parliament must approve within 2 months, by simple majority; then lasts 6 months.
    • Maximum period: 3 years, with approval every 6 months.UPPSC
    • Beyond 1 year needs National Emergency in force + Election Commission's certificate (44th Amendment, 1978).
    • S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994): proclamation open to court review; Assembly not dissolved before Parliament approves.
    • First used in Punjab, 1951; then PEPSU, 1953.UPPSC

    Check Key gives PEPSU as first; the explanation says Punjab (1951) came before PEPSU (1953).

    • Times imposed till 2019: Manipur 10, Uttar Pradesh 9, Bihar 8, Odisha 6.
    • Governor's Rule existed only in Jammu & Kashmir (Section 92 of its constitution), ended 2019.
    • Article 352 is not about failure of machinery in a State.

    Financial Emergency: Article 360

    • Article 360: declared when financial stability or credit of India is threatened.
    • Parliament must approve within 2 months; then continues till revoked.
    • President can order pay cuts, even for Supreme Court and High Court judges.
    • President may ask States to reserve Money Bills for him.
    • Article 360 has never been used.UPPSC ×2
    • Financial Emergency declared so far: never.UPPSC
    • K.M. Nambiar called the President's emergency power "a fraud on the Constitution".UPPSC

    Chapter 32

    The Finance Commission

    The Finance Commission under Article 280: members and work.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. It recommends how Centre and States share net tax proceeds.PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; Lower Sub (Spl) ’10; Lower Sub Mains ’13; UDA/LDA ’024 papers
    2. Set up every 5 years, or earlier if President wishes.PCS Mains ’08, ’10, ’113 papers
    3. Main job: recommend Centre-State tax sharing and principles of grants-in-aid to States.PCS Pre ’93, ’06; UDA/LDA ’063 papers
    4. State Finance Commission: constitutional body under Article 243-I.PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Pre ’15, ’163 papers
    5. Article 280(1): chairman + four other members; reports to President, not NITI Aayog.PCS Pre ’23; PCS Mains (Spl) ’082 papers

    Finance Commission: basics

    • Article 280: President appoints the Finance Commission.UPPSC
    • Set up every 5 years, or earlier if President wishes.UPPSC ×3
    • It recommends how Centre and States share net tax proceeds.UPPSC ×4
    • Also: grants-in-aid principles, funds for Panchayats and Municipalities, matters President refers.
    • Recommendations are advisory; it is a constitutional body.
    • President appoints chairman and members; Parliament fixes their qualifications by law (Article 280(2)).UPPSC
    • Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951: chairman = person experienced in public affairs.
    • Four members: High Court judge-qualified, government finance expert, administrator, economist.
    • A judge member is not compulsory; chairman can be reappointed.
    • First Finance Commission: order 22 November 1951, set up 6 April 1952, chairman K.C. Neogy.
    • 14th (Y.V. Reddy): States' share raised from 32% to 42%, for 2015–20.
    • 15th (N.K. Singh): two reports, 2020–21 and 2021–26.
    • 16th: set up 31 December 2023, chairman Arvind Panagariya.

    Finance Commission: members and work

    • Article 280(1): chairman + four other members; reports to President, not NITI Aayog.UPPSC ×2
    • Main job: recommend Centre-State tax sharing and principles of grants-in-aid to States.UPPSC ×3
    • Also advises on raising State funds for Panchayats and Municipalities.
    • It does not allow withdrawals from Consolidated Fund; Parliament does.
    • Article 281: President lays its recommendations before each House.
    Finance CommissionPeriodChairman
    12th2005–10C. Rangarajan
    13th2010–15Vijay Kelkar; report 2010UPPSC
    14th2015–20Y.V. Reddy; formed January 2013, report 15 December 2014UPPSC
    15th2020–26N.K. Singh; formed 27 November 2017UPPSC
    • State Finance Commission: constitutional body under Article 243-I.UPPSC ×3
    • Governor sets it up every 5 years to review Panchayat finances (73rd Amendment, 1992).
    • Union Finance Commission can recommend aid for Panchayats (Article 280(3)(bb)).
    • M.V. Mathur (3rd Finance Commission member) suggested merging Finance and Planning Commissions.

    Chapter 33

    The Planning Commission/NITI Aayog

    Planning Commission, NITI Aayog and the National Development Council.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Not a constitutional body, nor statutory.PCS Pre ’13, ’14; PCS Mains ’03, ’04, ’08, ’10; RO/ARO Mains ’137 papers
    2. Extra-constitutional and non-statutory body.PCS Pre ’18; Lower Sub ’152 papers
    3. National Development Council (NDC) formed 6 August 1952 by executive order.PCS Mains ’16; RO/ARO Mains ’162 papers
    4. NDC gives guidelines for the Plan, reviews progress, suggests ways to meet targets; not money allocation.PCS Mains ’05, ’102 papers
    5. Set up 15 March 1950 by a Union Cabinet resolution.PCS Pre ’991 paper

    Planning Commission

    • Set up 15 March 1950 by a Union Cabinet resolution.UPPSC
    • Not a constitutional body, nor statutory.UPPSC ×7
    • UPSC, State PSCs (Article 315), Finance Commission, Election Commission are constitutional bodies.
    • Formed on advice of advisory planning board under K.C. Neogy.
    • Prime Minister was ex-officio chairman; first: Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    • First Deputy Chairman: Gulzarilal Nanda.
    • Deputy Chairman ranked equal to a Cabinet Minister.UPPSC
    • Work: assess resources, prepare five-year plans, advise on States' annual plans.
    • About 70% of Centre's grants to States went on its advice.

    NITI Aayog

    • PM Narendra Modi abolished the Planning Commission (announced 15 August 2014).UPPSC
    • NITI Aayog formed 1 January 2015 by Union Cabinet resolution.UPPSC
    • NITI = National Institution for Transforming India; a policy think-tank.
    • Extra-constitutional and non-statutory body.UPPSC ×2
    • No full-time chairman: PM is ex-officio chairperson; works on cooperative federalism.UPPSC
    • PM appoints the Vice-Chairperson, who has Cabinet Minister rank.
    • First Vice-Chairman: Arvind Panagariya (2015–17); current: Suman K. Bery.
    • CEO: B.V.R. Subrahmanyam.
    • Governing Council: PM, all CMs, CMs of Delhi and Puducherry, Lt. Governors of other UTs; not Governors.UPPSC
    • National Development Council, Planning Commission, Zonal Councils: not mentioned in Constitution.

    National Development Council

    • Planning Commission Deputy Chairman had the rank of a Cabinet Minister.UPPSC
    • Deputy Chairmen: Manmohan Singh (1985–87), Pranab Mukherjee (1991–96), Montek Singh Ahluwalia (2004–14); never P. Chidambaram.UPPSC
    • Planning Commission called "economic cabinet" of Union and States; it framed five-year plans.UPPSC
    • National Development Council (NDC) formed 6 August 1952 by executive order.UPPSC ×2
    • NDC, not Planning Commission, is the highest decision-making body for planning.UPPSC
    • NDC: non-constitutional, non-statutory; should meet at least twice a year.
    • Members: PM (chairman), Union Cabinet ministers, all CMs, UT heads, Planning Commission/NITI members.
    • Planning Commission Secretary was also NDC Secretary.
    • NDC gives guidelines for the Plan, reviews progress, suggests ways to meet targets; not money allocation.UPPSC ×2
    • NDC gives final approval to five-year plans.UPPSC
    • NDC coordinates between Planning Commission and State Governments.UPPSC

    Chapter 34

    Lokpal and Important Commissions

    Lokpal, Lokayukta, human rights bodies, vigilance, Public Service Commissions and civil services reform.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Constitution Review Commission (22 February 2000): chairman M.N. Venkatachaliah; advisory report; not approved by Parliament.PCS Pre ’03; PCS Mains ’02; UDA/LDA ’023 papers
    2. NHRC set up 12 October 1993: statutory, not constitutional.PCS Mains ’04, ’072 papers
    3. Article 323: UPSC gives annual report to President; State PSC to Governor.Lower Sub ’13; UDA/LDA (Spl) ’102 papers
    4. Indian model of Ombudsman = Lokpal.PCS Mains ’141 paper
    5. Its chairman: Morarji Desai; K. Hanumanthaiah from 1967.RO/ARO ’171 paper

    Lokpal

    • Ombudsman (citizens' complaints officer) first created in Sweden, 1809.
    • Indian model of Ombudsman = Lokpal.UPPSC
    • First Administrative Reforms Commission (set up 5 January 1966, till 1970) first proposed Lokpal and Lokayukta.
    • Its chairman: Morarji Desai; K. Hanumanthaiah from 1967.UPPSC
    • First Lokpal Bill introduced in 1968 (4th Lok Sabha); passed there 1969, then lapsed.UPPSC
    • Lokpal Bill 2011: introduced 4 August 2011 by V. Narayanasamy; sent to Standing Committee; called "weak" by civil society.UPPSC
    • Civil society drafters: Anna Hazare, Arvind Kejriwal, Shanti Bhushan, Santosh Hegde, Prashant Bhushan.UPPSC
    • Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: in force 16 January 2014.
    • Lokpal = chairperson + at most 8 members; appointed by President.
    • Selection Committee: PM (chair), Lok Sabha Speaker, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, CJI or nominee judge, one eminent jurist.UPPSC
    • Rajya Sabha Chairman is not on the Selection Committee.
    • Act covers Indian public servants inside and outside India; PM is within Lokpal's reach.
    • Chairperson/member: minimum age 45; cannot be MP or MLA.
    • Chairperson may be CJI, Supreme Court judge or eminent person.
    • First Lokpal: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose.
    • Lokpal chairperson from 10 March 2024: Justice Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar.UPPSC

    Lokayukta

    • Maharashtra: first State to set up Lokayukta (Act 1971, in force 25 October 1972).UPPSC
    • Odisha passed first Lokayukta Act (1970) but it started 1983; abolished it first, 1993.
    • Later: Bihar 1973, Uttar Pradesh 1975, Madhya Pradesh 1982, Andhra Pradesh 1983, Karnataka 1984, Assam 1986.
    • UP Lokayukta (Act 1975) reports to the Governor, who lays it before both Houses.UPPSC
    • UP Lokayukta tenure: 5 years or age 70 (from 26 February 2024).UPPSC

    Check Tenure was 8 years when the question was asked; the key matches the 2024 amendment.

    • Uttarakhand: first State to pass Lokayukta Bill in 2011 (1 November).UPPSC
    • Governor appoints Lokayukta on CM's advice.
    • CM under Lokayukta in Himachal, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab.
    • Rajasthan Lokayukta Act, 1973: Section 7 matters open to inquiry; Section 8 matters barred.
    • Narpat Mal Lodha Committee (Rajasthan, 2014): review of Lokayukta Act.

    Minorities and other bodies

    • "Minority" is not defined in the Constitution; Minority Commission is statutory, not constitutional.UPPSC
    • National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992: in force 17 May 1993.
    • Six notified minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis (1993), Jains (27 January 2014).
    • Article 350B (7th Amendment, 1956): one Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities for all India, appointed by President.UPPSC
    • Article 350A: mother-tongue teaching at primary stage.
    • National Commission for Women Act, 1990 (30 August 1990): Section 10 lists functions.
    • Secondary Education Commission (1952–53): chairman A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar.
    • Vohra Committee (1993): nexus of politicians, criminals and bureaucrats.UPPSC
    • Rajamannar Committee: recommended ending IAS and IPS.
    • First Law Commission of free India (1955): chairman M.C. Setalvad.
    • Constitution Review Commission (22 February 2000): chairman M.N. Venkatachaliah; advisory report; not approved by Parliament.UPPSC ×3
    • Its final report: 31 March 2002.
    • Swaran Singh Committee (1976): led to 42nd Amendment; Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights; Fundamental Duties.
    • Central Pollution Control Board chairman: nominated by Central Government.
    • Kelkar Committee: PPP model; Bakshi Tek Chand Committee (1948): patent system.
    • Mandal Commission set up 1979 by Morarji Desai's Janata government.UPPSC
    • Chairman B.P. Mandal; task: identify socially and educationally backward classes.
    • Mandal report submitted in 1980.UPPSC
    • SC/ST Commission 1990: atrocities due to land alienation, bonded labour, debt, unpaid wages; not religion.

    Human rights: ideas and UDHR

    • Human Rights idea stresses dignity of man as a human being.UPPSC
    • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR): adopted by UN General Assembly 10 December 1948; 30 Articles.
    • 10 December = Human Rights Day; UDHR is not legally binding.
    • UDHR lacks right to privacy and universal basic income.
    • UDHR reflected in Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles (Article 45), Fundamental Duties.
    • First generation rights (UDHR Articles 3–21): civil and political.
    • Second generation (Articles 22–27): right to work, education; ending social discrimination.
    • Third generation: community and collective rights.
    • "Right to the City": proposed by Henri Lefebvre, 1968; not an agreed human right.

    National Human Rights Commission

    • Protection of Human Rights Ordinance issued under Article 123; Act in force 28 September 1993.
    • NHRC set up 12 October 1993: statutory, not constitutional.UPPSC ×2
    • Human rights in Act = life, liberty, equality, dignity.
    • Chairperson: former CJI or Supreme Court judge (2019 amendment); term 3 years or age 70.UPPSC

    Check When asked (2015), the head had to be a former CJI and the term was 5 years.

    • Three human-rights-expert members, at least one woman; also ex-officio members (chairpersons of other national commissions).
    • No further government job after tenure.
    • President appoints on advice of 6-member committee: PM, Lok Sabha Speaker, Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman, Opposition leaders of both Houses, Home Minister.
    • Powers only recommendatory; has civil court powers; cannot punish.
    • Section 12: functions, including research and support to NGOs.
    • Armed forces cases: NHRC only seeks report from Central Government.
    • "Armed forces" in Act excludes State armed forces; Section 2(m) defines public servant.
    • First chairman: Justice Ranganath Misra (1993–96); current: Justice V. Ramasubramanian since 30 December 2024.
    • Human Rights Court prosecutor: advocate with 7 years' practice (Section 31).

    State Human Rights Commission

    • Chairperson: Chief Justice or judge of a High Court.
    • Appointed by Governor; Section 22 committee: CM (chair), Speaker, State Home Minister, Opposition Leader.
    • With a Council: its Chairman and Opposition Leader join the committee.
    • Sitting judge appointed after consulting High Court Chief Justice.
    • Governor names acting chairperson; annual report goes to State Government.
    • 25 States have such Commissions.

    Vigilance and information bodies

    • Central Vigilance Commission: set up February 1964 on Santhanam Committee (1962–64) advice.
    • CVC is in no Article of the Constitution; statutory since 2003.UPPSC
    • CBI 1963; Enforcement Directorate 1956; Prevention of Corruption Act 1988, not 1985.UPPSC

    Check Key gives only the 1985 pair; the explanation says Enforcement Directorate–2000 is also wrong.

    • Inter-State Council 1990.
    • Central Information Commission: under Right to Information Act, 2005.
    • RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019: Central Government fixes tenure and pay of Information Commissioners.

    Public Service Commissions

    • Articles 315–323 (Part XIV): UPSC and State PSCs.
    • UPSC is a constitutional body (Article 315).UPPSC
    • UPSC functions come from Constitution, Parliament's laws, executive rules and conventions.UPPSC
    • Article 320: functions; 320(3)(c): consulted on disciplinary matters; Article 321: functions extended by law.
    • Article 315(2): Parliament creates Joint PSC when concerned States pass resolutions.UPPSC
    • Article 316: President appoints UPSC and Joint PSC members; Governor appoints State PSC members.
    • Article 317: State PSC member removed only by President after Supreme Court inquiry.UPPSC
    • So Parliament has no role in removing UPSC Chairman, unlike judges and CAG.UPPSC
    • Other removal grounds: insolvency, outside paid job, infirmity.
    • Article 322: expenses charged on Consolidated Fund.
    • Article 323: UPSC gives annual report to President; State PSC to Governor.UPPSC ×2
    • UPSC has no control over State PSCs.

    PSC removal and functions

    • Art 317: only President removes UPSC or State PSC chairman/member, though Governor appoints State PSC members.
    • Misbehaviour ground: President refers to Supreme Court; removal after its inquiry report (procedure under Art 145).
    • Other grounds, Art 317(3): insolvent (bankrupt), paid job outside office, unfit by infirmity of mind or body.
    • Parliament has no role in removing UPSC chairman; it has for judges and CAG.
    • Art 320: PSC functions; Art 320(3)(c): PSC consulted on all disciplinary matters of civil servants.
    • PSC consulted on recruitment method, appointment and promotion principles; not on transferring civil servants.
    • Art 315(4): UPSC may serve a state's needs on Governor's request, with President's approval.UPPSC
    • Art 321: Parliament or State Legislature may extend PSC functions by law; for UP PSC, UP State Legislature.UPPSC
    • Art 322: UPSC expenses charged on Consolidated Fund of India; State PSC on Consolidated Fund of State.UPPSC
    • Art 323(2): State PSC submits annual report to Governor.
    • Art 318: regulations on service conditions of PSC members and staff.

    PSC history, civil service facts

    • Government of India Act 1919 → first Public Service Commission, set up 1 October 1926 (chairman + 4 members).UPPSC
    • Government of India Act 1935 named it Federal Public Service Commission.
    • Madhya Pradesh PSC: formed under Section 118(3), States Reorganisation Act 1956; maximum 5 members.
    • First woman UPSC chairman: Rose Millian Bethew (1992–96).
    • Art 310: Doctrine of Pleasure; Union servants hold office at President's pleasure, state servants at Governor's.
    • Bureaucracy in India = agency to implement public policy.
    • UPSC committee to review civil services exam (July 2000): chairman Prof. Sukhadeo Thorat (as keyed; the book gives no explanation).

    Civil services reform

    • P.C. Hota Committee on Civil Services Reforms: set up February 2004; report within six months.UPPSC
    • Civil Services Day: 21 April; first held 2006 at Vigyan Bhawan.
    • Date marks Sardar Patel's address to first batch of civil servants, Metcalf House, 21 April 1947.

    Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

    • Part XXI (Art 369–392): temporary, transitional and special provisions.

    Jammu and Kashmir

    • J&K was left out of the definition of "State" in Art 152 (Part VI).

    Special Category Status

    • Special Category Status (SCS): not in Constitution; began 1969 on 5th Finance Commission's advice.
    • First SCS states (1969): Jammu and Kashmir, Assam, Nagaland.
    • Granted by National Development Council; 11 states in all; Bihar never got it.
    • The 11: Assam, Nagaland, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Uttarakhand, Telangana.
    • Gadgil Formula tests: hilly terrain, low population density or large tribal population, border location, backwardness, weak state finances.

    Chapter 36

    Election Commission

    The Election Commission, election law and reforms, delimitation and the right to vote.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 61st Amendment Act 1988 cut voting age 21 → 18 by amending Art 326; in force 28 March 1989.PCS Pre ’00; PCS Mains (Spl) ’04, ’08; PCS Mains ’07, ’105 papers
    2. Art 324: Election Commission (EC), a permanent, independent body, set up 25 January 1950.PCS Pre ’16; PCS Mains ’10, ’173 papers
    3. Right to vote and to be elected = legal (statutory) right under RPA 1951, not fundamental or constitutional.PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’10; UDA/LDA ’133 papers
    4. Proportional representation gives all groups due share, so ensures representation of minorities.PCS Pre ’13; Lower Sub ’13; Lower Sub Mains ’133 papers
    5. CEC removed only in same manner and on same grounds as Supreme Court judge, Art 324(5).PCS Pre ’91; PCS Mains ’022 papers

    Election Commission: set-up

    • Part XV (Art 324–329): elections.
    • Art 324: Election Commission (EC), a permanent, independent body, set up 25 January 1950.UPPSC ×3
    • Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) + other Election Commissioners; President fixes number and appoints them, Art 324(2).
    • Now three members: CEC + 2 Election Commissioners; continuously multi-member since 1 October 1993.
    • All have equal powers; decisions by majority; salary same as Supreme Court judge.
    • Tenure: 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier.UPPSC
    • CEC or Election Commissioner resigns by writing to President.
    • CEC removed only in same manner and on same grounds as Supreme Court judge, Art 324(5).UPPSC ×2
    • Other Election Commissioner or Regional Commissioner: removed by President only on CEC's recommendation.UPPSC
    • EC is independent for free and fair polls; still, removal power lies with executive.UPPSC
    • Table of precedence: CEC ranks 9A, with UPSC chairman and Comptroller and Auditor General.

    Election Commission: functions

    • EC conducts elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President; supervises, directs, controls electoral rolls.UPPSC
    • EC does not recommend President's Rule where free and fair polls are not possible.
    • Making provisions (law) for elections to legislatures is not an EC function.UPPSC
    • EC does not elect Speaker, Deputy Speaker or Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman; the Houses elect them.UPPSC
    • Panchayat and municipal elections: State Election Commission (Art 243K, 243ZA); election disputes: judiciary.
    • Election notification: President for Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha, Governor for state legislature, on EC's recommendation; not issued by EC.UPPSC
    • EC fixes schedule of general and bye-elections, allots symbols, settles splits/mergers of recognised parties.
    • Art 103: President decides disqualification of an MP after taking EC's opinion and acts on it; decision final.UPPSC ×2
    • Art 192: same advisory role of EC for state legislators.
    • Model Code of Conduct: framed by EC, not enacted by Parliament; applies once election schedule is announced.UPPSC
    • Security deposit lost if candidate gets not more than one-sixth of valid votes.
    • Representation of the People Act (RPA) 1951, Section 8(3): jail of 2+ years → disqualified, plus 6 years after release.
    • Direct election on adult suffrage: Lok Sabha, Assemblies.
    • Proportional representation by single transferable vote: President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha, Legislative Council.

    Right to vote

    • Right to vote and to be elected = legal (statutory) right under RPA 1951, not fundamental or constitutional.UPPSC ×3
    • Kuldip Nayar vs Union of India: Supreme Court held vote is only a statutory right.
    • Art 326: Lok Sabha and Assembly elections on adult suffrage (all adults vote).UPPSC
    • 61st Amendment Act 1988 cut voting age 21 → 18 by amending Art 326; in force 28 March 1989.UPPSC ×5

    Check One key calls it "61st Amendment, 1989"; the Act is of 1988 and came into force in 1989.

    • 18-year-olds first voted in Lok Sabha general election of November 1989.UPPSC
    • State legislature election principles: adult suffrage, one electoral roll per constituency, no exclusion by religion, race, sex; parties free to set own norms.UPPSC
    • Postal ballot from home: age raised 80 → 85 on 1 March 2024 (Rule 27A, Conduct of Elections Rules 1961).
    • 2024 Lok Sabha poll: home voting first for 85+ and persons with 40%+ disability.
    • One Nation One Election needs changes in Art 83, 85, 172, 174, 356.
    • High-Level Committee on Simultaneous Elections (2 September 2023): chairman Ram Nath Kovind; secretary Niten Chandra.
    • Members: Amit Shah, Ghulam Nabi Azad, N.K. Singh, Subhash C. Kashyap, Harish Salve, Sanjay Kothari; special invitee Arjun Ram Meghwal.
    • Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury was named but declined.
    • Exit poll = survey of voters after they vote; opinion poll = survey before election.
    • Lok Sabha election 2009: 714 million electors.UPPSC

    Election law and delimitation

    • RPA 1951 Section 33: a candidate may contest from at most two constituencies (since 1996 amendment).
    • Devi Lal contested three Lok Sabha seats in 1991.
    • RPA (Amendment) Act 1996 followed Dinesh Goswami Committee (electoral reforms; advised state funding of elections).
    • 1996 changes: insulting National Flag or Constitution → 6-year disqualification; higher security deposit; no countermanding on candidate's death.
    • Delimitation Commission: set up by Central Government under Parliament's law; redraws constituencies after census; "one vote, one value".
    • It decides which seats are reserved; its orders cannot be challenged in court or modified by Lok Sabha/Assembly.
    • Commissions: 1952, 1963, 1973, 2002 (four under Delimitation Acts); fifth on 6 March 2020 for J&K.
    • 2002 Commission chairman: Justice Kuldip Singh; 2020: Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai.
    • Lok Sabha reserved seats (2008 order): 84 SC, 47 ST out of 543.
    • Proportional representation gives all groups due share, so ensures representation of minorities.UPPSC ×3
    • Proportional representation not needed where a two-party system has developed.
    • Voting is a statutory right, not a legal duty; low turnout brings no re-election or penalty.

    Election reforms and firsts

    • Order: EVM (1982, Parur, Kerala) → voter photo identity card EPIC (1993) → VVPAT (4 September 2013, Noksen, Nagaland) → NOTA (Supreme Court order, 27 September 2013).UPPSC
    • M3 = third-generation EVM/VVPAT in use; holds 384 candidates; tamper detection, self-diagnostics.
    • EC first became a three-member body on 16 October 1989; those posts lasted till 1 January 1990.UPPSC
    • First CEC: Sukumar Sen (21 March 1950–19 December 1958); first and only woman CEC: V.S. Ramadevi (1990).UPPSC
    • National Voters' Day: 25 January (EC's foundation day), since 2011.UPPSC

    Chapter 37

    Political Parties

    Political parties: recognition, founding years, anti-defection law and the party system.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 52nd Amendment 1985 added Tenth Schedule: anti-defection law, bans floor crossing (changing party).PCS Pre ’92, ’96; PCS Mains ’08; UDA/LDA ’064 papers
    2. India has no fixed party system; too many parties, fed by caste and regionalism.PCS Pre ’00; PCS Mains ’04; Lower Sub (Spl) ’043 papers
    3. Communist Party of India (CPI) · 26 December 1925, Kanpur · first set up 17 October 1920 at TashkentPCS Mains ’11; RO/ARO Mains ’172 papers
    4. Condition 3: recognised state party in at least four states.PCS Pre ’001 paper
    5. Or 8% of total state votes, even with no seat.PCS Pre ’141 paper

    Party registration and recognition

    • Party system = part of the political system; it forms and runs government.
    • RPA 1951: EC registers parties; all parties are registered parties.
    • EC recognises national/state parties under Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order 1968.
    • National party, condition 1: 6% valid votes in four or more states + 4 Lok Sabha seats.
    • Condition 2: 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11) from at least three states.
    • Condition 3: recognised state party in at least four states.UPPSC
    • State party (any one): 3 seats or 3% of Assembly seats, whichever more; or 1 Lok Sabha seat per 25 allotted to state.
    • Or 6% votes + 1 Lok Sabha seat; or 6% votes + 2 Assembly seats.
    • Or 8% of total state votes, even with no seat.UPPSC

    Check Key says (c) 8%; the explanation notes UPPSC's own key gave (d) None of the above.

    • Six national parties at present: INC, BJP, BSP, CPI(M), Aam Aadmi Party, National People's Party.
    • Trinamool Congress got national status on 2 September 2016; no longer national.
    • 1999 general election: 6 national and 48 state parties.
    • Shiromani Akali Dal = regional party of Punjab.UPPSC
    • Telugu Desam = regional party of Andhra Pradesh, not national.UPPSC
    • Samajwadi Party: not national; formed 4 October 1992, Lucknow, under Mulayam Singh Yadav.

    Elections and party system

    • United Front government (1996–97) did not include BSP, Samata Party, Haryana Vikas Party.
    • BJP vote share: 7.4% (1984), 11.4% (1989), 22.4% (1991).
    • 2004 Lok Sabha: Congress 145, BJP 138, CPI(M) 43 seats.
    • 13th Lok Sabha: CPM 32, TDP 29, BSP 14, BJD 10 seats.UPPSC
    • 1989 election: Congress largest (197 seats) but Janata Dal coalition ruled under V.P. Singh; end of "Congress System".
    • BJP-led coalition's National Agenda: policy guidance, promises, guiding principles; a coalition must respect all partners.UPPSC
    • India has no fixed party system; too many parties, fed by caste and regionalism.UPPSC ×3
    • Growth of strong regional parties shows regional aspirations.UPPSC
    • First-past-the-post: winner needs only relative majority; governments hold majority of seats, not of votes.
    • 33% seats for women in legislatures needs a constitutional amendment; Art 330–334 cover no women.
    • Kerala: ruled in turn by Congress and CPI(M), both national parties.
    • Pressure group: tries to influence policy, puts up no candidates; example, a trade union.
    • Inner-party democracy = periodic elections within a party to choose its office bearers.UPPSC
    • Rajni Kothari called India's early system a "one-party dominant system"; wrote 'Politics in India', 'Caste in Indian Politics', 'Rethinking Democracy'.

    Anti-defection law

    • 52nd Amendment 1985 added Tenth Schedule: anti-defection law, bans floor crossing (changing party).UPPSC ×4
    • Passed by Parliament 15 February 1985; in force 1 March 1985; amended Art 101, 102, 190, 191.UPPSC
    • Political parties got constitutional recognition first in 1985, through Tenth Schedule.UPPSC
    • Law covers en-bloc defection, small defection in one spell, voting against party; not large defections in several spells.UPPSC
    • Merger valid when two-thirds of the legislature party agree.
    • Speaker or Chairman decides defection cases, not President; law fixes no time limit.
    • Nominated member is disqualified if he joins a party after six months.
    • Presiding officer may give up party on election and rejoin after leaving office: no disqualification.
    • "Political party" is named in Tenth Schedule.
    • Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passed an anti-defection law in 1979.

    Parties: other facts

    • First-past-the-post: most votes wins; explains mismatch of vote share and seats.
    • Recognised Opposition party needs one-tenth of Lok Sabha seats (at least 54).
    • Kamaraj Plan (1963, Congress president K. Kamaraj): to make Indian National Congress vibrant.UPPSC
    • Bhu-Poratam (struggle for land): Andhra Pradesh, by Bharatiya Khet Mazdoor Union and communist parties.
    • Business class is not a social base of communist parties.
    • Electoral Bond Scheme: notified 2 January 2018; buyer Indian citizen or body; valid 15 days; credited same day.
    • Bonds only for parties registered under Section 29A RPA 1951 with at least 1% votes; sold by SBI's 11 branches.

    Chapter 38

    Constitutional Amendments

    How the Constitution is amended, major amendments up to the 106th, and the basic structure doctrine.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala, 1973: Supreme Court gave the "basic structure" doctrine.PCS Pre ’05, ’16, ’20, ’224 papers
    2. 69th · 1991 · Delhi made National Capital TerritoryPCS Pre ’22; PCS Mains ’09; Lower Sub ’153 papers
    3. 91st · 2003 (in force 1 January 2004) · ministers incl. PM/CM at most 15% of Lok Sabha/Assembly: Art 75(1A), 164(1A)PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’04, ’173 papers
    4. Art 368, Part XX: Parliament's power and procedure to amend the Constitution.PCS Mains ’08; GIC ’102 papers
    5. Bill starts only in either House of Parliament; not in state legislatures, not by President.PCS Pre ’24; UDA/LDA ’132 papers

    Amendment procedure

    • Art 368, Part XX: Parliament's power and procedure to amend the Constitution.UPPSC ×2
    • Parliament may add, vary or repeal any provision, but cannot change the basic structure.UPPSC
    • Bill starts only in either House of Parliament; not in state legislatures, not by President.UPPSC ×2
    • No prior recommendation of President needed.
    • Each House passes it separately by special majority: majority of total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting.UPPSC
    • No joint sitting; if one House rejects, the bill is dropped.UPPSC
    • President must assent, no veto: "shall give his assent" added by 24th Amendment 1971.
    • Three ways: simple majority; special majority; special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures.
    • Simple majority (not counted under Art 368): new states, names/boundaries, Legislative Councils, salaries of President, Governors, judges.
    • Half the states must ratify changes to federal provisions, Supreme Court's powers, amendment process; not formation of new states.UPPSC
    Needs ratification by half the statesSubject
    Art 54, 55election of President and its manner
    Art 73, 162extent of Union and state executive power
    Art 241High Courts for Union Territories
    Art 279AGST Council (added after 101st Amendment 2016)
    Part V Chapter IV; Part VI Chapter VUnion Judiciary; High Courts in states
    Part XI Chapter IUnion–state legislative relations
    Seventh Scheduleany of the three Lists
    Representation of statesin Parliament
    Art 368the amending power itself
    • No ratification needed for President's qualification, tenure, office conditions or Governor's office conditions (Art 158).
    • State legislature may pass or reject the ratification resolution; it cannot amend it.
    • 3rd Amendment 1954: first amendment ratified by states (Concurrent List entry 33).
    • Amendment process borrowed from South Africa's Constitution.

    • EWS = citizens outside classes of Art 15(4), 15(5), 16(4).
    • 106th: starts after delimitation following first census after the Act; lasts 15 years; covers one-third of SC/ST seats too.
    • 98 amendments implemented by May 2013; 104th by January 2020.UPPSC

    Basic structure and cases

    • Golaknath vs State of Punjab (27 February 1967): Supreme Court first limited Parliament's amending power.UPPSC
    • Order: Golaknath 1967 → 24th Amendment (5 November 1971) → Kesavananda Bharati 1973 → 42nd Amendment 1976.UPPSC
    • Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala, 1973: Supreme Court gave the "basic structure" doctrine.UPPSC ×4
    • Basic structure = features so essential that Parliament cannot abrogate them under Art 368.
    • Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.UPPSC
    • 25th Amendment 1971: law giving effect to Art 39(b), (c) not void for abridging Art 14, 19, 31.UPPSC
    • 42nd Amendment put all Directive Principles above Art 14, 19, 31; Minerva Mills 1980 struck this, kept Art 39(b), (c) priority.

    Chapter 39

    Official Language

    Official language provisions and the Eighth Schedule.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. 350A · Mother-tongue teaching at primary stage for linguistic minority children; added by 7th Amendment, 1956PCS Pre ’02, ’03; Lower Sub ’023 papers
    2. Census 2001 mother tongues: Bengali 8.11% > Telugu 7.19% > Marathi 6.99% > Tamil 5.91% (after Hindi 41.03%).PCS Pre ’98, ’012 papers
    3. Art 343(2): English to continue for Union's official purposes for 15 years from commencement.PCS Pre ’231 paper
    4. First Official Language Commission (Article 344): 7 June 1955, chairman B.G. Kher; report 1956.PCS Pre ’981 paper
    5. Eighth Schedule now lists 22 languages; originally 14.GIC ’101 paper

    Official language

    • Part XVII (Art 343–351): official language; four heads: Union, regional languages, judiciary, texts of laws and special directives.
    • Art 343: Union's official language is Hindi in Devanagari script; numerals in international form of Indian numerals.
    • Art 343(2): English to continue for Union's official purposes for 15 years from commencement.UPPSC
    • Art 344: President forms Official Language Commission after 5 years, then 10 years, from commencement.
    • First Official Language Commission: 1955, chairman B.G. Kher.
    • Art 344(4): parliamentary committee of 30: 20 from Lok Sabha, 10 from Rajya Sabha.
    • Art 345: State Legislature may by law adopt state language(s) or Hindi; till then English continues.
    • Art 346: language between states, and between a state and the Union.
    • Art 347: language spoken by a section of a state's population.
    • Art 348(1)(a): Supreme Court and High Court proceedings in English.
    • Art 348(2): Governor, with President's prior consent, may allow Hindi or state language in High Court.
    • Art 350A: instruction in mother tongue at primary stage.
    • Art 350B: Special Officer for linguistic minorities; appointed by and reports to President.
    • Constituent Assembly adopted Hindi on 14 September 1949 → Hindi Diwas.
    • Eighth Schedule: 14 languages at first; 22 now.
    • Added: Sindhi (21st Amendment 1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali (71st, 1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (92nd, 2003).
    • The phrase "official language of India" is nowhere in the Constitution; only "of the Union".
    • Amending Art 343, 344, 346, 348(1) needs special majority under Art 368(2); no state ratification.

    Official language and Eighth Schedule

    • Part XVII, Articles 343–351: official language; four heads: Union, regional languages, judiciary and law texts, special directives.
    • Article 343(1): Union official language = Hindi in Devanagari script; numerals in international form.
    • Article 343(2): English to continue for all Union official purposes for 15 years.
    • Hindi adopted as official language on 14 September 1949; 14 September = Hindi Diwas.
    • Hindi = official language of Union, not national language; "official language of India" appears nowhere in Constitution.
    • Article 343(3): Parliament may by law (simple majority) continue English; used for Official Language Act, 1963.
    • Official Language Act, 1963, Section 3: English also used along with Hindi from 26 January 1965.
    • Changing Articles 343, 344, 346, 348 themselves needs Article 368 special majority; no State ratification.

    Chapter 40

    Panchayati Raj and Community Development

    Village and city self-government under the 73rd and 74th Amendments, and district planning.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. P.K. Thungan · 1988 · Constitutional statusPCS Pre ’21, ’22; PCS Mains ’17; RO/ARO Mains ’17; Lower Sub Mains ’155 papers
    2. 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave Panchayati Raj constitutional status.PCS Pre ’22; PCS Mains ’04; Lower Sub Mains ’153 papers
    3. 73rd Act came into force on 24 April 1993; third tier of government added.PCS Pre ’10, ’20; PCS Mains ’123 papers
    4. Its report (November 1957) recommended "democratic decentralisation" = Panchayati Raj.PCS Pre ’13; PCS Mains ’10; UDA/LDA ’063 papers
    5. It first recommended three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district).PCS Pre ’24; PCS Mains ’12, ’173 papers

    73rd Amendment basics

    • Article 40 (Directive Principle): State shall organise village panchayats as units of self-government.UPPSC
    • 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave Panchayati Raj constitutional status.UPPSC ×3
    • It added Part IX "The Panchayats" (Articles 243 to 243-O, 16 Articles) and the 11th Schedule.
    • 73rd Act came into force on 24 April 1993; third tier of government added.UPPSC ×3
    • National Panchayati Raj Day: 24 April; first celebrated 2010.UPPSC
    • Panchayati Raj Day 2025 main event: Lohna Uttar Gram Panchayat, Madhubani (Bihar).
    • 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992, PM P.V. Narasimha Rao) = watershed for local governance.UPPSC
    • First attempt: 64th Amendment Bill, in Lok Sabha July 1989.
    • 11th Schedule: 29 subjects for Panchayats; rural sports not among them.UPPSC ×2
    • Article 243G: State Legislature may give Panchayats powers for economic development and social justice plans.
    • Panchayati Raj = State List subject, entry 5 of Seventh Schedule.UPPSC ×2
    • State Government takes the decision to hold Panchayat elections (Article 243K).UPPSC
    • Madhya Pradesh: first State to implement the 73rd Amendment.
    • 73rd Act did not provide regular pay to members or a two-child bar.
    • Panchayati Raj = local self-governance, democratic decentralisation, three-tier with bio-relations (organic links).UPPSC
    • It is called "grass-root democracy".UPPSC
    • Adopted to decentralise democratic power.UPPSC
    • Main purpose: let people take part in development administration.UPPSC
    • Local government features: statutory status, local participation, own taxes; not central control.UPPSC
    • 73rd Amendment revived rural local bodies and cut political interference in them.UPPSC
    • Judicial power not decentralised; States give the framework practical shape.
    • Public order and judicial review are not local body functions.
    • State controls local bodies in law-making, finance and staff; not citizens' complaints.
    • Bihar Nyaya Panchayats once could jail; Bihar Panchayati Raj Act, 2006 allows no imprisonment.

    Structure, term and reservation

    Gram Sabha and PESA

    • Gram Sabha = persons on electoral rolls of a village within a Panchayat area.UPPSC
    • Gram Sabha powers are fixed by State Legislature law (Article 243A), not by the Centre.UPPSC
    • Gram Sabha: permanent, largest body; only it can cancel its own decisions.
    • PESA (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas Act) passed in 1996, on Bhuria Committee report.UPPSC
    • PESA in 10 Fifth Schedule States: Andhra, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal, Jharkhand, MP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Telangana.
    • PESA aims: self-governance, traditional rights, freedom from exploitation; no autonomous regions.
    • Under PESA, Gram Sabha owns minor forest produce and can stop land transfer.
    • Its consent needed for minor mineral leases only, not other minerals.
    • PESA Gram Sabha chaired by an ST member chosen by consensus, else oldest ST woman.
    • Chhattisgarh Gram Sabha: meets every three months; quorum 1/10, one-third of them women.
    • Chhattisgarh Gram Panchayat: 10 to 20 wards, one elected Panch each; none nominated.
    • MP: without Sarpanch and Up-Sarpanch, a Panch elected by members present presides over Gram Sabha.
    • Rajasthan Panchayati Raj Act, 1994, Section 89: "Gram Sevak" renamed "Gram Vikas Adhikari".

    History and committees

    • Charles Metcalfe (1830): village communities are "little republics".
    • Lord Ripon = father of local self-government in India; Viceroy from 1880.
    • First Municipal Corporation: Madras, 1688.
    • Gandhi suggested the name "Panchayati Raj" for rural local government.UPPSC
    • Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (January 1957, by National Development Council) reviewed Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953).
    • Its report (November 1957) recommended "democratic decentralisation" = Panchayati Raj.UPPSC ×3
    • It first recommended three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district).UPPSC ×3
    • Balwant Rai Mehta = "Architect of Panchayati Raj".UPPSC ×2
    • Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur, Rajasthan.UPPSC ×2
    • Rajasthan = first State with Panchayati Raj; Andhra Pradesh second.UPPSC ×3

    Elections and finance

    • State Election Commission (Article 243K) supervises, directs and controls all Panchayat elections and rolls.UPPSC ×3
    • Governor appoints the State Election Commissioner.UPPSC
    • SEC is a constitutional authority; Election Commission of India has no role in local elections.UPPSC
    • Article 243ZA: the same SEC conducts municipal elections.
    • Rajasthan SEC: July 1994, single member; MP SEC: 1 February 1994.
    • Governor sets up State Finance Commission every 5 years to review Panchayat finances (Article 243I).UPPSC
    • State Finance Commission advises on sharing taxes between State and local bodies.UPPSC
    • It also advises on taxes and fees Panchayats may levy; reports to Governor.
    • Union Finance Commission (Article 280) suggests ways to add to State funds for local bodies.UPPSC
    • Constitutional authorities: SEC, State Finance Commission, District Panchayat; State Electoral Officer is not.UPPSC ×2

    Municipalities

    • 74th Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Municipalities; not about Panchayats.UPPSC ×2
    • It added Part IX-A (Articles 243P–243ZG) for urban local bodies; in force 1 June 1993.UPPSC ×2
    • It added 12th Schedule (18 subjects), restructured municipalities, reserved women's seats; applies to all States.UPPSC
    • Article 243Q: three types: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).
    • Eight kinds of urban bodies: Municipal Corporation, Municipality, Notified Area Committee, Town Area Committee, Cantonment Board, Township, Port Authority, Special Purpose Agency.
    • Article 243P(d): Governor notifies a municipal area.UPPSC
    • Article 243T(3): 1/3 of directly elected municipal seats for women; minimum age 21 (Article 243V).UPPSC
    • Article 243T(1): SC/ST seats; Article 243W: powers of Municipalities; Article 243Y: finance review.
    • Article 243U: Municipality term 5 years, so Mayor's term 5 years.UPPSC

    • Census urban area: population 5,000+, 75% male workers non-farm, density 400 per sq km.UPPSC
    • Candidate for Municipal Council must be on its voters' list.
    • Rajasthan Municipal Act, 2009: State nominates up to 6 (board), 8 (council), 12 (corporation).

    • U.P. Municipality chairman: elected by all voters on the municipal roll, from among ward electors.UPPSC
    • Ghaziabad has a Nagar Nigam, not Nagarpalika Parishad; Kanpur Nagar Nigam; Kakori Nagar Panchayat; Lucknow has Cantonment Board.UPPSC
    • 73rd and 74th Amendments created State Election Commission, State Finance Commission, District Planning Committee; not Property Tax Board.UPPSC

    United Nations

    • UN Charter signed 26 June 1945 by 50 nations at San Francisco; Poland 51st member.
    • UN born 24 October 1945 = United Nations Day.
    • Security Council: 15 members; 5 permanent (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) with veto; 10 elected for 2 years.
    • Elected for 2021–22: India, Ireland, Kenya, Mexico, Norway; Canada lost.UPPSC
    • Demand to democratise UN is about the Security Council.
    • April 2024: USA vetoed Palestine's full membership; UK and Switzerland abstained.
    • USA = largest payer for UN peacekeeping (about 28%); peacekeepers use force in self-defence and defence of mandate.
    • UN Credentials Committee: 9 members, appointed by General Assembly each session.
    • UN good governance: 8 features: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus, equity and inclusiveness, effectiveness and efficiency, accountability.
    • UN official languages (6): English, French, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese, Russian; Hindi is not.UPPSC ×2
    • Working languages: English and French.
    • International Mother Language Day, 21 February: declared by UNESCO, November 1999.
    • Atal Bihari Vajpayee: first to speak in Hindi at UN, 4 October 1977 (as Foreign Minister).
    • June 2022 UN multilingualism resolution first mentioned Hindi, Urdu, Bengali.
    • South Sudan: newest, 193rd country, 9 July 2011; capital Juba.UPPSC
    • Switzerland joined UN only on 10 September 2002.
    • International Court of Justice: set up June 1945; seat The Hague, Netherlands.UPPSC
    • Indian ICJ judges: B.N. Rau, Nagendra Singh, R.S. Pathak, Dalveer Bhandari (2012–2027).
    • ILO: 1919, under Treaty of Versailles; headquarters Geneva.

    Awards, days and culture

    • Bharat Ratna started 1954; first: C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan, C.V. Raman.UPPSC
    • Bharat Ratna: maximum three a year; not a title under Article 18; PM recommends.
    • Bharat Ratna 2024 (five): Karpuri Thakur, L.K. Advani, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Charan Singh, M.S. Swaminathan.
    • Non-Indian Bharat Ratnas: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987), Nelson Mandela (1990).
    • Padma Awards: from 1954; paused 1978–79 and 1993–97.
    • Param Vir Chakra: started 26 January 1950; four Indra Vajra replicas; 21 winners.
    • Gandhi Peace Prize: 1995; jury = PM (chair), CJI, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, two others; 2021 to Gita Press.
    • Outstanding Parliamentarian Award: 1995; M.M. Joshi 2009, Arun Jaitley 2010, Karan Singh 2011, Sharad Yadav 2012.
    • Joyita Mondal (West Bengal): first transgender judge, Lok Adalat.UPPSC
    • All India Radio motto: "Bahujan Hitaya, Bahujan Sukhaya".UPPSC

    • First Festival of India abroad: Britain, 1982.UPPSC
    • Pravasi Bharatiya Divas: 9 January (Gandhi's 1915 return); began 2003; every two years since 2015.UPPSC
    • National Voters' Day 25 January; Constitution Day 26 November; Human Rights Day 10 December.UPPSC
